docs.title: About this book
docs.text:
Generated by Nikhil Kumar Rajput

A complete course in server-side web programming: PHP, string handling, HTML forms with GET and POST, MySQL and the CRUD operations, and jQuery with AJAX and JSON, written for a university course and fully worked with listings, outputs, solved problems and exercises with answers.

docs.title: Unit 4: Database: MySQL Connectivity
docs.text:
A form handler that forgets everything the moment it replies is not yet an application. This unit adds the memory: a relational database, MySQL, and the small set of PHP functions that send SQL to it and bring rows back. It teaches the SQL statements for creating a database and its tables and for the four operations on data (create, retrieve, update and delete), then connects PHP to MySQL, builds a complete CRUD application, and ends with the most important security lesson of the course, SQL injection and the prepared statement that prevents it.

It corresponds to Unit 4 of the course, Database: Connectivity with MySQL, which is allotted 15 lecture hours, the largest share of the course.

Learning outcomes

  • Create a database and tables with sensible column types, a primary key and AUTO_INCREMENT.
  • Write INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE statements, including WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT, GROUP BY and JOIN.
  • Connect PHP to MySQL with mysqli, in both the procedural and the object style, and report a failure properly instead of showing a blank page.
  • Loop over a result set and turn it into an HTML table.
  • Insert what a form submitted, and update or delete an existing row.
  • Explain SQL injection, demonstrate it, and stop it with a prepared statement.

docs.title: 4.1 Why a web application needs a database
docs.text:
The idea, first

Unit 3 built a registration form. Submit it and the data is gone the instant the reply is sent: nothing on the server remembers it. You could write the values to a text file, and for about a week that would work — until two people submit at the same moment, or you want the students from Delhi with more than 70 marks sorted by name, or somebody's name contains a comma.

A database solves all three at once. It stores rows in tables with declared types, answers questions about them in a language designed for questions, and handles simultaneous writers without you thinking about it. SQL is that language, and MySQL is the program that speaks it — the M in XAMPP, and the one the course names.

So there are two skills here, and they are worth keeping separate in your head. SQL is a language you write and test in phpMyAdmin, with no PHP anywhere near it. Connectivity is the small set of PHP functions that send a string of SQL to MySQL and hand back the rows. Almost every problem a student has in this unit is actually a broken SQL string, and the fastest way to find that out is to paste the query into phpMyAdmin and watch MySQL say why.

The sample database

The examples in this unit use a small college database with seven students and four courses; its definition is given in Section 4.3. The outputs shown were produced by running the statements and programs against that data, in the order in which they appear, so a statement that changes the data (such as the INSERT in Listing 4.3) is reflected in the listings after it, until the data is put back to the original seven students after Listings 4.9 and 4.10. Every PHP program of this unit starts from the original seven students.

Listing 4.1. Looking at the sample data

SELECT * FROM students;

Result:

| roll    | name        | course | marks | email          | city     |
+---------+-------------+--------+-------+----------------+----------+
| 2231045 | Zoya Khan   | BSCCS  | 82    | zoya@ex.ac.in  | Delhi    |
| 2231046 | Aman Verma  | BSCCS  | 67    | aman@ex.ac.in  | Noida    |
| 2231047 | Riya Singh  | BAECO  | 91    | riya@ex.ac.in  | Delhi    |
| 2231048 | Dev Kapoor  | BAECO  | 55    | dev@ex.ac.in   | Gurugram |

docs.title: 4.2 The relational model, in one page
docs.text: Word Means In our database Database a named collection of tables college Table rows all of the same shape students, courses Row / record / tuple one thing one student Column / field / attribute one property, with a declared type marks INT Primary key the column that identifies a row uniquely; never repeated, never null roll Foreign key a column holding another table's primary key students.course → courses.code NULL "no value recorded" — not zero, not the empty string a student with no email yet Index a lookup structure that makes a WHERE fast created automatically for the primary key

docs.title: Choosing a column type
docs.text: Type Holds Use for INT a whole number, about ±2 billion roll numbers, marks, counts BIGINT a much larger whole number phone numbers stored as numbers — though see below VARCHAR(n) text up to n characters, stored compactly names, emails, and phone numbers — a leading zero must survive, and you never do arithmetic on a phone number CHAR(n) exactly n characters, padded fixed codes: a state code, Y/N TEXT long text, up to 64 KB an address, a comment, an article DECIMAL(8,2) an exact number with 2 decimal places money — never FLOAT, which cannot represent 0.10 exactly FLOAT / DOUBLE approximate measurements, averages DATE YYYY-MM-DD date of birth DATETIME / TIMESTAMP date and time when a row was created BOOLEAN really TINYINT(1): 0 or 1 is_active ENUM('a','b') one of a fixed list gender, status Constraint Means PRIMARY KEY unique and not null; one per table AUTO_INCREMENT MySQL fills it in, one higher each time NOT NULL a value must be supplied UNIQUE no two rows may share it — an email column wants this DEFAULT x used when the INSERT omits the column FOREIGN KEY … REFERENCES the value must exist in the other table

docs.title: With phpMyAdmin
docs.text:
1. Start Apache and MySQL in XAMPP, then open http://localhost/phpmyadmin/.
  2. New in the left sidebar → name the database college → collation utf8mb4_general_ci → Create.
  3. Choose the database, then the SQL tab, and paste the CREATE TABLE below. Do it this way rather than through the form: the statement is what you will be examined on, and it is what you can save in a file and re-run.

schema.sql

CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS college;
USE college;

CREATE TABLE students (
    roll    INT          PRIMARY KEY,
    name    VARCHAR(50)  NOT NULL,
    course  VARCHAR(10),
    marks   INT          DEFAULT 0,
    email   VARCHAR(60)  UNIQUE,
    city    VARCHAR(30)
);

The definition used for the examples in this unit. Note the trailing semicolon on each statement — phpMyAdmin needs it when you paste several at once.

Listing 4.2. Create a table of your own

CREATE TABLE books (
    id       INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    title    VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
    author   VARCHAR(50),
    price    DECIMAL(8,2),
    in_stock INT DEFAULT 0
);

INSERT INTO books (title, author, price, in_stock) VALUES
('Learning PHP, MySQL & JavaScript', 'Robin Nixon',  1899.00, 4),
('PHP: The Complete Reference',      'Steven Holzner', 950.50, 2),
('JavaScript and jQuery',            'Jon Duckett',  1250.00, 0);

SELECT * FROM books;

Result:

Query OK, table books created
Query OK, 3 rows affected (last insert id 3)
+----+----------------------------------+----------------+-------+----------+
| id | title                            | author         | price | in_stock |
+----+----------------------------------+----------------+-------+----------+
| 1  | Learning PHP, MySQL & JavaScript | Robin Nixon    | 1899  | 4        |
| 2  | PHP: The Complete Reference      | Steven Holzner | 950.5 | 2        |
| 3  | JavaScript and jQuery            | Jon Duckett    | 1250  | 0        |
+----+----------------------------------+----------------+-------+----------+
3 rows in set

DESCRIBE books; shows what MySQL made of the definition. The new table sits beside the two that already existed.

AUTO_INCREMENT is what you want for most keys

students.roll is a natural key — it means something outside the database, so you supply it. books.id is a surrogate key: it means nothing, MySQL fills it in, and you never have to ask "what number comes next". After an insert, mysqli_insert_id() tells you the value it chose.

docs.title: 4.4 C — Create: INSERT
docs.text:
-- name the columns; this is the form to write
INSERT INTO students (roll, name, course, marks)
VALUES (2231052, 'Ishan Roy', 'BSCCS', 71);

-- several rows in one statement: faster, and one round trip
INSERT INTO students (roll, name, course, marks) VALUES
    (2231053, 'Nikita Rao', 'BCOM',  63),
    (2231054, 'Omar Sheikh','BAECO', 79);

-- omitting the column list means "every column, in the declared order"
INSERT INTO students VALUES (2231055, 'Priya Das', 'BAENG', 84, 'priya@ex.ac.in', 'Delhi');

Always name the columns. The last form breaks silently the day someone adds a column to the table.

Listing 4.3. Insert, then look

INSERT INTO students (roll, name, course, marks, email, city)
VALUES (2231052, 'Ishan Roy', 'BSCCS', 71, 'ishan@ex.ac.in', 'Delhi');

SELECT roll, name, course, marks FROM students ORDER BY roll DESC LIMIT 3;

Result:

Query OK, 1 row affected (last insert id 3)
+---------+-------------+--------+-------+
| roll    | name        | course | marks |
+---------+-------------+--------+-------+
| 2231052 | Ishan Roy   | BSCCS  | 71    |
| 2231051 | Meera Joshi | BCOM   | 88    |
| 2231050 | Kabir Nath  | BSCCS  | 38    |
+---------+-------------+--------+-------+
3 rows in set

Inserting a roll number that already exists is refused with Duplicate entry … for key 'PRIMARY', which is the primary key doing its job.

docs.title: Choosing rows: WHERE
docs.text:
Operator Example Matches = <> < > <= >= marks >= 60 the obvious AND OR NOT marks > 60 AND city = 'Delhi' combinations LIKE name LIKE 'A%' % is any run of characters, _ is exactly one IN course IN ('BSCCS','BCOM') any of a list BETWEEN marks BETWEEN 40 AND 59 inclusive at both ends IS NULL email IS NULL = NULL never matches anything — null is not equal to null

Listing 4.4. WHERE, every form

SELECT name, course, marks, city
FROM students
WHERE marks >= 70 AND city = 'Delhi'
ORDER BY marks DESC;

Result:

+-------------+--------+-------+-------+
| name        | course | marks | city  |
+-------------+--------+-------+-------+
| Riya Singh  | BAECO  | 91    | Delhi |
| Meera Joshi | BCOM   | 88    | Delhi |
| Zoya Khan   | BSCCS  | 82    | Delhi |
| Sara Ali    | BCOM   | 74    | Delhi |
| Ishan Roy   | BSCCS  | 71    | Delhi |
+-------------+--------+-------+-------+
5 rows in set

Changing one clause at a time shows what each does. The last query is the one to remember: comparing with = NULL silently returns nothing, which is why IS NULL exists.

Listing 4.5. LIKE, IN and BETWEEN

SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE name LIKE 'R%';

SELECT name, course FROM students WHERE course IN ('BSCCS', 'BCOM') ORDER BY name;

SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks BETWEEN 40 AND 74 ORDER BY marks;

Result:

+------------+-------+
| name       | marks |
+------------+-------+
| Riya Singh | 91    |
+------------+-------+
1 row in set
+-------------+--------+
| name        | course |
+-------------+--------+
| Aman Verma  | BSCCS  |
| Ishan Roy   | BSCCS  |
| Kabir Nath  | BSCCS  |
| Meera Joshi | BCOM   |
| Sara Ali    | BCOM   |
| Zoya Khan   | BSCCS  |
+-------------+--------+
6 rows in set
+------------+-------+
| name       | marks |

| Dev Kapoor | 55    |
| Aman Verma | 67    |
| Ishan Roy  | 71    |

LIKE '%a%' finds names containing an a, and LIKE '____' (four underscores) finds names of exactly four characters.

docs.title: Ordering, limiting and counting
docs.text:
Listing 4.6. ORDER BY, LIMIT and the top-n query

SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 3;

Result:

+-------------+-------+
| name        | marks |
+-------------+-------+
| Riya Singh  | 91    |
| Meera Joshi | 88    |
| Zoya Khan   | 82    |
+-------------+-------+
3 rows in set

LIMIT 3 after ORDER BY marks DESC is the standard "top three" query. LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20 is page three of a paginated list — you will use it at the end of this unit.

docs.title: Aggregates and GROUP BY
docs.text:
An aggregate function turns many rows into one number. GROUP BY says "do that once per group" instead of once for the whole table.

Function Gives Note COUNT(*) how many rows counts rows, nulls and all COUNT(email) how many rows have a non-null email the difference between the two is the number of nulls SUM(marks) the total ignores nulls AVG(marks) the mean ignores nulls, which is usually what you want MIN / MAX smallest / largest works on text too

Listing 4.7. GROUP BY, with and without HAVING

SELECT course,
       COUNT(*)          AS students,
       ROUND(AVG(marks)) AS average,
       MAX(marks)        AS best
FROM students
GROUP BY course
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY average DESC;

Result:

+--------+----------+---------+------+
| course | students | average | best |
+--------+----------+---------+------+
| BCOM   | 2        | 81      | 88   |
| BAECO  | 2        | 73      | 91   |
| BSCCS  | 4        | 65      | 82   |
+--------+----------+---------+------+
3 rows in set

WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after. That single sentence answers most exam questions on this topic.

docs.title: JOIN: reading two tables at once
docs.text:
students.course holds a course code. The readable title lives in courses. A join brings them together for one query, without ever storing the title twice.

Listing 4.8. INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN

SELECT s.name, s.marks, c.title, c.fee
FROM students s
INNER JOIN courses c ON s.course = c.code
WHERE s.marks >= 70
ORDER BY s.marks DESC;

SELECT c.title, COUNT(s.roll) AS enrolled
FROM courses c
INNER JOIN students s ON s.course = c.code
GROUP BY c.title
ORDER BY enrolled DESC;

Result:

+-------------+-------+----------------------------+-------+
| name        | marks | title                      | fee   |
+-------------+-------+----------------------------+-------+
| Riya Singh  | 91    | B.A. (H) Economics         | 14500 |
| Meera Joshi | 88    | B.Com. (H)                 | 15800 |
| Zoya Khan   | 82    | Computer Science (Honours) | 21000 |
| Sara Ali    | 74    | B.Com. (H)                 | 15800 |
| Ishan Roy   | 71    | Computer Science (Honours) | 21000 |
+-------------+-------+----------------------------+-------+
5 rows in set
+----------------------------+----------+
| title                      | enrolled |
+----------------------------+----------+
| Computer Science (Honours) | 4        |
| B.A. (H) Economics         | 2        |
| B.Com. (H)                 | 2        |
+----------------------------+----------+
3 rows in set

Changing INNER to LEFT in the second query makes B.A. (H) English appear with an enrolled count of 0, because no student takes it. That is the whole difference: INNER keeps only matches, LEFT keeps every row of the left-hand table.

docs.title: 4.6 U and D — UPDATE and DELETE
docs.text:
The WHERE clause is not optional

UPDATE students SET marks = 0; sets every student's marks to zero. DELETE FROM students; empties the table. There is no undo and no confirmation. The professional habit: write the statement as a SELECT first, look at the rows it returns, and only then change the first word.

Listing 4.9. Check with SELECT, then UPDATE

-- 1. look before you leap
SELECT roll, name, marks FROM students WHERE marks < 40;

-- 2. the same WHERE, now doing the work
UPDATE students SET marks = marks + 5 WHERE marks < 40;

-- 3. check
SELECT roll, name, marks FROM students WHERE roll = 2231050;

-- 4. several columns at once
UPDATE students SET city = 'New Delhi', email = 'zoya.khan@ex.ac.in' WHERE roll = 2231045;
SELECT * FROM students WHERE roll = 2231045;

Result:

+---------+------------+-------+
| roll    | name       | marks |
+---------+------------+-------+
| 2231050 | Kabir Nath | 38    |
+---------+------------+-------+
1 row in set
Query OK, 1 row affected
+---------+------------+-------+
| roll    | name       | marks |
+---------+------------+-------+
| 2231050 | Kabir Nath | 43    |
+---------+------------+-------+
1 row in set
Query OK, 1 row affected
+---------+-----------+--------+-------+--------------------+-----------+
| roll    | name      | course | marks | email              | city      |
+---------+-----------+--------+-------+--------------------+-----------+
| 2231045 | Zoya Khan | BSCCS  | 82    | zoya.khan@ex.ac.in | New Delhi |
+---------+-----------+--------+-------+--------------------+-----------+
1 row in set

The first statement shows exactly which rows the WHERE clause catches, the second changes those and only those, and the third proves it.

Listing 4.10. DELETE, carefully

SELECT * FROM students WHERE roll = 2231050;

DELETE FROM students WHERE roll = 2231050;

SELECT COUNT(*) AS remaining FROM students;

Result:

+---------+------------+--------+-------+----------------+-------+
| roll    | name       | course | marks | email          | city  |
+---------+------------+--------+-------+----------------+-------+
| 2231050 | Kabir Nath | BSCCS  | 38    | kabir@ex.ac.in | Noida |
+---------+------------+--------+-------+----------------+-------+
1 row in set
Query OK, 1 row affected
+-----------+
| remaining |
+-----------+
| 6         |
+-----------+
1 row in set

mysqli_affected_rows() — or the row count this console prints — is how a PHP program knows whether the delete actually matched anything. A DELETE that matches nothing is not an error.

docs.title: 4.7 Connectivity: PHP talking to MySQL
docs.text:
PHP has three ways to reach MySQL. The course means mysqli, and it has two styles that do the same thing.

Extension Looks like Verdict mysqli procedural mysqli_query($conn, $sql) What most textbooks and exam papers use. Start here mysqli object oriented $conn->query($sql) The same extension, shorter to type. Know both — you will meet both PDO $pdo->prepare($sql) Works with other databases too, and has the nicest prepared statements. Not in this course, but worth a look ~~mysql_*~~ ~~mysql_connect()~~ Removed from PHP in 2015. If a tutorial uses it, the tutorial is at least ten years old and its security advice is too

docs.title: The four lines that connect
docs.text:
Listing 4.11. Connect, procedurally

<?php
$host = "localhost";
$user = "root";
$pass = "";          // XAMPP's default: root with no password
$db   = "college";

$conn = mysqli_connect($host, $user, $pass, $db);

if (!$conn) {
    die("Connection failed: " . mysqli_connect_error());
}

echo "Connected to '$db'.\n";

// Always tell MySQL the character set, or Hindi names come back as ????
mysqli_set_charset($conn, "utf8mb4");

$result = mysqli_query($conn, "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM students");
$row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result);
echo "It holds {$row['n']} students.\n";

mysqli_close($conn);

Output:

Connected to 'college'.
It holds 7 students.

Giving a database name that does not exist makes the connection report the failure instead of the page silently doing nothing. That die() is the difference between a five-minute bug and a two-hour one.

Listing 4.12. The same thing, object style

<?php
$conn = new mysqli("localhost", "root", "", "college");

if ($conn->connect_error) {
    die("Connection failed: " . $conn->connect_error);
}

$result = $conn->query("SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 2");

echo "Top two:\n";
while ($row = $result->fetch_assoc()) {
    echo "  {$row['name']} — {$row['marks']}\n";
}

echo "Rows in that result: ", $result->num_rows, "\n";
$conn->close();

Output:

Top two:
  Riya Singh — 91
  Meera Joshi — 88
Rows in that result: 2

Identical behaviour, fewer characters. The rule for reading either: procedural functions take the connection as their first argument; the object style has it as the thing before the arrow.

Put the connection in its own file

Every page needs it, and the password should appear once. Save db.php with the four variables and the mysqli_connect, then require "db.php"; at the top of every other page. Leave off the closing ?>, or a stray newline will break header() — exactly the bug from Unit 3.

A curiosity worth knowing

A ?> inside a // comment still closes the PHP block. // no closing ?> tag here ends PHP mode at the ?> and sends " tag here" to the browser. The tokeniser looks for the closing tag before it looks for the end of the line. Block comments /* … */ are not affected, so write it that way if you must mention the tag at all.

Listing 4.13. db.php, and a page that requires it

index.php

<?php
require "db.php";      // $conn is now available

$sql = "SELECT name, course, marks FROM students WHERE marks >= 70 ORDER BY marks DESC";
$result = mysqli_query($conn, $sql);

if (!$result) {
    die("Query failed: " . mysqli_error($conn));
}

printf("%-14s %-8s %s\n", "NAME", "COURSE", "MARKS");
echo str_repeat("-", 32), "\n";

while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)) {
    printf("%-14s %-8s %3d\n", $row["name"], $row["course"], $row["marks"]);
}

echo "\n", mysqli_num_rows($result), " row(s).\n";

db.php

<?php
// db.php — the only file that knows the password.
// This file deliberately ends without a closing tag.

$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

if (!$conn) {
    die("Connection failed: " . mysqli_connect_error());
}

mysqli_set_charset($conn, "utf8mb4");

Output:

NAME           COURSE   MARKS
--------------------------------
Riya Singh     BAECO     91
Meera Joshi    BCOM      88
Zoya Khan      BSCCS     82
Sara Ali       BCOM      74

4 row(s).

There are two files, db.php and a page that requires it. This is how every page in your project should begin.

docs.title: The fetch functions
Handling errors like an adult
docs.text:
Listing 4.15. What a broken query actually does

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

// A table that does not exist
$result = mysqli_query($conn, "SELECT * FROM studnets");

if (!$result) {
    echo "The query failed, and MySQL said why:\n";
    echo "  error : ", mysqli_error($conn), "\n";
    echo "  number: ", mysqli_errno($conn), "\n";
} else {
    echo "unreachable\n";
}

echo "\nA syntax error reads differently:\n";
$result = mysqli_query($conn, "SELCT name FROM students");
if (!$result) echo "  ", mysqli_error($conn), "\n";

echo "\nAnd a query that is fine but matches nothing is NOT an error:\n";
$result = mysqli_query($conn, "SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 1000");
var_dump($result === false);
echo "  rows: ", mysqli_num_rows($result), "\n";

Output:

The query failed, and MySQL said why:
  error : Table 'college.studnets' doesn't exist
  number: 1146

A syntax error reads differently:
  SQL syntax error: statement starts with 'SELCT'

And a query that is fine but matches nothing is NOT an error:
bool(false)
  rows: 0

A failed mysqli_query returns false. Passing that to mysqli_fetch_assoc is a TypeError — which is where "my page is blank" comes from. Check the return value, every time.

Two different 'nothing's

$result === false means the query failed — a typo, a missing table, no permission. mysqli_num_rows($result) === 0 means the query worked and matched no rows. Beginners conflate them and then report "database error" to a user who simply searched for something that is not there.

docs.title: 4.8 From a result set to an HTML table
docs.text:
This is the payoff. The loop from Unit 1, the escaping from Unit 2, and the query from this unit, together.

Listing 4.16. The classic report page

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");
if (!$conn) die("Connection failed: " . mysqli_connect_error());

$sql = "SELECT s.roll, s.name, c.title, s.marks
        FROM students s
        INNER JOIN courses c ON s.course = c.code
        ORDER BY s.marks DESC";

$result = mysqli_query($conn, $sql);
if (!$result) die("Query failed: " . mysqli_error($conn));
?>

<h3>Merit list</h3>

<?php if (mysqli_num_rows($result) === 0): ?>

  <p>No students found.</p>

<?php else: ?>

  <table>
    <tr><th>Roll</th><th>Name</th><th>Course</th><th>Marks</th><th>Result</th></tr>
    <?php $total = 0; while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)): $total += $row["marks"]; ?>
      <tr>
        <td><?= (int) $row["roll"] ?></td>
        <td><?= htmlspecialchars($row["name"]) ?></td>
        <td><?= htmlspecialchars($row["title"]) ?></td>
        <td style="text-align:right"><?= (int) $row["marks"] ?></td>
        <td style="color:<?= $row["marks"] >= 40 ? "#1a7f4b" : "#c0392b" ?>">
          <?= $row["marks"] >= 40 ? "Pass" : "Fail" ?></td>
      </tr>
    <?php endwhile; ?>
    <tr>
      <th colspan="3">Average</th>
      <th style="text-align:right"><?= round($total / mysqli_num_rows($result), 1) ?></th>
      <th></th>
    </tr>
  </table>

<?php endif; ?>

<p><?= mysqli_num_rows($result) ?> students listed.</p>

Output sent to the browser:

<h3>Merit list</h3>

  <table>
    <tr><th>Roll</th><th>Name</th><th>Course</th><th>Marks</th><th>Result</th></tr>
          <tr>
        <td>2231047</td>
        <td>Riya Singh</td>
        <td>B.A. (H) Economics</td>
        <td style="text-align:right">91</td>
        <td style="color:#1a7f4b">
          Pass</td>
      </tr>
          <tr>
        <td>2231051</td>
        <td>Meera Joshi</td>
        <td>B.Com. (H)</td>
        <td style="text-align:right">88</td>
        <td style="color:#1a7f4b">

       <a href="index.php">cancel</a></p>
</form>

save.php

<?php
require "db.php";

if ($_SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] !== "POST") {
    header("Location: index.php");
    exit;
}

$editing = ($_POST["editing"] ?? "0") === "1";
$roll    = (int) ($_POST["roll"] ?? 0);
$name    = trim($_POST["name"] ?? "");
$course  = trim($_POST["course"] ?? "");
$marks   = (int) ($_POST["marks"] ?? 0);

// Validate before touching the database — Unit 3's habit, unchanged
$errors = [];
if ($roll < 1000000)                            $errors[] = "Roll number looks wrong";
if ($name === "")                               $errors[] = "Name is required";
if ($marks < 0 || $marks > 100)                 $errors[] = "Marks must be 0-100";

if ($errors) {
    echo "<h3 style='color:#c0392b'>Not saved</h3><ul>";
    foreach ($errors as $e) echo "<li>", htmlspecialchars($e), "</li>";
    echo "</ul><p><a href='form.php'>← back to the form</a></p>";
    exit;
}

if ($editing) {
    $sql  = "UPDATE students SET name = ?, course = ?, marks = ? WHERE roll = ?";
    $stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn, $sql);
    mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "ssii", $name, $course, $marks, $roll);
} else {
    $sql  = "INSERT INTO students (roll, name, course, marks) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)";
    $stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn, $sql);
    mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "issi", $roll, $name, $course, $marks);
}

if (!mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt)) {
    echo "<h3 style='color:#c0392b'>Database error</h3>";
    echo "<p>", htmlspecialchars(mysqli_error($conn)), "</p>";
    echo "<p><a href='form.php'>← back</a></p>";
    exit;
}

$what = $editing ? "updated" : "added";
header("Location: index.php?msg=" . urlencode("Record for roll $roll $what."));
exit;

<?php
require "db.php";

$roll = isset($_GET["roll"]) ? (int) $_GET["roll"] : 0;

// A real delete should be a POST. This page therefore asks first, and the
// confirmation button is what actually does the work.
if ($_SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] === "POST") {
    $roll = (int) ($_POST["roll"] ?? 0);
    $stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn, "DELETE FROM students WHERE roll = ?");
    mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "i", $roll);
    mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt);

    $n = mysqli_affected_rows($conn);
    $msg = $n ? "Deleted roll $roll." : "No record with roll $roll.";
    header("Location: index.php?msg=" . urlencode($msg));
    exit;
}

$stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn, "SELECT name FROM students WHERE roll = ?");
mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "i", $roll);
mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt);
$row = mysqli_fetch_assoc(mysqli_stmt_get_result($stmt));

if (!$row) {
    header("Location: index.php?msg=" . urlencode("No such record."));
    exit;
}
?>

docs.title: 4.10 SQL injection, and prepared statements
docs.text:
The problem, first

Building a query by pasting a variable into a string means the user's text becomes part of your program, not just your data. Type an apostrophe into a search box and the query breaks. Type the right sequence of characters and the query does something else entirely — returns every row, ignores the password check, or drops the table.

Listing 4.18. A login that anyone can walk through

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");
mysqli_query($conn, "CREATE TABLE users (id INT, username VARCHAR(20), password VARCHAR(20))");
mysqli_query($conn, "INSERT INTO users VALUES (1,'zoya','s3cret'), (2,'admin','h4rd-t0-guess')");

// What an attacker types into the form:
$username = "admin";
$password = "anything' OR '1'='1";

// The vulnerable way — string concatenation
$sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '$username' AND password = '$password'";

echo "The query that actually ran:\n  $sql\n\n";

$result = mysqli_query($conn, $sql);

if ($result && mysqli_num_rows($result) > 0) {
    $row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result);
    echo "LOGGED IN as {$row['username']} — with the wrong password.\n";
} else {
    echo "Access denied.\n";
}

Output:

The query that actually ran:
  SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = 'admin' AND password = 'anything' OR '1'='1'

LOGGED IN as zoya — with the wrong password.

The password is wrong, and the login succeeds. Read the assembled query in the output: the ' closes the string early, OR '1'='1' is always true, and -- comments out the rest. Nothing exotic happened; the input simply became code.

Listing 4.19. The same attack against a prepared statement

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");
mysqli_query($conn, "CREATE TABLE users (id INT, username VARCHAR(20), password VARCHAR(20))");
mysqli_query($conn, "INSERT INTO users VALUES (1,'zoya','s3cret'), (2,'admin','h4rd-t0-guess')");

$username = "admin";
$password = "anything' OR '1'='1";

// 1. the query, with ? where the values go — no variables in the string at all
$sql  = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ? AND password = ?";
$stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn, $sql);

// 2. the values, sent separately.  "ss" = two strings
mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "ss", $username, $password);

// 3. run it
mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt);
$result = mysqli_stmt_get_result($stmt);

if ($result && mysqli_num_rows($result) > 0) {
    echo "logged in\n";
} else {
    echo "Access denied — the apostrophe was treated as part of the password.\n";
}

// And the honest login still works:
$password = "h4rd-t0-guess";
mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "ss", $username, $password);
mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt);
echo mysqli_num_rows(mysqli_stmt_get_result($stmt)) ? "The real password works.\n" : "";

Output:

Access denied — the apostrophe was treated as part of the password.
The real password works.

Identical input, and the login fails as it should. The query and the data travelled separately, so the apostrophe was never anything but a character in a password.

Letter in bind_param Means i integer s string — use this for anything you are unsure about d double (a float) b blob, sent in chunks

The letters must be in the same order as the ? marks, and there must be exactly as many. "issi" means: first value an integer, then two strings, then an integer.

A placeholder stands for a value, never for a name

SELECT * FROM ? WHERE ? = ? is not valid. Table names, column names and the direction of an ORDER BY cannot be bound. When those must vary — a sortable table, for instance — check them against a whitelist, exactly as Unit 3 did with the sort parameter.

Listing 4.20. Whitelisting what cannot be bound

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

// pretend these came from the URL
$sort  = "marks";
$dir   = "desc";
$minimum = "60";

// column and direction: not bindable, so check them against a list
$allowedSort = ["roll", "name", "marks"];
if (!in_array($sort, $allowedSort, true)) $sort = "roll";
$dir = strtolower($dir) === "desc" ? "DESC" : "ASC";

// the value: bindable, so bind it
$sql  = "SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks >= ? ORDER BY $sort $dir";
$stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn, $sql);
mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "i", $minimum);
mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt);

echo "Query: $sql\n\n";
$result = mysqli_stmt_get_result($stmt);
while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)) {
    printf("  %-14s %3d\n", $row["name"], $row["marks"]);
}

Output:

Query: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks >= ? ORDER BY marks DESC

  Riya Singh      91
  Meera Joshi     88
  Zoya Khan       82
  Sara Ali        74
  Aman Verma      67

Two rules: values go in placeholders, names come from a list you wrote. Between them they cover every query you will need on this course.

What about mysqli_real_escape_string()?

It escapes quotes for you and it does work, which is why older textbooks teach it. But it must be applied to every single value, every time, and one forgotten call is a hole — while a prepared statement cannot be forgotten halfway. Use prepared statements; know what real_escape_string is, because an exam may ask.

docs.title: 4.11 Solved problems
docs.text:
Example 4.1: 'My INSERT does nothing and shows no error'

Problem. A student's registration page runs, the browser shows the success message, and phpMyAdmin shows no new row. Diagnose it systematically.

Step 1 — is the query even being checked?

The usual cause is mysqli_query($conn, $sql); with the return value thrown away, followed unconditionally by "Registered successfully". The message is printed whether or not anything happened. Always write if (!mysqli_query(...)) die(mysqli_error($conn));.

Step 2 — print the SQL and read it

echo $sql; and look. Nine times in ten the answer is visible: an empty value where a variable should be (the form field's name does not match), or VALUES (, , ), or quotes in the wrong place.

Step 3 — paste that SQL into phpMyAdmin

If MySQL rejects it there, the problem is the SQL and PHP is innocent. If MySQL accepts it there, the problem is in PHP — usually the wrong database, or a connection that failed silently.

Step 4 — the two silent killers

A NOT NULL column with no default, receiving nothing. And a duplicate primary key — MySQL says "Duplicate entry", but only if you are looking at mysqli_error().

Answer. Check the return of every query; echo the SQL; run it in phpMyAdmin

Listing 4.21. Debugging an insert, step by step

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

// A form where the field is called "sname" but the code reads "name"
$_POST = ["sname" => "Test Student", "roll" => "2231099"];

$name = $_POST["name"] ?? "";     // <- the bug: wrong key, so empty
$roll = (int) ($_POST["roll"] ?? 0);

$sql = "INSERT INTO students (roll, name, course, marks)
        VALUES ($roll, '$name', 'BSCCS', 50)";

echo "The SQL being sent:\n  $sql\n\n";   // step 2: look at it

if (!mysqli_query($conn, $sql)) {          // step 1: check the result
    echo "MySQL refused it:\n  ", mysqli_error($conn), "\n";
} else {
    echo "Inserted. Rows affected: ", mysqli_affected_rows($conn), "\n";
}

echo "\nNow with the right key:\n";
$name = $_POST["sname"];
$sql = "INSERT INTO students (roll, name, course, marks)
        VALUES (2231098, '$name', 'BSCCS', 50)";
echo mysqli_query($conn, $sql) ? "  inserted\n" : ("  " . mysqli_error($conn) . "\n");

Output:

The SQL being sent:
  INSERT INTO students (roll, name, course, marks)
        VALUES (2231099, '', 'BSCCS', 50)

Inserted. Rows affected: 1

Now with the right key:
  inserted

Example 4.2: A name with an apostrophe breaks the page

Problem. Inserting "O'Brien" produces You have an error in your SQL syntax near 'Brien'. Explain, and give two fixes.

Step 1 — see the query MySQL saw

INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES ('O'Brien'). The apostrophe in the name closed the string after O, so Brien' is left over and means nothing. MySQL is right to complain.

Step 2 — the escaping fix

mysqli_real_escape_string($conn, $name) turns it into O\'Brien, which MySQL reads as one string containing an apostrophe. It needs the connection, because the correct escaping depends on the character set.

Step 3 — the real fix

A prepared statement. The name never enters the SQL text at all, so there is nothing to escape and nothing to forget.

Step 4 — why this matters beyond Irish surnames

The same character that breaks the query for an honest user is the one an attacker uses deliberately. A page that cannot store "O'Brien" is a page that can be injected — they are the same bug seen from two sides.

Answer. Prepared statement; or mysqli_real_escape_string on every value, without exception

Listing 4.22. O'Brien, three ways

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");
$name = "O'Brien";

echo "1. Straight into the string:\n";
$sql = "INSERT INTO students (roll, name, marks) VALUES (2231090, '$name', 60)";
echo "   $sql\n";
echo mysqli_query($conn, $sql) ? "   ok\n" : "   " . mysqli_error($conn) . "\n";

echo "\n2. With real_escape_string:\n";
$safe = mysqli_real_escape_string($conn, $name);
$sql = "INSERT INTO students (roll, name, marks) VALUES (2231091, '$safe', 60)";
echo "   $sql\n";
echo mysqli_query($conn, $sql) ? "   ok\n" : "   " . mysqli_error($conn) . "\n";

echo "\n3. With a prepared statement:\n";
$stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn, "INSERT INTO students (roll, name, marks) VALUES (?, ?, ?)");
$roll = 2231092; $marks = 60;
mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "isi", $roll, $name, $marks);
echo mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt) ? "   ok — and no escaping anywhere in sight\n"
                                : "   " . mysqli_error($conn) . "\n";

$r = mysqli_query($conn, "SELECT roll, name FROM students WHERE roll > 2231089");
while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($r)) echo "   stored: {$row['roll']} {$row['name']}\n";

Output:

1. Straight into the string:
   INSERT INTO students (roll, name, marks) VALUES (2231090, 'O'Brien', 60)
   unterminated string literal in SQL

2. With real_escape_string:
   INSERT INTO students (roll, name, marks) VALUES (2231091, 'O\'Brien', 60)
   ok

3. With a prepared statement:
   ok — and no escaping anywhere in sight
   stored: 2231091 O'Brien
   stored: 2231092 O'Brien

Example 4.3: Paginating a long list

Problem. A table has 500 students. Show 5 per page, with working "previous" and "next" links.

Step 1 — the two numbers

LIMIT $perPage OFFSET $offset, where $offset = ($page - 1) * $perPage. Page 1 has offset 0, page 2 has offset 5. Getting that arithmetic wrong by one is the classic bug.

Step 2 — how many pages

A second query, SELECT COUNT(*), gives the total. ceil($total / $perPage) is the number of pages — ceil, because 11 rows at 5 per page needs 3 pages, not 2.2.

Step 3 — clamp the page number

$page comes from the URL, so it can be 0, −4 or "abc". Cast it to an integer and force it into range, or the offset goes negative and MySQL errors.

Step 4 — why not fetch everything and slice in PHP?

Because that transfers 500 rows to show 5, and at 50,000 rows it exhausts memory. Let the database do the work it is built for.

Answer. LIMIT n OFFSET (page-1)*n, plus a COUNT(*) for the number of pages

Listing 4.23. Pagination that works

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

$perPage = 3;

// 1. how many rows are there altogether?
$countRow = mysqli_fetch_assoc(mysqli_query($conn, "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM students"));
$total = (int) $countRow["n"];
$pages = max(1, (int) ceil($total / $perPage));

// 2. which page was asked for, and is it sane?
$page = (int) ($_GET["page"] ?? 1);
if ($page < 1)      $page = 1;
if ($page > $pages) $page = $pages;

// 3. the window of rows
$offset = ($page - 1) * $perPage;
$sql = "SELECT roll, name, marks FROM students ORDER BY roll LIMIT $perPage OFFSET $offset";
$result = mysqli_query($conn, $sql);
?>

<h3>Students — page <?= $page ?> of <?= $pages ?></h3>

<table>
  <tr><th>Roll</th><th>Name</th><th>Marks</th></tr>
<?php while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)): ?>
  <tr>
    <td><?= (int) $row["roll"] ?></td>
    <td><?= htmlspecialchars($row["name"]) ?></td>
    <td style="text-align:right"><?= (int) $row["marks"] ?></td>
  </tr>
<?php endwhile; ?>
</table>

<p>
  <?php if ($page > 1): ?>
    <a href="index.php?page=<?= $page - 1 ?>">← previous</a>
  <?php endif; ?>

  <?php for ($p = 1; $p <= $pages; $p++): ?>
    <?php if ($p === $page): ?>
      <b>[<?= $p ?>]</b>
    <?php else: ?>
      <a href="index.php?page=<?= $p ?>"><?= $p ?></a>
    <?php endif; ?>
  <?php endfor; ?>

  <?php if ($page < $pages): ?>
    <a href="index.php?page=<?= $page + 1 ?>">next →</a>
  <?php endif; ?>
</p>

<p style="color:#666;font-size:14px">Showing rows <?= $offset + 1 ?>–<?= min($offset + $perPage, $total) ?>
   of <?= $total ?>. The database returns three rows, not <?= $total ?>.</p>

Example 4.4: Searching, safely

Problem. Add a search box that finds students whose name contains what was typed. Make it injection-proof.

Step 1 — LIKE with wildcards

"Contains" is LIKE '%text%'. "Starts with" is LIKE 'text%', which is much faster on a large table because an index can be used — worth knowing even though it is not what was asked.

Step 2 — where the % signs go

Not in the SQL. Bind the whole pattern: $pattern = "%" . $q . "%"; then bind $pattern. Writing LIKE '%?%' in the SQL does not work — the ? inside quotes is a literal question mark, not a placeholder.

Step 3 — the empty search

An empty box should show everything, or nothing, but must not error. %% matches every row, which is a reasonable answer.

Step 4 — and escape it on the way out

The search term is echoed back into the page ("Results for …"), so it needs htmlspecialchars() — two different defences for two different destinations.

Answer. Bind "%$q%" as one value; never put ? inside quotes

Listing 4.24. A safe search box

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

$q = trim($_GET["q"] ?? "");
?>

<h3>Search students</h3>

<form action="index.php" method="get">
  <input type="text" name="q" size="26" value="<?= htmlspecialchars($q, ENT_QUOTES) ?>"
         placeholder="part of a name">
  <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

<?php
$pattern = "%" . $q . "%";          // the wildcards go in the VALUE
$sql  = "SELECT roll, name, course, marks FROM students
         WHERE name LIKE ? ORDER BY name";
$stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn, $sql);
mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "s", $pattern);
mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt);
$result = mysqli_stmt_get_result($stmt);
$n = mysqli_num_rows($result);
?>

<p><?= $n ?> result<?= $n === 1 ? "" : "s" ?>
   <?= $q !== "" ? "for “" . htmlspecialchars($q) . "”" : "(everyone)" ?></p>

<?php if ($n): ?>
<table>
  <tr><th>Roll</th><th>Name</th><th>Course</th><th>Marks</th></tr>
<?php while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)): ?>
  <tr>

    <td><?= htmlspecialchars($row["name"]) ?></td>
    <td><?= htmlspecialchars($row["course"]) ?></td>
    <td style="text-align:right"><?= (int) $row["marks"] ?></td>
