docs.title: 4.12 Common mistakes to avoid
docs.text:
• Do not build queries by pasting variables into strings. Use prepared statements — every time, not just for logins.
  • Do not ignore the return value of mysqli_query(). Check it and print mysqli_error($conn) while you are developing.
  • Do not confuse "the query failed" (false) with "the query matched nothing" (num_rows === 0).
  • Do not write UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE. Write it as a SELECT first.
  • Do not compare with = NULL. Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL.
  • Do not put a placeholder inside quotes: LIKE '%?%' is a literal question mark. Bind the whole pattern instead.
  • Do not try to bind a table or column name. Whitelist those.
  • Do not store money in a FLOAT. Use DECIMAL(10,2).
  • Do not store a phone number as an INT — a leading zero disappears and you will never add two phone numbers together.
  • Do not put a SELECT inside a loop when a JOIN would do it in one query. Ten students should not mean eleven queries.
  • Do not forget mysqli_set_charset($conn, "utf8mb4") if any name might not be in English.
  • Do not echo a database value without htmlspecialchars(). The database is not a source of trusted text — someone's form put it there.

docs.title: 4.13 Summary
docs.text:
The key points of the unit, each stated as something you should now be able to do.

  • You can say why a database rather than a file: declared types, a language for asking questions, and safe simultaneous writers.
  • You can name the parts — database, table, row, column, primary key, foreign key, null — and choose a column type on purpose, including the two that are asked about in vivas: DECIMAL for money and VARCHAR for phone numbers.
  • You can create a database and a table, with a primary key, NOT NULL, DEFAULT and AUTO_INCREMENT, and you know why you should paste the statement into phpMyAdmin rather than click through its form.
  • You can write all four CRUD statements, and the whole SELECT in the right clause order, with WHERE, LIKE, IN, BETWEEN, IS NULL, ORDER BY and LIMIT.
  • You can aggregate and group, you know that WHERE filters rows before grouping while HAVING filters groups after, and you can join two tables — including the LEFT JOIN that keeps the rows with no match.
  • You can connect from PHP in either style, check for failure, loop a result set with while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)), and turn it into an escaped HTML table.
  • You can write the four-file CRUD application — list, form, save, delete — with validation before the write and a redirect after it.
  • You can demonstrate SQL injection, explain in one sentence why it works (the data became part of the program), and close it with a prepared statement; and you know that table and column names cannot be bound and must be whitelisted instead.
  • You can debug the three failures that account for most lost lab time: an unchecked query, an apostrophe in the data, and a variable that was empty because the form field had a different name.

docs.title: 4.14 Exercises
docs.text: Try each exercise on paper before you open its answer.

docs.title: Write the query
docs.text:
Exercise 4.1. List the name and marks of every student who scored more than 70, highest first.

Answer

A query that does it:

SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > 70 ORDER BY marks DESC

On the students and courses data of this chapter it returns:

+-------------+-------+
| name        | marks |
+-------------+-------+
| Riya Singh  | 91    |
| Meera Joshi | 88    |
| Zoya Khan   | 82    |
| Sara Ali    | 74    |
+-------------+-------+
4 rows in set

Note > rather than >= — 'more than 70' excludes 70 itself. Read the wording of an exam question carefully; this is where marks are lost.

Exercise 4.2. List the name and city of every student from Delhi or Noida, sorted by name.

Answer

A query that does it:

SELECT name, city FROM students WHERE city IN ('Delhi','Noida') ORDER BY name

On the students and courses data of this chapter it returns:

+-------------+-------+
| name        | city  |
+-------------+-------+
| Aman Verma  | Noida |
| Kabir Nath  | Noida |
| Meera Joshi | Delhi |
| Riya Singh  | Delhi |
| Sara Ali    | Delhi |
| Zoya Khan   | Delhi |
+-------------+-------+
6 rows in set

IN reads better than city = 'Delhi' OR city = 'Noida' and scales to a long list, but both are correct.

Exercise 4.3. For each course, show the course code and the number of students in it, as a column called total. Sort by course code.

Answer

A query that does it:

SELECT course, COUNT(*) AS total FROM students GROUP BY course ORDER BY course

On the students and courses data of this chapter it returns:

+--------+-------+
| course | total |
+--------+-------+
| BAECO  | 2     |
| BCOM   | 2     |
| BSCCS  | 3     |
+--------+-------+
3 rows in set

Every column in the SELECT list must either be in the GROUP BY or be inside an aggregate function. Adding name here would be meaningless — which student's name would it show?

Exercise 4.4. Show the name of each student together with the title of their course, taking the title from the courses table. Sort by name.

Answer

A query that does it:

SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s INNER JOIN courses c ON s.course = c.code ORDER BY s.name

On the students and courses data of this chapter it returns:

+-------------+----------------------------+
| name        | title                      |
+-------------+----------------------------+
| Aman Verma  | Computer Science (Honours) |
| Dev Kapoor  | B.A. (H) Economics         |
| Kabir Nath  | Computer Science (Honours) |
| Meera Joshi | B.Com. (H)                 |
| Riya Singh  | B.A. (H) Economics         |
| Sara Ali    | B.Com. (H)                 |
| Zoya Khan   | Computer Science (Honours) |
+-------------+----------------------------+
7 rows in set

The ON clause names the two columns that hold the same value — the foreign key and the primary key it points at. Forget it and you get every student paired with every course.

Exercise 4.5. Show the three highest-scoring students: their name and marks, best first.

Answer

A query that does it:

SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 3

On the students and courses data of this chapter it returns:

+-------------+-------+
| name        | marks |
+-------------+-------+
| Riya Singh  | 91    |
| Meera Joshi | 88    |
| Zoya Khan   | 82    |
+-------------+-------+
3 rows in set

ORDER BY then LIMIT — the limit is applied last, after sorting, which is what makes this the 'top n' idiom.

Exercise 4.6. For each city, show the city and the average marks rounded to a whole number, as avg_marks — but only for cities with more than one student. Sort by city.

Answer

A query that does it:

SELECT city, ROUND(AVG(marks)) AS avg_marks FROM students GROUP BY city HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY city

On the students and courses data of this chapter it returns:

+-------+-----------+
| city  | avg_marks |
+-------+-----------+
| Delhi | 84        |
| Noida | 53        |
+-------+-----------+
2 rows in set

The condition is about the group, not about individual rows, so it must be HAVING. Putting COUNT(*) > 1 in a WHERE clause is an error — WHERE runs before any grouping has happened.

docs.title: Write it — query and print
docs.text:
Exercise 4.7. Connect to college, then print the name and marks of every student in course BSCCS, ordered by marks descending, one per line as Name: marks.

Expected:Zoya Khan: 82Aman Verma: 67Kabir Nath: 38

Starting point:

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

// your code here

Your script is tested with these cases:

Case Expected output BSCCS students Zoya Khan: 82 Aman Verma: 67 Kabir Nath: 38 Answer

A solution:

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

$sql = "SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE course = 'BSCCS' ORDER BY marks DESC";
$result = mysqli_query($conn, $sql);

if (!$result) die(mysqli_error($conn));

while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)) {
    echo $row["name"], ": ", $row["marks"], "\n";
}

Note the quoting: the SQL string is in double quotes so 'BSCCS' can be in single quotes inside it. Getting this the wrong way round is the commonest cause of a syntax error from MySQL.

The while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)) loop is the single most important line in this unit. Learn it as one piece.

Exercise 4.8. Print one line per course: the course code, then a colon and a space, then the number of students in it — ordered by code. Use SQL to do the counting, not PHP.

Expected:BAECO: 2BCOM: 2BSCCS: 3

Starting point:

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

// your code here

Your script is tested with these cases:

Case Expected output counts per course BAECO: 2 BCOM: 2 BSCCS: 3 Answer

A solution:

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

$sql = "SELECT course, COUNT(*) AS total
        FROM students
        GROUP BY course
        ORDER BY course";

$result = mysqli_query($conn, $sql);

while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)) {
    echo $row["course"], ": ", $row["total"], "\n";
}

An aggregate needs an alias — AS total — or the column would be called COUNT(*) and awkward to read in PHP.

Counting in SQL sends one row per course over the wire. Counting in PHP would fetch all seven students and count them in a loop: more code, more memory, and much slower when the table has fifty thousand rows.

Exercise 4.9. Print the name of the top scorer and their marks, in the form Riya Singh scored 91. There is exactly one row to fetch, so do not write a loop.

Starting point:

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

// your code here
Answer

A solution:

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

$sql = "SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 1";
$result = mysqli_query($conn, $sql);
$row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result);

if ($row) {
    echo $row["name"], " scored ", $row["marks"];
}

One fetch_assoc, no loop, and a check that the row exists — because LIMIT 1 on an empty table still returns a valid result with no rows in it.

SELECT MAX(marks) would give you the number but not the name. To get the row that holds the maximum, sort and take one.

docs.title: Quick check — connectivity and safety
docs.text:
Exercise 4.10. mysqli_query() returned false. What does that mean?

  • (a) The query failed — a typo, a missing table, or a permission problem. mysqli_error($conn) says which
  • (b) The query ran and matched no rows
  • (c) The connection was lost
  • (d) The table is empty
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Correct. A query that runs but matches nothing returns a valid result object whose num_rows is 0.
  • (b) That case gives a result object, not false. Confusing the two produces 'database error' messages for empty searches.
  • (c) Possible, but not what false specifically means.
  • (d) An empty table still gives a valid, empty result.

Exercise 4.11. Which of these is safe from SQL injection?

  • (a) $sql = "SELECT * FROM s WHERE id = ?"; …bind_param("i", $id);
  • (b) $sql = "SELECT * FROM s WHERE id = $id";
  • (c) $sql = "SELECT * FROM s WHERE id = '" . htmlspecialchars($id) . "'";
  • (d) $sql = "SELECT * FROM s WHERE id = '" . strip_tags($id) . "'";
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Correct. The query is sent to MySQL first, then the value separately; the value can never be parsed as SQL.
  • (b) Concatenation. Even with an integer this is a habit that fails the moment the value is a string.
  • (c) htmlspecialchars protects HTML, not SQL. It does not escape a backslash or an apostrophe for MySQL — it converts an apostrophe to ', which changes the data and still does not make it safe.
  • (d) strip_tags removes HTML tags. An apostrophe is not a tag.

Exercise 4.12. Which loop reads every row of a result set?

  • (a) while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)) { … }
  • (b) for ($i = 0; $i < mysqli_num_rows($result); $i++) { $row = $result[$i]; }
  • (c) foreach ($result as $row) { … }
  • (d) while (mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)) { echo $row; }
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Right. Each call returns the next row and finally null, which ends the loop.
  • (b) A result set is not an array and cannot be indexed.
  • (c) This one actually works in modern PHP because mysqli_result is iterable — but the while loop is what the textbooks and exam papers use, and it works everywhere.
  • (d) It fetches but never assigns, so $row is never set.

Exercise 4.13. What is wrong with UPDATE students SET marks = 90;?

  • (a) No WHERE clause — it sets every student's marks to 90
  • (b) Nothing
  • (c) marks needs quotes
  • (d) It should be SET marks == 90
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Correct, and there is no undo. Write it as a SELECT first and look at the rows before changing the first word.
  • (b) It is valid SQL, which is exactly the danger.
  • (c) Column names are not quoted with apostrophes; that would make it the literal string 'marks'.
  • (d) SQL uses a single = for assignment and for comparison.

Exercise 4.14. Where does the difference between WHERE and HAVING lie?

  • (a) WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after
  • (b) They are interchangeable
  • (c) HAVING is for text and WHERE for numbers
  • (d) HAVING is faster
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Exactly. That is why WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 is an error — at WHERE time no group exists yet.
  • (b) They coincide only when there is no GROUP BY at all.
  • (c) Neither cares about type.
  • (d) If anything the reverse: WHERE reduces the rows before the work of grouping begins.

Exercise 4.15. In mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "ssi", $a, $b, $c), what does "ssi" say?

  • (a) The first two values are strings and the third is an integer
  • (b) The statement has three tables
  • (c) Nothing — it is a label
  • (d) Sort ascending, string, integer
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Correct, and there must be exactly one letter per ? in the query, in the same order.
  • (b) It describes the bound values, nothing else.
  • (c) MySQL uses it to send each value with the right type.
  • (d) The letters are types: i, s, d and b.

docs.title: Put it in order — a prepared INSERT
docs.text:
Exercise 4.16. These lines insert a student safely. Put them in the only order that runs.

mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "isi", $roll, $name, $marks);
$sql = "INSERT INTO students (roll, name, marks) VALUES (?, ?, ?)";
$roll = 2231060; $name = "Ira Bose"; $marks = 77;
mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt);
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");
$stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn, $sql);
echo mysqli_affected_rows($conn), " row inserted";
<?php
Answer

The lines in working order:

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");
$sql = "INSERT INTO students (roll, name, marks) VALUES (?, ?, ?)";
$stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn, $sql);
mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "isi", $roll, $name, $marks);
$roll = 2231060; $name = "Ira Bose"; $marks = 77;
mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt);
echo mysqli_affected_rows($conn), " row inserted";

It prints:

1 row inserted

The surprising one is that bind_param comes before the values are assigned. It binds by reference: it remembers the variables, and reads them when execute runs. Both orders work here, but binding first is the form you will see in textbooks, and it is why the same statement can be executed repeatedly with new values.

docs.title: Fill the blanks — connect and fetch
docs.text:
Exercise 4.17. Complete the standard connect-query-loop. It should print each name and mark on its own line.

The blanks are marked ___1___, ___2___ and so on.

<?php
$conn = ___1___("localhost", "root", "", "college");

if (!$conn) {
    die("Connection failed: " . mysqli_connect_error());
}

$sql = "SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY roll LIMIT 2";
$result = ___2___($conn, $sql);

while ($row = ___3___($result)) {
    echo $row[___4___], " - ", $row["marks"], "\n";
}
Answer
  • Blank 1: mysqli_connect
  • Blank 2: mysqli_query
  • Blank 3: mysqli_fetch_assoc
  • Blank 4: "name" (also 'name')
<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

if (!$conn) {
    die("Connection failed: " . mysqli_connect_error());
}

$sql = "SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY roll LIMIT 2";
$result = mysqli_query($conn, $sql);

while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)) {
    echo $row["name"], " - ", $row["marks"], "\n";
}

It prints:

Zoya Khan - 82
Aman Verma - 67

Four functions and one loop. Once these are muscle memory, the rest of Unit 4 is SQL rather than PHP.

Exercise 4.18. Complete the prepared statement so the roll number is bound as an integer.

The blanks are marked ___1___, ___2___ and so on.

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");
$roll = 2231047;

$sql  = "SELECT name FROM students WHERE roll = ___1___";
$stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn, $sql);
mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "___2___", $roll);
mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt);

$result = ___3___($stmt);
$row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result);
echo $row["name"];
Answer
  • Blank 1: ?
  • Blank 2: i
  • Blank 3: mysqli_stmt_get_result
<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");
$roll = 2231047;

$sql  = "SELECT name FROM students WHERE roll = ?";
$stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn, $sql);
mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "i", $roll);
mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt);

$result = mysqli_stmt_get_result($stmt);
$row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result);
echo $row["name"];

It prints:

Riya Singh

Note that the ? has no quotes around it. Writing '?' makes it a literal question mark and the query then matches nothing.

docs.title: Write it — CRUD in PHP
docs.text:
Exercise 4.19. Insert a new student — roll 2231099, name Ira Bose, course BCOM, marks 77 — using a prepared statement, then print the number of rows affected and nothing else.

Expected output: 1

Starting point:

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

// your code here
Answer

A solution:

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

$roll = 2231099;
$name = "Ira Bose";
$course = "BCOM";
$marks = 77;

$sql = "INSERT INTO students (roll, name, course, marks) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)";
$stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn, $sql);
mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "issi", $roll, $name, $course, $marks);
mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt);

echo mysqli_affected_rows($conn);

"issi" — integer, string, string, integer — in the same order as the four question marks.

mysqli_affected_rows() takes the connection, not the statement or the result. That argument catches everyone once.

Exercise 4.20. Give every student in BAECO five extra marks, then print the number of rows changed, then on the next line the new marks of roll 2231047.

Expected:296

Starting point:

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

// your code here

Your script is tested with these cases:

Case Expected output grace marks 2 96 Answer

A solution:

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

mysqli_query($conn, "UPDATE students SET marks = marks + 5 WHERE course = 'BAECO'");
echo mysqli_affected_rows($conn), "\n";

$r = mysqli_query($conn, "SELECT marks FROM students WHERE roll = 2231047");
$row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($r);
echo $row["marks"];

SET marks = marks + 5 — the column may appear on both sides, and MySQL reads the old value. Fetching every row into PHP, adding 5 and writing each back would take seven queries instead of one.

This is the difference between using a database and using it as a filing cabinet: the arithmetic happens where the data already is.

Exercise 4.21. Delete every student who scored below 40, then print how many were removed, then the number of students remaining, on two lines.

Expected:16

Starting point:

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

// your code here

Your script is tested with these cases:

Case Expected output cull and count 1 6 Answer

A solution:

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

mysqli_query($conn, "DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 40");
echo mysqli_affected_rows($conn), "\n";

$r = mysqli_query($conn, "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM students");
$row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($r);
echo $row["n"];

COUNT(*) needs an alias to be read conveniently in PHP — $row["n"] rather than $row["COUNT(*)"].

Every program in this unit starts from a fresh copy of the seven-student data, which is why the counts are the same however many times it is run.

Exercise 4.22. Print the title of each course and the number of students taking it, one per line as Title: n, in order of title. Courses with nobody enrolled must appear with 0.

Expected:B.A. (H) Economics: 2B.A. (H) English: 0B.Com. (H): 2Computer Science (Honours): 3

Starting point:

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

// your code here

Your script is tested with these cases:

Case Expected output enrolment per course B.A. (H) Economics: 2 B.A. (H) English: 0 B.Com. (H): 2 Computer Science (Honours): 3 Answer

A solution:

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

$sql = "SELECT c.title, COUNT(s.roll) AS total
        FROM courses c
        LEFT JOIN students s ON s.course = c.code
        GROUP BY c.title
        ORDER BY c.title";

$result = mysqli_query($conn, $sql);

while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)) {
    echo $row["title"], ": ", $row["total"], "\n";
}

Two things make the zero appear. LEFT JOIN keeps every course even when no student matches — an INNER JOIN would drop English entirely. And COUNT(s.roll) rather than COUNT(*): the unmatched row still exists, so COUNT(*) would count it as 1.

This pair — LEFT JOIN plus COUNT of a column from the right-hand table — is the standard way to ask 'how many of these does each of those have, including none'.

docs.title: Predict the output — result sets
docs.text:
Exercise 4.23. What does this script print?

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");
$r = mysqli_query($conn, "SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 1000");
var_dump($r === false);
var_dump(mysqli_num_rows($r));
var_dump(mysqli_fetch_assoc($r));

Hint: A query that matches nothing is not a query that failed.

Answer

The script prints:

bool(false)
int(0)
NULL

The result object is real, it simply holds no rows, and the first fetch returns null. Treating this as an error is the bug that makes a search page report 'database error' when the search term is not there.

Exercise 4.24. What does this script print?

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");
$r = mysqli_query($conn, "SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY roll LIMIT 2");
$a = mysqli_fetch_assoc($r);
$b = mysqli_fetch_assoc($r);
$c = mysqli_fetch_assoc($r);
echo $a["name"], "|", $b["name"], "|";
var_dump($c);

Hint: Each fetch moves to the next row. What happens after the last one?

Answer

The script prints:

Zoya Khan|Aman Verma|NULL

The cursor advances with each call and returns null when it runs out — which is exactly what makes while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($r)) terminate.

Exercise 4.25. What does this script print?

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");
mysqli_query($conn, "UPDATE students SET marks = 100 WHERE course = 'BSCCS'");
echo mysqli_affected_rows($conn), "\n";
mysqli_query($conn, "UPDATE students SET marks = 100 WHERE course = 'BSCCS'");
echo mysqli_affected_rows($conn), "\n";

Hint: The second UPDATE matches the same rows. Does it change them?

Answer

The script prints:

3
0

MySQL reports rows changed, not rows matched. Running the same update twice affects three rows and then none, because the second time the values are already what you asked for. Do not use affected_rows to test whether a WHERE matched anything.

docs.title: Practice problems
docs.text:
Exercise 4.26. Write the CREATE TABLE for a library table: an auto-incrementing id, a title that cannot be null, an author, a price to two decimal places, and an issued flag defaulting to 0.

Answer 
CREATE TABLE library (
    id      INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    title   VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    author  VARCHAR(60),
    price   DECIMAL(8,2),
    issued  TINYINT(1) DEFAULT 0
);

DECIMAL(8,2) stores a price exactly, with up to six digits before the decimal point and two after; a FLOAT would introduce rounding error into money. AUTO_INCREMENT requires the column to be a key, which PRIMARY KEY provides.

Exercise 4.27. Write the SQL for: all students whose name starts with a vowel; the average marks per city; the student with the second-highest marks; every course with no students in it.

Answer 
-- names starting with a vowel
SELECT roll, name FROM students
WHERE name LIKE 'A%' OR name LIKE 'E%' OR name LIKE 'I%'
   OR name LIKE 'O%' OR name LIKE 'U%';

-- average marks per city
SELECT city, AVG(marks) AS average FROM students GROUP BY city;

-- second-highest marks
SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;

-- courses with no students
SELECT c.title
FROM courses c
LEFT JOIN students s ON s.course = c.code
WHERE s.roll IS NULL;

On the seven students of this chapter the results are: Aman Verma; Delhi 83.75, Noida 52.5, Gurugram 55; Meera Joshi (88); and B.A. (H) English.

The LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 form returns the second row, so if two students tie for the top mark it returns the other of the two. The LEFT JOIN … WHERE s.roll IS NULL form keeps every course and then selects those for which the join found no student.

Exercise 4.28. Explain the difference between COUNT(*), COUNT(email) and COUNT(DISTINCT city) on our students table, and give the three numbers.

Answer
  • COUNT(*) counts rows, whatever they contain: 7.
  • COUNT(email) counts the rows in which email is not NULL: 7, because every student has an email address. A student with no email would be left out.
  • COUNT(DISTINCT city) counts the different non-NULL values of city: 3 (Delhi, Noida and Gurugram).

Exercise 4.29. Write a PHP page that shows a dropdown of courses (from the courses table) and lists the students of whichever is chosen.

Answer 
<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

$selected = $_GET["course"] ?? "";
$courses  = mysqli_query($conn, "SELECT code, title FROM courses ORDER BY title");
?>
<form method="get" action="">
  <select name="course">
    <option value="">-- choose a course --</option>
<?php while ($c = mysqli_fetch_assoc($courses)): ?>
    <option value="<?= htmlspecialchars($c["code"]) ?>"<?= $c["code"] === $selected ? " selected" : "" ?>>
      <?= htmlspecialchars($c["title"]) ?></option>
<?php endwhile; ?>
  </select>
  <button type="submit">Show</button>
</form>

<?php
if ($selected !== "") {
    $stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn, "SELECT roll, name, marks FROM students WHERE course = ? ORDER BY name");
    mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "s", $selected);
    mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt);
    $result = mysqli_stmt_get_result($stmt);

    if (mysqli_num_rows($result) === 0) {
        echo "<p>No students in this course.</p>";
    } else {
        echo "<ul>\n";
        while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)) {
            echo "  <li>", htmlspecialchars($row["name"]), " (", (int) $row["marks"], ")</li>\n";
        }
        echo "</ul>\n";
    }
}

Choosing BSCCS lists Aman Verma (67), Kabir Nath (38) and Zoya Khan (82). The chosen course comes from the URL, so it is bound as a parameter and never pasted into the SQL, and the dropdown is generated from the table so it can never offer a course that does not exist.

Exercise 4.30. Take the CRUD application of Listing 4.17 and add a "search" box that filters the list, keeping the search term when you page through the results.

Answer

Three changes are needed on the list page. Read the term, use it in a prepared LIKE query, and put it into every pagination link.

$q       = trim($_GET["q"] ?? "");
$pattern = "%" . $q . "%";                   // the wildcards go in the value

$stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn,
    "SELECT roll, name, course, marks FROM students
     WHERE name LIKE ? ORDER BY roll LIMIT ? OFFSET ?");
mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "sii", $pattern, $perPage, $offset);

<form method="get" action="">
  <input type="text" name="q" value="<?= htmlspecialchars($q, ENT_QUOTES) ?>">
  <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

<a href="?<?= htmlspecialchars(http_build_query(["q" => $q, "page" => $p])) ?>"><?= $p ?></a>

http_build_query encodes the term correctly, so a search for O'Brien survives the click to page 2. The total used to count the pages must come from the same filtered query (SELECT COUNT(*) … WHERE name LIKE ?), or the page numbers will not match the results.

Exercise 4.31. Why does mysqli_affected_rows() return 0 after an UPDATE that set a column to the value it already had? When would that matter?

Answer

By default MySQL reports the number of rows that were actually changed, not the number that were matched by the WHERE clause. An UPDATE that writes the value a column already holds changes nothing, so the count is 0 even though the row was found.

It matters when a program treats 0 as "no such record". A user who opens an edit form and presses Save without changing anything would be told that the record was not found. The cure is to test for failure with mysqli_errno(), or to connect with the MYSQLI_CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS flag, which makes MySQL report matched rows instead.

Exercise 4.32. Rewrite the vulnerable login from Listing 4.18 using a prepared statement and password_hash() / password_verify(), and explain why storing plain passwords is worse than the injection hole.

Answer

When the account is created, store only the hash:

$hash = password_hash($password, PASSWORD_DEFAULT);
$stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn, "INSERT INTO users (username, password) VALUES (?, ?)");
mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "ss", $username, $hash);
mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt);

At login, fetch the row by username only, and let password_verify do the comparison:

$stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn, "SELECT password FROM users WHERE username = ?");
mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "s", $username);
mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt);
$row = mysqli_fetch_assoc(mysqli_stmt_get_result($stmt));

if ($row && password_verify($password, $row["password"])) {
    echo "Logged in.";
} else {
    echo "Access denied.";
}

The injection hole is a flaw in one query, and fixing that query closes it. Plain-text passwords are a flaw in the data itself: anyone who ever obtains a copy of the table, through a backup, a leaked file or a different injection, reads every user's password at once, and because people reuse passwords, the damage spreads to their accounts on other sites. A hash cannot be reversed, so the same leak gives the attacker far less.

Exercise 4.33. A page shows ten students and, for each, runs another query to fetch their course title, which makes eleven queries in total. Rewrite it with one query, and explain what the original is called.

Answer 
SELECT s.name, c.title
FROM students s
JOIN courses c ON c.code = s.course
ORDER BY s.name;

One query returns every student with the title of their course, and the page loops over that single result set. The original pattern, one query to get the list followed by one more query for each row, is called the N+1 query problem: with ten students it makes eleven round trips to the database, and with a thousand students it makes a thousand and one.

docs.title: Examination questions
docs.text: These are questions in the shapes this course uses, grouped by the marks they carry. A two-mark question wants a definition and one concrete example, a five-mark question wants structure, and a ten-mark question wants an answer with parts.

docs.title: Two-mark questions
docs.text:
Exercise 4.34. (2 marks) Write the syntax to connect PHP to MySQL and check the connection.

Answer 
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

if (!$conn) {
    die("Connection failed: " . mysqli_connect_error());
}

Object style: $conn = new mysqli("localhost","root","","college"); then test $conn->connect_error. Four arguments: host, user, password, database.

Exercise 4.35. (2 marks) What does mysqli_query() return?

Answer

For a SELECT, a result object. For INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, true. On failure, false.

The distinction that matters: a query that ran but matched no rows still returns a valid result whose mysqli_num_rows() is 0 — that is not a failure.

Exercise 4.36. (2 marks) Difference between mysqli_num_rows() and mysqli_affected_rows().

Answer
  • mysqli_num_rows($result) — how many rows a SELECT returned. Takes the result.
  • mysqli_affected_rows($conn) — how many rows an INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE changed. Takes the connection.

Note that an UPDATE which sets a column to the value it already held reports 0 affected rows: MySQL counts rows changed, not rows matched.

Exercise 4.37. (2 marks) What is a primary key? How does it differ from a foreign key?

Answer

A primary key is the column that identifies a row uniquely: never repeated, never null, one per table. A foreign key is a column holding the primary key of another table, which is what makes a join possible and what keeps the two tables consistent.

roll   INT PRIMARY KEY                       -- in students
course VARCHAR(10), FOREIGN KEY (course) REFERENCES courses(code)

Exercise 4.38. (2 marks) What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?

Answer

WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after. That is why an aggregate cannot appear in a WHERE clause — at that point no group exists yet.

SELECT course, COUNT(*) FROM students
WHERE  marks >= 40        -- rows first
GROUP BY course
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;      -- then groups

docs.title: Five-mark questions
docs.text:
Exercise 4.39. (5 marks) Explain the CRUD operations with SQL syntax and an example of each.

Answer Operation SQL Example Create INSERT INTO t (cols) VALUES (…) INSERT INTO students (roll,name) VALUES (2231045,'Zoya') Retrieve SELECT cols FROM t WHERE … SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks >= 40 Update UPDATE t SET col = v WHERE … UPDATE students SET marks = 85 WHERE roll = 2231045 Delete DELETE FROM t WHERE … DELETE FROM students WHERE roll = 2231045

State the warning: an UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause affects every row and cannot be undone. The professional habit is to write the statement as a SELECT first, look at the rows it matches, and only then change the first word.

Exercise 4.40. (5 marks) What is SQL injection? Explain with an example and give the remedy.

Answer

What it is. When a query is built by pasting user input into a string, the input becomes part of the program rather than staying data, and the user can change what the query does.

Example. A login built like this:

$sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '$user' AND password = '$pass'";

If the visitor types anything' OR '1'='1 as the password, the query that actually runs is:

SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = 'admin' AND password = 'anything' OR '1'='1'

'1'='1' is always true, so a row is returned and the login succeeds with the wrong password.

The remedy — a prepared statement. The query and the data travel separately, so the data can never be parsed as SQL:

$sql  = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ? AND password = ?";
$stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn, $sql);
mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "ss", $user, $pass);
mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt);
$result = mysqli_stmt_get_result($stmt);

Two more points: mysqli_real_escape_string() also works but must be applied to every value without exception, so it is easier to get wrong; and a placeholder can stand for a value only — a table or column name must be checked against a whitelist instead.

Unit 4 demonstrates the attack and the fix, live.

Exercise 4.41. (5 marks) Explain JOIN with an example. Differentiate INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN.

Answer

A join combines rows from two tables using a column they share — a foreign key and the primary key it points at.

SELECT s.name, c.title
FROM students s
INNER JOIN courses c ON s.course = c.code;
INNER JOIN LEFT JOIN Keeps only rows that match in both tables every row of the left table, matched or not Unmatched rows dropped kept, with NULL in the right-hand columns Use for "students with their course" "every course and how many students, including those with none"

A worked contrast: a course with no students appears in a LEFT JOIN with a null count and vanishes entirely from an INNER JOIN. Note also that COUNT(*) would count the unmatched row as 1, so the correct form is COUNT(s.roll).

docs.title: Ten-mark questions
docs.text:
Exercise 4.42. (10 marks) Write a PHP program to connect to MySQL, create a table, insert records and display them in an HTML table.

Answer

1. The SQL, run once in phpMyAdmin:

CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS college;
USE college;

CREATE TABLE students (
    roll   INT         PRIMARY KEY,
    name   VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    course VARCHAR(10),
    marks  INT DEFAULT 0
);

2. Connect — in its own file, so the password appears once:

<?php  // db.php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");
if (!$conn) die("Connection failed: " . mysqli_connect_error());

3. Insert, with a prepared statement:

<?php
require "db.php";

$sql  = "INSERT INTO students (roll, name, course, marks) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)";
$stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn, $sql);
mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "issi", $roll, $name, $course, $marks);

$roll = 2231045; $name = "Zoya Khan"; $course = "BSCCS"; $marks = 82;

if (mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt)) {
    echo "The record is added in the database!";
} else {
    echo "Error: " . mysqli_error($conn);
}

4. Retrieve and display:

<?php
$result = mysqli_query($conn, "SELECT roll, name, course, marks
                               FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC");
if (!$result) die("Query failed: " . mysqli_error($conn));
?>

<table border="1">
  <tr><th>Roll</th><th>Name</th><th>Course</th><th>Marks</th></tr>
  <?php while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)): ?>
    <tr>
      <td><?= (int) $row["roll"] ?></td>
      <td><?= htmlspecialchars($row["name"]) ?></td>
      <td><?= htmlspecialchars($row["course"]) ?></td>
      <td><?= (int) $row["marks"] ?></td>
    </tr>
  <?php endwhile; ?>
</table>

<p><?= mysqli_num_rows($result) ?> students.</p>

The marks are in the details: checking the return value of every query, using a prepared statement, escaping every value on the way out, and the while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)) loop — which works because each call returns the next row and finally null.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
AJAX. Asking the server for data in the background, with JavaScript, and updating part of the page without reloading it (Unit 5).

Anchor (regular expression). The symbols ^ and $, which tie a pattern to the start and the end of the string; without them a validation pattern matches somewhere in the input rather than all of it (Section 2.5).

Array. PHP's one compound structure: an ordered map from keys to values. With integer keys 0, 1, 2 … it behaves as a list; with chosen keys it is an associative array (Section 1.6).

Callback. A function passed to another function, to be called later; in jQuery, the function that runs when a request has finished or an event has occurred (Unit 5).

Casting. Converting a value to another type on purpose, as in (int)"12" (Section 1.5).

Client side and server side. Code that runs in the visitor's browser (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, jQuery) as against code that runs on the web server before the reply is sent (PHP). The browser never receives PHP (Section 1.1).

Cookie. A small piece of data that the server asks the browser to store and to send back with later requests (Section 3.10).

CRUD. The four operations on stored data: create, retrieve (read), update and delete. In SQL they are INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE (Unit 4).

Cross-site scripting (XSS). A flaw in which text supplied by one visitor is printed unescaped into a page and run as script in the browsers of other visitors. The defence is to escape output (Section 2.7).

Database. An organised collection of tables that a database server such as MySQL stores and answers questions about (Unit 4).

Debounce. Waiting until a burst of events, such as typing, has paused before acting on it, so that one request is sent instead of one per keystroke (Unit 5).

Delegation. Attaching an event handler to an element that always exists, such as a list, so that it also handles clicks on children that were added later (Section 5.5).

DOM. The Document Object Model: the tree of elements that the browser builds from a page, which JavaScript and jQuery read and change (Unit 5).

Escaping. Replacing the characters that have a special meaning in a context (for HTML, <, >, & and the quotation marks) by harmless equivalents. In PHP, htmlspecialchars() (Section 2.7).

Foreign key. A column whose values are primary-key values of another table, such as students.course pointing to courses.code (Section 4.2).

GET and POST. The two ways a form sends its values: appended to the address (GET), or in the body of the request (POST) (Unit 3).

Heredoc. A way of writing a long string with quotation marks in it, between <<<EOT and a closing marker (Section 2.2).

htdocs. The folder of a XAMPP installation from which the Apache server serves files (Section 1.2).

Interpolation. The substitution of the value of a variable into a double-quoted string (Section 2.2).

JOIN. An SQL operation that combines rows of two tables whose key columns match; INNER JOIN keeps only matches and LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table (Section 4.5).

JSON. JavaScript Object Notation: a text format for objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null, used to carry data between server and browser. PHP produces it with json_encode and reads it with json_decode (Section 5.6).

jQuery. A JavaScript library that selects elements, changes them, handles events and makes AJAX calls with short, uniform syntax (Unit 5).

Localhost. The name by which your own computer refers to itself; the address http://localhost/ reaches the web server running on it (Section 1.2).

mysqli. The PHP extension used throughout this book to talk to MySQL, in a procedural and an object-oriented style (Section 4.7).

NULL. The value of a variable that has none; in a database, "no value recorded", which is neither zero nor the empty string (Sections 1.5 and 4.2).

Post/redirect/get. The pattern of finishing a successful POST with a redirect, so that refreshing the resulting page does not submit the form again (Section 3.10).

Prepared statement. An SQL statement sent to the server with placeholders, and the values sent separately, so that the values can never be read as SQL (Section 4.10).

Primary key. The column, or columns, that identify a row uniquely; never repeated and never null (Section 4.2).

Query string. The part of an address after the ?, holding name=value pairs separated by & (Section 3.3).

Result set. The rows returned by a SELECT, which PHP reads one at a time with a fetch function (Section 4.7).

Sanitising. Transforming a value so that it is safe in the place where it is about to be used; compare with validating, which decides whether a value is acceptable at all (Section 3.8).

Selector. In jQuery, a string such as "#id", ".class" or "tr:even" that chooses the elements to work on (Section 5.3).

Session. Data about a visitor that the server keeps between requests, found again by an identifier that the browser sends in a cookie (Section 3.10).

SQL. Structured Query Language, the language in which a relational database is asked questions and given instructions (Unit 4).

SQL injection. An attack in which text typed by a visitor becomes part of an SQL statement and changes its meaning. A prepared statement prevents it (Section 4.10).

Superglobal. A built-in PHP array available in every scope, such as $_GET, $_POST, $_SERVER, $_SESSION and $_FILES (Section 3.5).

Type juggling. PHP's automatic conversion of a value to the type an operator needs, the source of many surprises in comparisons (Section 1.5).

Validation. Checking on the server that a submitted value is acceptable and rejecting it if it is not. Client-side checks are a convenience; only the server's check counts (Section 3.7).

XAMPP. A bundle of the Apache web server, MySQL (MariaDB), PHP and Perl for a personal computer (Section 1.2).

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text: A reader who has never written PHP should begin with Unit 1 and read straight through, running every listing. A reader who knows the language and has an examination close should work through the Summary of each unit, then the multiple-choice and predict-the-output exercises, then the examination questions, and keep the Reference unit beside them.

docs.title: Unit 3: Handling HTML Forms with PHP
docs.text:
Forms are how a visitor talks to a web application. This unit shows how a form is written, how its values travel to the server by GET and by POST, how PHP receives them in the superglobal arrays, and how a script must treat them: validate them, escape them, and, where the application needs to remember a visitor from one request to the next, keep them in a session or a cookie.

It corresponds to Unit 3 of the course, Handling HTML Forms with PHP, which is allotted 12 lecture hours, the second largest share of the course. Most of the working code in the later units is a form handler of the kind developed here.

Learning outcomes

  • Write an HTML form whose fields actually reach PHP — and explain why the name attribute is the only one that matters for that.
  • Describe exactly what travels over the network for a GET and for a POST, and choose between them for a given job with a reason.
  • Read every kind of input — text, radio, checkbox groups, multi-selects, textareas, hidden fields — out of $_GET and $_POST without warnings.
  • Name the superglobals and say what each holds.
  • Validate on the server, report every error at once, and redisplay the form with the user's answers still in it.
  • Explain why client-side validation is not validation, and demonstrate an XSS hole and its fix.
  • Use header() for the post/redirect/get pattern, and sessions to remember a user between requests.

docs.title: 3.1 A form is a parcel of named values
docs.text:
The idea, first

A form is a way for the browser to send you a small parcel of named values. That is all it is. The browser collects one value per named field, packs them into a request, and asks the server for a page — passing the parcel along. PHP unpacks it into an array. Everything else in this unit is detail about the packing.

There are exactly two ways to pack the parcel. GET writes the values into the web address after a question mark, where they are visible in the address bar, saved in history, and short. POST puts them in the body of the request, where they are not visible in the address bar and can be as large as you like. That is the whole of "GET versus POST"; the rest of what people say about it follows from those two sentences.

And one thing that is not detail at all: everything in that parcel is a lie until you check it. The browser is a program on someone else's computer. The maxlength you set, the required you added, the dropdown that only offered three choices — all of it can be edited or ignored before the request is sent. Client-side validation is a courtesy to honest users. Server-side validation is the only validation there is, which is why the course lists "validate server-side data" as an outcome of the course.

Figure 3.1. The whole mechanism. The name attribute becomes the array key; the typed value becomes the array value; every value arrives as a string.

docs.title: 3.2 Creating a form
3.3 Submitting with GET
docs.text:
GET appends the values to the address as a query string: a ?, then name=value pairs joined by &, with anything unusual percent-encoded.

Listing 3.2. A GET form — watch the address bar

index.php

<h3>Search the college directory</h3>

<form action="search.php" method="get">
  <p>
    <label for="q">Name contains</label>
    <input type="text" id="q" name="q" value="Zoya Khan">
  </p>
  <p>
    <label for="d">Department</label>
    <select id="d" name="dept">
      <option value="cs">Computer Science</option>
      <option value="eco" selected>Economics</option>
      <option value="eng">English</option>
    </select>
  </p>
  <p><button type="submit">Search</button></p>
</form>

search.php

<h3>Results</h3>

<?php if (empty($_GET["q"])): ?>
  <p>Nothing searched for yet.</p>
<?php else: ?>
  <p>Looking for <b><?= htmlspecialchars($_GET["q"]) ?></b>
     in <b><?= htmlspecialchars($_GET["dept"] ?? "all departments") ?></b>.</p>
<?php endif; ?>

<h4>The address this page was fetched with</h4>
<pre><?= htmlspecialchars($_SERVER["REQUEST_URI"]) ?></pre>

<h4>$_GET</h4>
<pre><?php print_r($_GET); ?></pre>

<p>Because everything is in the address, this page can be
   <b>bookmarked</b> and <b>shared</b> — and that is exactly what you want for a
   search results page.</p>

<p><a href="index.php">← search again</a></p>

Output sent to the browser:

<h3>Search the college directory</h3>

<form action="search.php" method="get">
  <p>
    <label for="q">Name contains</label>
    <input type="text" id="q" name="q" value="Zoya Khan">
  </p>
  <p>
    <label for="d">Department</label>
    <select id="d" name="dept">
      <option value="cs">Computer Science</option>
      <option value="eco" selected>Economics</option>
      <option value="eng">English</option>
    </select>
  </p>
  <p><button type="submit">Search</button></p>
</form>

Submitting the form requests search.php?q=Zoya+Khan&dept=eco, and the reply is:

The reply:

<h3>Results</h3>

  <p>Looking for <b>Zoya Khan</b>
     in <b>eco</b>.</p>

<h4>The address this page was fetched with</h4>
<pre>/search.php?q=Zoya%20Khan&dept=eco</pre>

<h4>$_GET</h4>
<pre>Array
(
    [q] => Zoya Khan
    [dept] => eco
)
</pre>

<p>Because everything is in the address, this page can be
   <b>bookmarked</b> and <b>shared</b> — and that is exactly what you want for a
   search results page.</p>

<p><a href="index.php">← search again</a></p>

Notice the encoding in the query string: a space becomes + and @ becomes %40. That encoding is why you must never build a URL by pasting values together by hand.

docs.title: A query string does not need a form
docs.text:
Any link can carry parameters. This is how "next page", "sort by marks" and "edit record 17" links work, and you will use it constantly in Unit 4.

Listing 3.3. Links as parameters

<?php
$students = [
    ["roll" => 2231045, "name" => "Zoya Khan",  "marks" => 82],
    ["roll" => 2231046, "name" => "Aman Verma", "marks" => 67],
    ["roll" => 2231047, "name" => "Riya Singh", "marks" => 91],
    ["roll" => 2231048, "name" => "Dev Kapoor", "marks" => 55],
];

$sort = $_GET["sort"] ?? "roll";
$dir  = $_GET["dir"]  ?? "asc";

// Never trust a parameter: check it against a list of what is allowed
$allowed = ["roll", "name", "marks"];
if (!in_array($sort, $allowed, true)) $sort = "roll";
$dir = $dir === "desc" ? "desc" : "asc";

usort($students, function ($a, $b) use ($sort, $dir) {
    $r = $a[$sort] <=> $b[$sort];
    return $dir === "desc" ? -$r : $r;
});

function link_for($col, $sort, $dir) {
    $next = ($col === $sort && $dir === "asc") ? "desc" : "asc";
    $arrow = $col === $sort ? ($dir === "asc" ? " ↑" : " ↓") : "";
    return "<a href=\"index.php?sort=$col&dir=$next\">" . ucfirst($col) . "$arrow</a>";
}
?>

<h3>Class list — click a heading to sort</h3>
<table>
  <tr>
    <th><?= link_for("roll",  $sort, $dir) ?></th>
    <th><?= link_for("name",  $sort, $dir) ?></th>
    <th><?= link_for("marks", $sort, $dir) ?></th>
  </tr>
<?php foreach ($students as $s): ?>
  <tr>
    <td><?= $s["roll"] ?></td>
    <td><?= htmlspecialchars($s["name"]) ?></td>
    <td><?= $s["marks"] ?></td>
  </tr>
<?php endforeach; ?>
</table>

<p style="color:#666">sorting by <b><?= htmlspecialchars($sort) ?></b>,
   <?= htmlspecialchars($dir) ?></p>

Output sent to the browser:

<h3>Class list — click a heading to sort</h3>
<table>
  <tr>
    <th><a href="index.php?sort=roll&dir=asc">Roll</a></th>
    <th><a href="index.php?sort=name&dir=asc">Name</a></th>
    <th><a href="index.php?sort=marks&dir=asc">Marks ↓</a></th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>2231047</td>
    <td>Riya Singh</td>
    <td>91</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>2231045</td>
    <td>Zoya Khan</td>
    <td>82</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>2231046</td>
    <td>Aman Verma</td>
    <td>67</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>2231048</td>
    <td>Dev Kapoor</td>
    <td>55</td>
  </tr>
</table>

<p style="color:#666">sorting by <b>marks</b>,
   desc</p>

Following the Name heading link requests index.php?sort=name&dir=asc:

The reply:

<h3>Class list — click a heading to sort</h3>
<table>
  <tr>
    <th><a href="index.php?sort=roll&dir=asc">Roll</a></th>
    <th><a href="index.php?sort=name&dir=desc">Name ↑</a></th>
    <th><a href="index.php?sort=marks&dir=asc">Marks</a></th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>2231046</td>
    <td>Aman Verma</td>
    <td>67</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>2231048</td>
    <td>Dev Kapoor</td>
    <td>55</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>2231047</td>
    <td>Riya Singh</td>
    <td>91</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>2231045</td>
    <td>Zoya Khan</td>
    <td>82</td>
  </tr>
</table>

<p style="color:#666">sorting by <b>name</b>,
   asc</p>

Each heading is an ordinary link of the form <a href="index.php?sort=name&dir=asc">, and PHP reads the query string out of $_GET exactly as if a form had sent it.

Whitelist every parameter you use in a decision

$sort comes from the address bar, so a visitor can put anything there. The three lines that check it against $allowed are the difference between a sort link and a hole. In Unit 4 the same value would go near an SQL query, where the consequences are much worse.

docs.title: 3.4 Submitting with POST
docs.text:
POST sends the values in the request body instead of the address. Nothing about how PHP reads them changes; only $_GET becomes $_POST.

Listing 3.4. The same form, both ways

index.php

<h3>Log in</h3>

<!-- change method="post" to method="get" and run again -->
<form action="check.php" method="post">
  <p><label for="u">Username</label>
     <input type="text" id="u" name="username" value="zoya"></p>
  <p><label for="p">Password</label>
     <input type="password" id="p" name="password" value="hunter2"></p>
  <p><button type="submit">Sign in</button></p>
</form>

<p style="color:#666;font-size:14px">With <code>get</code> the password will appear in the
   address bar, in the browser's history, and in the server's log file. That is the
   reason logins are always <code>post</code>.</p>

check.php

<h3>What arrived</h3>

<p>Request method: <b><?= $_SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] ?></b></p>
<p>Query string: <code><?= htmlspecialchars($_SERVER["QUERY_STRING"]) ?: "(empty)" ?></code></p>

<h4>$_GET</h4>
<pre><?php print_r($_GET); ?></pre>

<h4>$_POST</h4>
<pre><?php print_r($_POST); ?></pre>

<h4>$_REQUEST — both, merged</h4>
<pre><?php print_r($_REQUEST); ?></pre>

<p><a href="index.php">← back</a></p>

Output sent to the browser:

<h3>Log in</h3>

<!-- change method="post" to method="get" and run again -->
<form action="check.php" method="post">
  <p><label for="u">Username</label>
     <input type="text" id="u" name="username" value="zoya"></p>
  <p><label for="p">Password</label>
     <input type="password" id="p" name="password" value="hunter2"></p>
  <p><button type="submit">Sign in</button></p>
</form>

<p style="color:#666;font-size:14px">With <code>get</code> the password will appear in the
   address bar, in the browser's history, and in the server's log file. That is the
   reason logins are always <code>post</code>.</p>

With method="post", as written, the handler check.php sees the values in $_POST and an empty query string:

The reply:

<h3>What arrived</h3>

<p>Request method: <b>POST</b></p>
<p>Query string: <code>(empty)</code></p>

<h4>$_GET</h4>
<pre>Array
(
)
</pre>

<h4>$_POST</h4>
<pre>Array
(
    [username] => zoya
    [password] => hunter2
)
</pre>

<h4>$_REQUEST — both, merged</h4>
<pre>Array
(
    [username] => zoya
    [password] => hunter2
)
</pre>

<p><a href="index.php">← back</a></p>

Change the form to method="get" and the same two values travel in the address instead. The handler now sees:

The reply:

<h3>What arrived</h3>

<p>Request method: <b>GET</b></p>
<p>Query string: <code>username=zoya&password=hunter2</code></p>

<h4>$_GET</h4>
<pre>Array
(
    [username] => zoya
    [password] => hunter2
)
</pre>

<h4>$_POST</h4>
<pre>Array
(
)
</pre>

<h4>$_REQUEST — both, merged</h4>
<pre>Array
(
    [username] => zoya
    [password] => hunter2
)
</pre>

<p><a href="index.php">← back</a></p>

Changing method="post" to method="get" in the form changes the request line and changes which superglobal is filled. This one experiment is the whole of "GET versus POST".

docs.title: GET versus POST
docs.text:
GET POST Data travels in the URL, after ? the request body Visible in the address bar Yes No Saved in browser history / bookmarkable Yes No Appears in server logs and Referer headers Yes No Size limit ~2000 characters in practice (a browser and server limit, not a rule of HTTP) Effectively unlimited (post_max_size, 8 MB by default) Can send a file No Yes, with enctype="multipart/form-data" Cached by browsers and proxies Yes No Re-submitted on refresh Silently The browser asks first Read in PHP from $_GET $_POST Use it for Asking for something: search, filter, sort, page number, "show record 17" Changing something: register, log in, save, delete, upload Is it more secure? Neither is secure. POST merely keeps values out of the address bar and the logs; the body is just as readable to anyone watching the network. Only HTTPS makes a request private

The rule of thumb: Safe and idempotent → GET. Otherwise → POST.

A GET should be safe: repeating it changes nothing. If pressing refresh twice would place two orders, enrol a student twice, or delete two rows, the request had to be a POST. This is not a style preference — search engines and browsers pre-fetch GET links, and a "delete" link with a GET behind it has emptied more than one database.

docs.title: 3.5 The PHP global variables
docs.text:
A superglobal is an array PHP fills in for you before your script runs. They are visible everywhere — inside functions too, with no global declaration, which is what makes them "super".

Superglobal Holds Filled from $_GET query-string parameters the text after ? in the address $_POST submitted form fields the request body $_REQUEST GET, POST and cookies merged convenient, and best avoided — you lose track of where a value came from $_SERVER information about the request and the server Apache and PHP $_SESSION values remembered between requests for one visitor the server, after session_start() $_COOKIE cookies the browser sent back the Cookie header $_FILES uploaded files a multipart POST $_ENV environment variables the operating system $GLOBALS every global variable, by name PHP itself

Listing 3.5. What is in $_SERVER

<?php
$interesting = [
    "REQUEST_METHOD" => "GET or POST — the test at the top of every form handler",
    "PHP_SELF"       => "this script's path — used as a self-posting form's action",
    "SCRIPT_NAME"    => "the same thing, but safe from a certain injection trick",
    "QUERY_STRING"   => "everything after the ? in the address",
    "REQUEST_URI"    => "path and query together",
    "HTTP_HOST"      => "the host the browser asked for",
    "REMOTE_ADDR"    => "the visitor's IP address",
    "DOCUMENT_ROOT"  => "where htdocs lives on disk",
];

foreach ($interesting as $key => $why) {
    printf("%-16s %-28s %s\n", $key, $_SERVER[$key] ?? "(not set)", $why);
}

Output:

REQUEST_METHOD   GET                          GET or POST — the test at the top of every form handler
PHP_SELF         /server.php                  this script's path — used as a self-posting form's action
SCRIPT_NAME      /server.php                  the same thing, but safe from a certain injection trick
QUERY_STRING     page=2                       everything after the ? in the address
REQUEST_URI      /server.php?page=2           path and query together
HTTP_HOST        localhost                    the host the browser asked for
REMOTE_ADDR      127.0.0.1                    the visitor's IP address
DOCUMENT_ROOT    /var/www/html                where htdocs lives on disk

On a real server this array has forty or more entries. These are the ones you will use; the rest are worth a look with print_r($_SERVER) on your own machine.

docs.title: The self-processing form
docs.text:
Most real forms post back to the page they came from: one file holds both the form and the code that handles it. That is what makes it possible to redisplay the form with the errors marked and the answers still in place.

Listing 3.6. One file, both jobs

<?php
$message = "";

// Has this page been reached by a submission, or by someone just opening it?
if ($_SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] === "POST") {
    $a = (float) ($_POST["a"] ?? 0);
    $b = (float) ($_POST["b"] ?? 0);
    $message = "$a + $b = " . ($a + $b);
}
?>

<h3>Add two numbers</h3>

<?php if ($message): ?>
  <p style="background:#eef8f2;border-left:5px solid #1a7f4b;padding:8px">
    <b><?= htmlspecialchars($message) ?></b></p>
<?php endif; ?>

<form action="" method="post">
  <p><label for="a">First</label>
     <input type="text" id="a" name="a" value="<?= htmlspecialchars($_POST["a"] ?? "") ?>"></p>
  <p><label for="b">Second</label>
     <input type="text" id="b" name="b" value="<?= htmlspecialchars($_POST["b"] ?? "") ?>"></p>
  <p><button type="submit">Evaluate</button></p>
</form>

Output sent to the browser:

<h3>Add two numbers</h3>

<form action="" method="post">
  <p><label for="a">First</label>
     <input type="text" id="a" name="a" value=""></p>
  <p><label for="b">Second</label>
     <input type="text" id="b" name="b" value=""></p>
  <p><button type="submit">Evaluate</button></p>
</form>

Entering 12 and 30 and pressing Evaluate posts the form back to the same file:

The reply:

<h3>Add two numbers</h3>

  <p style="background:#eef8f2;border-left:5px solid #1a7f4b;padding:8px">
    <b>12 + 30 = 42</b></p>

<form action="" method="post">
  <p><label for="a">First</label>
     <input type="text" id="a" name="a" value="12"></p>
  <p><label for="b">Second</label>
     <input type="text" id="b" name="b" value="30"></p>
  <p><button type="submit">Evaluate</button></p>
</form>

The same file draws the form and handles it, and the if at the top decides which. Notice that the form's action is empty, which is the simplest and safest way to post to the same page.

action='', $_SERVER['PHP_SELF'], or nothing

All three post to the same page. action="" is the simplest and is completely safe. If you use PHP_SELF — as many textbooks do — you must escape it: action="<?= htmlspecialchars($_SERVER['PHP_SELF']) ?>", because on some server setups an attacker can append markup to the path and get it echoed into your page. action="" avoids the whole question.

docs.title: 3.6 Every kind of input, and how it arrives
docs.text:
Text fields are easy. The ones worth practising are the ones that can send nothing at all, or send several values at once.

Listing 3.7. The full form — one of everything

index.php

<h3>One of every input</h3>

<form action="show.php" method="post">
  <p><label for="a">Text</label>
     <input type="text" id="a" name="sname" value="Zoya Khan"></p>

  <p><label for="b">Number</label>
     <input type="number" id="b" name="marks" value="82" min="0" max="100"></p>

  <p><label for="c">Email</label>
     <input type="email" id="c" name="email" value="zoya@ex.ac.in"></p>

  <p><label for="d">Date</label>
     <input type="date" id="d" name="dob" value="2005-08-14"></p>

  <p><label>Gender</label>
     <label><input type="radio" name="gender" value="F" checked> Female</label>
     <label><input type="radio" name="gender" value="M"> Male</label>
     <label><input type="radio" name="gender" value="O"> Other</label></p>

  <p><label>Single checkbox</label>
     <label><input type="checkbox" name="hosteller" value="yes"> Hosteller</label></p>

  <p><label>Subjects (note the [] in the name)</label>
     <label><input type="checkbox" name="subjects[]" value="PHP" checked> PHP</label>
     <label><input type="checkbox" name="subjects[]" value="MySQL" checked> MySQL</label>
     <label><input type="checkbox" name="subjects[]" value="jQuery"> jQuery</label></p>

  <p><label for="e">Course</label>
     <select id="e" name="course">
       <option value="">-- choose --</option>
       <option value="CS Hon" selected>Computer Science</option>
       <option value="BA Eco">B.A. Economics</option>
     </select></p>

docs.title: 3.7 Validating on the server
docs.text:
Client-side validation stops honest mistakes early and is worth adding. Server-side validation is what actually protects you. Both, always — and never only the first.

Listing 3.8. Client-side checks are advisory

index.php

<h3>A well-guarded form</h3>

<form action="handle.php" method="post">
  <p><label for="r">Roll (7 digits)</label>
     <input type="text" id="r" name="rollno" required pattern="\d{7}" maxlength="7"
            value="2231045"></p>
  <p><label for="m">Marks (0-100)</label>
     <input type="number" id="m" name="marks" required min="0" max="100" value="82"></p>
  <p><button type="submit">Submit honestly</button></p>
</form>

<p style="color:#666;font-size:14px">Every attribute above is enforced by the browser
   and by nothing else. Anyone can send a request without using this page at all.</p>

handle.php

<?php
// What the browser promised
$roll  = $_POST["rollno"] ?? "";
$marks = $_POST["marks"]  ?? "";

// What the server must nevertheless check
$errors = [];
if (!preg_match('/^\d{7}$/', $roll))                 $errors[] = "Roll must be exactly 7 digits";
if (!is_numeric($marks) || $marks < 0 || $marks > 100) $errors[] = "Marks must be 0-100";
?>

<h3>Server-side result</h3>

<?php if ($errors): ?>
  <ul style="color:#c0392b">
    <?php foreach ($errors as $e): ?><li><?= htmlspecialchars($e) ?></li><?php endforeach; ?>
  </ul>
<?php else: ?>
  <p style="color:#1a7f4b">Both values passed the server's own checks.</p>
<?php endif; ?>

<p>Received: roll <code><?= htmlspecialchars($roll) ?></code>,
   marks <code><?= htmlspecialchars($marks) ?></code></p>

<p><a href="index.php">← back</a></p>

Output sent to the browser:

<h3>A well-guarded form</h3>

<form action="handle.php" method="post">
  <p><label for="r">Roll (7 digits)</label>
     <input type="text" id="r" name="rollno" required pattern="\d{7}" maxlength="7"
            value="2231045"></p>
  <p><label for="m">Marks (0-100)</label>
     <input type="number" id="m" name="marks" required min="0" max="100" value="82"></p>
  <p><button type="submit">Submit honestly</button></p>
</form>

<p style="color:#666;font-size:14px">Every attribute above is enforced by the browser
   and by nothing else. Anyone can send a request without using this page at all.</p>

A request that never touched the form, sent by a program with a short roll number and marks of 150, goes straight past the checks made in the browser, and the server catches both:

The reply:

<h3>Server-side result</h3>

  <ul style="color:#c0392b">
    <li>Roll must be exactly 7 digits</li><li>Marks must be 0-100</li>  </ul>

<p>Received: roll <code>123</code>,
   marks <code>150</code></p>

<p><a href="index.php">← back</a></p>

The form has required, maxlength="7" and a pattern, yet the handler receives whatever it is sent. A user can bypass these attributes with the browser's developer tools, or with a tool such as curl; the point is that the server must check for itself.

docs.title: The tools
docs.text:
Check How Present at all isset($_POST["x"]) Not blank trim($_POST["x"] ?? "") !== "" — not empty(), which rejects "0" Letters and spaces only preg_match('/^[A-Za-z ]+$/', $name) Exactly n digits preg_match('/^\d{7}$/', $roll) A number in a range is_numeric($m) && $m >= 0 && $m <= 100 An email address filter_var($e, FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL) An integer filter_var($n, FILTER_VALIDATE_INT) — returns the int, or false A URL filter_var($u, FILTER_VALIDATE_URL) One of a fixed set in_array($v, ["CS Hon", "BA Eco"], true) Two fields match $p1 === $p2 — with === A date checkdate($m, $d, $y), or compare with strtotime()

filter_var returns the value, not true

filter_var("0", FILTER_VALIDATE_INT) returns the integer 0, which is falsy — so if (filter_var(...)) rejects a legitimate zero. Test it with !== false.

docs.title: The sticky, self-validating form
docs.text:
This is the pattern to learn by heart. One file; validate on POST; if anything is wrong, fall through and redraw the form with the messages beside the fields and the user's answers still in place. Losing a user's typing because of one bad field is the fastest way to lose the user.

Listing 3.9. The complete registration form

<?php
$fields = ["sname" => "", "rollno" => "", "email" => "", "phone" => "",
           "course" => "", "gender" => "", "subjects" => []];
$errors = [];
$done   = false;

if ($_SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] === "POST") {

    // 1. collect and clean
    foreach ($fields as $k => $default) {
        if (is_array($default)) $fields[$k] = $_POST[$k] ?? [];
        else                    $fields[$k] = trim($_POST[$k] ?? "");
    }

    // 2. check, collecting every problem rather than stopping at the first
    if ($fields["sname"] === "")                                  $errors["sname"]  = "Name is required";
    elseif (!preg_match('/^[A-Za-z ]{3,50}$/', $fields["sname"])) $errors["sname"]  = "3-50 letters and spaces only";

    if (!preg_match('/^\d{7}$/', $fields["rollno"]))              $errors["rollno"] = "Roll number must be exactly 7 digits";

    if (!filter_var($fields["email"], FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL))     $errors["email"]  = "That is not a valid email address";

    if (!preg_match('/^[6-9]\d{9}$/', $fields["phone"]))          $errors["phone"]  = "10 digits, starting 6-9";

    $courses = ["CS Hon", "BA Eco", "BCom"];
    if (!in_array($fields["course"], $courses, true))             $errors["course"] = "Choose a course";

    if (!in_array($fields["gender"], ["F", "M", "O"], true))      $errors["gender"] = "Choose one";

    if (count($fields["subjects"]) < 2)                           $errors["subjects"] = "Pick at least two subjects";

    // 3. if it all passed, this is where the database insert of Unit 4 goes
    $done = empty($errors);
}

// a small helper so the markup below stays readable
function e($s) { return htmlspecialchars((string) $s, ENT_QUOTES); }
function err($errors, $k) {
    return isset($errors[$k])
        ? '<span style="color:#c0392b;font-size:13px"> ⚠ ' . e($errors[$k]) . '</span>' : '';
}
?>

<?php if ($done): ?>

  <h3 style="color:#1a7f4b">Registered</h3>
  <p>Thank you, <b><?= e($fields["sname"]) ?></b>. Roll <?= e($fields["rollno"]) ?>,
     <?= e($fields["course"]) ?>, subjects <?= e(implode(", ", $fields["subjects"])) ?>.</p>
  <p><a href="index.php">Register someone else</a></p>

<?php else: ?>

  <h3>Student registration</h3>

  <?php if ($errors): ?>
    <p style="background:#fdf0ee;border-left:5px solid #c0392b;padding:8px">
      <b><?= count($errors) ?> problem<?= count($errors) === 1 ? "" : "s" ?></b>
      — nothing has been saved.</p>
  <?php endif; ?>

  <form action="" method="post">
    <p><label for="a">Name</label>
       <input type="text" id="a" name="sname" value="<?= e($fields["sname"]) ?>">
       <?= err($errors, "sname") ?></p>

    <p><label for="b">Roll number</label>
       <input type="text" id="b" name="rollno" value="<?= e($fields["rollno"]) ?>">
       <?= err($errors, "rollno") ?></p>

    <p><label for="c">Email</label>
       <input type="text" id="c" name="email" value="<?= e($fields["email"]) ?>">
       <?= err($errors, "email") ?></p>

    <p><label for="d">Phone</label>
       <input type="text" id="d" name="phone" value="<?= e($fields["phone"]) ?>">
       <?= err($errors, "phone") ?></p>

    <p><label for="f">Course</label>
       <select id="f" name="course">
         <option value="">-- choose --</option>
         <?php foreach (["CS Hon", "BA Eco", "BCom"] as $c): ?>
           <option value="<?= e($c) ?>" <?= $fields["course"] === $c ? "selected" : "" ?>>
             <?= e($c) ?></option>
         <?php endforeach; ?>
       </select>
       <?= err($errors, "course") ?></p>

    <p><label>Gender</label>
       <?php foreach (["F" => "Female", "M" => "Male", "O" => "Other"] as $v => $label): ?>
         <label><input type="radio" name="gender" value="<?= $v ?>"
                <?= $fields["gender"] === $v ? "checked" : "" ?>> <?= $label ?></label>
       <?php endforeach; ?>
       <?= err($errors, "gender") ?></p>

    <p><label>Subjects</label>
       <?php foreach (["PHP", "MySQL", "jQuery", "JSON"] as $s): ?>
         <label><input type="checkbox" name="subjects[]" value="<?= $s ?>"
                <?= in_array($s, $fields["subjects"], true) ? "checked" : "" ?>> <?= $s ?></label>
       <?php endforeach; ?>
       <?= err($errors, "subjects") ?></p>

    <p><button type="submit">Register</button></p>
  </form>

<?php endif; ?>

Output sent to the browser:

    <p><label for="a">Name</label>
       <input type="text" id="a" name="sname" value="">

    <p><label for="f">Course</label>

                    <option value="CS Hon" >
             CS Hon</option>

             BA Eco</option>

             BCom</option>
                </select>
       </p>

    <p><label>Gender</label>
                <label><input type="radio" name="gender" value="F"
                > Female</label>

                > Male</label>
                <label><input type="radio" name="gender" value="O"
                > Other</label>
              </p>

    <p><label>Subjects</label>
                <label><input type="checkbox" name="subjects[]" value="PHP"
                > PHP</label>
                <label><input type="checkbox" name="subjects[]" value="MySQL"

                > JSON</label>

Submitting a name of two letters, a five-digit roll number, a malformed email address, a short phone number, no course, no gender and only one subject redisplays the form with every error at once and with the typed values preserved:

The reply:

      <b>7 problems</b>
      — nothing has been saved.</p>

                > Female</label>

                checked> PHP</label>

Submitting correct values gives the confirmation:

The shape to memorise

1. Is this a POST? 2. Collect and trim every field into one array. 3. Check each one, adding to an $errors array — never returning early. 4. If $errors is empty, act; otherwise redraw the form with the values and the messages. Every form you write for the rest of this course is this shape.

docs.title: 3.8 Sanitising: what happens if you do not
docs.text:
Listing 3.10. A guest book with and without escaping

<?php
$comment = $_POST["comment"] ?? "";
?>

<h3>Guest book</h3>

<form action="" method="post">
  <p><input type="text" name="comment" size="46"
            value="<?= htmlspecialchars($comment, ENT_QUOTES) ?>"></p>
  <p><button type="submit">Post comment</button></p>
</form>

<p style="color:#666;font-size:14px">Try: <code><b>bold</b></code> or
   <code><img src=x onerror="alert(1)"></code></p>

<?php if ($comment !== ""): ?>
<table>
  <tr><th style="width:50%">Unsafe: echoed straight out</th>
      <th>Safe: htmlspecialchars()</th></tr>
  <tr>
    <td style="border:2px solid #c0392b"><?= $comment ?></td>
    <td style="border:2px solid #1a7f4b"><?= htmlspecialchars($comment) ?></td>
  </tr>
</table>
<?php endif; ?>

Output sent to the browser:

<h3>Guest book</h3>

<form action="" method="post">
  <p><input type="text" name="comment" size="46"
            value=""></p>
  <p><button type="submit">Post comment</button></p>
</form>

<p style="color:#666;font-size:14px">Try: <code><b>bold</b></code> or
   <code><img src=x onerror="alert(1)"></code></p>

Posting the comment <b>bold</b> shows the difference between the two columns:

The reply:

<h3>Guest book</h3>

<form action="" method="post">
  <p><input type="text" name="comment" size="46"
            value="<b>bold</b>"></p>
  <p><button type="submit">Post comment</button></p>
</form>

<p style="color:#666;font-size:14px">Try: <code><b>bold</b></code> or
   <code><img src=x onerror="alert(1)"></code></p>

<table>
  <tr><th style="width:50%">Unsafe: echoed straight out</th>
      <th>Safe: htmlspecialchars()</th></tr>
  <tr>
    <td style="border:2px solid #c0392b"><b>bold</b></td>
    <td style="border:2px solid #1a7f4b"><b>bold</b></td>
  </tr>
</table>

The unsafe column renders the comment as markup; the safe column shows it as text. Now imagine that the tag were <script> and that the page were seen by everyone in the college.

Where the value is going What protects it Into HTML text htmlspecialchars($v) Into an HTML attribute htmlspecialchars($v, ENT_QUOTES) — and always quote the attribute Into a URL urlencode($v) Into an SQL query a prepared statement — Unit 4 Into a shell command escapeshellarg() — and think again about whether you need to Into JavaScript json_encode($v) — Unit 5

Validation and sanitisation are different jobs

Validation asks "is this acceptable?" and rejects it if not — it happens on the way in. Sanitisation asks "is this safe here?" and transforms it — it happens on the way out, and what is safe depends entirely on where the value is going. A name may be perfectly valid and still need escaping before it goes into a page.

docs.title: 3.9 Uploading a file
docs.text:
A file is the one kind of input that does not arrive in $_POST. It needs a different encoding on the form, and it lands in its own superglobal.

Requirement Why enctype="multipart/form-data" on the form The default encoding cannot carry raw bytes. Forget this and $_FILES is simply empty — the single commonest upload bug method="post" A GET has no body to put the file in <input type="file" name="photo"> name becomes the key in $_FILES, as always

docs.title: What $_FILES holds
3.10 Remembering the user: sessions and cookies
docs.text:
HTTP has no memory. Each request arrives knowing nothing about the last, which is why a login has to be stored somewhere. A session stores it on the server and gives the browser only an ID; a cookie stores the value in the browser itself.

Session Cookie Stored on the server in the browser The user can read it No — only an opaque ID travels Yes, and edit it Size as large as you like about 4 KB Lifetime until the browser closes, or the server expires it whatever expiry you set — days, months Use for who is logged in, a shopping cart, a CSRF token "remember me", theme preference, language Started with session_start() at the very top of every page that uses it setcookie() before any output

Listing 3.12. A session that survives the round trip

index.php

<?php
session_start();

if (($_POST["action"] ?? "") === "login") {
    $_SESSION["user"]  = trim($_POST["username"] ?? "");
    $_SESSION["since"] = date("H:i:s");
}
if (($_GET["action"] ?? "") === "logout") {
    session_destroy();
    $_SESSION = [];
}
?>

<h3>Session demonstration</h3>

<?php if (!empty($_SESSION["user"])): ?>

  <p>Signed in as <b><?= htmlspecialchars($_SESSION["user"]) ?></b>
     since <?= htmlspecialchars($_SESSION["since"]) ?>.</p>
  <p><a href="profile.php">Visit another page →</a>  
     <a href="index.php?action=logout">Sign out</a></p>

<?php else: ?>

  <form action="" method="post">
