    <input type="hidden" name="action" value="login">
    <p><label for="u">Name</label>
       <input type="text" id="u" name="username" value="Zoya"></p>
    <p><button type="submit">Sign in</button></p>
  </form>

<?php endif; ?>

<h4>$_SESSION right now</h4>
<pre><?php print_r($_SESSION); ?></pre>

profile.php

<?php
session_start();

// The guard that goes at the top of every page that needs a login
if (empty($_SESSION["user"])) {
    echo "<p style='color:#c0392b'>Not signed in. <a href='index.php'>Go back</a></p>";
    exit;
}
?>

<h3>Profile page</h3>
<p>This is a different file, and it still knows you are
   <b><?= htmlspecialchars($_SESSION["user"]) ?></b> — nothing was posted to it.</p>
<p><a href="index.php">← back</a></p>

Output sent to the browser:

<h3>Session demonstration</h3>

  <form action="" method="post">
    <input type="hidden" name="action" value="login">
    <p><label for="u">Name</label>
       <input type="text" id="u" name="username" value="Zoya"></p>
    <p><button type="submit">Sign in</button></p>
  </form>

<h4>$_SESSION right now</h4>
<pre>Array
(
)
</pre>

Signing in as Zoya creates the session and then displays it:

The reply:

<h3>Session demonstration</h3>

  <p>Signed in as <b>Zoya</b>
     since 09:41:07.</p>
  <p><a href="profile.php">Visit another page →</a>  
     <a href="index.php?action=logout">Sign out</a></p>

<h4>$_SESSION right now</h4>
<pre>Array
(
    [user] => Zoya
    [since] => 09:41:07
)
</pre>

A later request for the same page, with no form data at all, still finds the name, because it is kept on the server against the session identifier:

The reply:

<h3>Session demonstration</h3>

  <p>Signed in as <b>Zoya</b>
     since 09:41:07.</p>
  <p><a href="profile.php">Visit another page →</a>  
     <a href="index.php?action=logout">Sign out</a></p>

<h4>$_SESSION right now</h4>
<pre>Array
(
    [user] => Zoya
    [since] => 09:41:07
)
</pre>

After signing in, a visit to another page and back again shows that the name is remembered without being sent each time, because it is stored on the server against the session identifier.

session_start() must come before any output

It sends a Set-Cookie header, and headers cannot follow content. One space before <?php, or a blank line after ?> in an included file, produces "Warning: session_start(): Cannot send session cookie — headers already sent". That message always means output escaped before you meant it to.

docs.title: Redirect after POST
docs.text:
A page that handles a POST and then prints the result has a problem: pressing refresh re-submits the form, and the record is saved twice. The fix is to finish a successful POST with a redirect, so the page the user ends up on was fetched with a GET.

Listing 3.13. Post / redirect / get

index.php

<?php
session_start();

if ($_SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] === "POST") {
    $note = trim($_POST["note"] ?? "");
    if ($note !== "") {
        $_SESSION["saved"] = $note;         // in Unit 4 this is an INSERT
        header("Location: done.php");       // then redirect
        exit;                               // ALWAYS exit after a redirect
    }
}
?>

<h3>Add a note</h3>
<form action="" method="post">
  <p><input type="text" name="note" size="40" value="Submit assignment by Friday"></p>
  <p><button type="submit">Save</button></p>
</form>

done.php

<?php session_start(); ?>

<h3 style="color:#1a7f4b">Saved</h3>
<p>Your note: <b><?= htmlspecialchars($_SESSION["saved"] ?? "(nothing)") ?></b></p>
<p>This page arrived by <b><?= $_SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] ?></b>, so refreshing it
   saves nothing a second time.</p>
<p><a href="index.php">← add another</a></p>

Output sent to the browser:

<h3>Add a note</h3>
<form action="" method="post">
  <p><input type="text" name="note" size="40" value="Submit assignment by Friday"></p>
  <p><button type="submit">Save</button></p>
</form>

Submitting the note makes the handler save it and redirect. The browser then makes a fresh GET request for done.php, whose reply is:

The reply:

-> redirected to done.php

<h3 style="color:#1a7f4b">Saved</h3>
<p>Your note: <b>Submit assignment by Friday</b></p>
<p>This page arrived by <b>GET</b>, so refreshing it
   saves nothing a second time.</p>
<p><a href="index.php">← add another</a></p>

The handler saves, then sends Location:, and the browser follows the redirect. The address the user ends up on is a plain GET, so refreshing it is harmless.

exit; after every header('Location: …')

header() only queues a header. Without exit, the rest of the script keeps running — inserting the row a second time, printing content, and possibly doing damage before the browser follows the redirect. It is one word and it is not optional.

docs.title: 3.11 Solved problems
docs.text:
Example 3.1: Why does my checkbox never arrive?

Problem. A student writes <input type="checkbox" name="agree"> and then if ($_POST["agree"] == "on") { … }. Ticked, it works. Unticked, the page shows a warning. Explain and fix.

Step 1 — what the browser sends

A ticked checkbox sends its value, defaulting to the string "on" when no value attribute is given. An unticked checkbox sends nothing whatsoever — there is no empty value, no "off"; the key simply does not exist in $_POST.

Step 2 — why the warning appears

$_POST["agree"] on a missing key is "Warning: Undefined array key", and the expression evaluates to null. The comparison then quietly fails, so the logic is right by accident and the log fills with warnings.

Step 3 — the fix

Ask whether it exists, not what it equals: if (isset($_POST["agree"])). Give the box an explicit value if you need to distinguish several boxes.

Step 4 — the group version

For several checkboxes with the same purpose, name them subjects[] and read $_POST["subjects"] ?? []. The ?? [] means the foreach that follows works even when nothing was ticked.

Answer. isset($_POST["agree"]) for one box; $_POST["subjects"] ?? [] for a group

Example 3.2: The form loses everything on one mistake

Problem. A registration form with eight fields rejects a bad email and redraws itself — empty. Users abandon it. What is wrong, and what does the fix look like?

Step 1 — why it happens

The form is redrawn from the original HTML, in which every value="" is blank. Nothing puts the submitted values back.

Step 2 — the fix for text fields

value="<?= htmlspecialchars($_POST['sname'] ?? '') ?>". The ?? covers the first visit, when there is no POST at all; the htmlspecialchars stops a quote in the value from ending the attribute and letting markup in.

Step 3 — the other controls

They each need their own word rather than a value: selected on the matching <option>, checked on the matching radio, and in_array($s, $chosen) to decide checked for each box in a group. The registration lab above shows all three.

Step 4 — why escaping is not optional here

Without it, a name containing a double quote — or a deliberately crafted " onmouseover="… — breaks straight out of the attribute. A sticky form that is not escaped is an XSS hole that the site's own users fill in.

Answer. Re-echo every submitted value, escaped, and add selected / checked for the rest

Example 3.3: 'Headers already sent'

Problem. A login page works, but header("Location: home.php") produces Warning: Cannot modify header information — headers already sent by (output started at /var/www/config.php:12). Diagnose it.

Step 1 — read the message properly

It names the file and line where output began: config.php line 12. That is the culprit, not the line with header() on it.

Step 2 — what counts as output

Anything at all: an echo, a stray character, a blank line before <?php, a newline after ?>, or a byte-order mark that an editor saved at the top of the file. Once a single byte has gone, the headers have been flushed and cannot change.

Step 3 — the fix

Delete the whitespace, and — the habit that prevents it for good — leave off the closing ?> in any file that contains only PHP. Then there is nothing after it to leak.

Step 4 — the same cause elsewhere

The identical warning from session_start() and setcookie() has the identical cause, because all three send headers.

Answer. Remove output before the header — usually a newline after ?> in an included file

Example 3.4: Two buttons on one form

Problem. A form needs "Save" and "Delete" buttons that submit to the same handler. How does the handler tell which was pressed?

Step 1 — a submit button is a field

Give each button the same name and a different value: <button name="action" value="save"> and value="delete". Only the button actually pressed is submitted, so $_POST["action"] holds one of the two.

Step 2 — branch on it, defensively

switch ($_POST["action"] ?? "") with a default that rejects anything unexpected. The value comes from the browser, so "delete_everything" is a request someone can make.

Step 3 — the trap with <button>

<button>Save</button> with no value sends an empty string in most browsers — the text between the tags is not the value. Always set value explicitly.

Answer. Same name, different value, then branch on $_POST["action"]

Listing 3.14. Two buttons, one handler

<?php
$msg = "";
if ($_SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] === "POST") {
    $id = (int) ($_POST["id"] ?? 0);
    switch ($_POST["action"] ?? "") {
        case "save":   $msg = "Saved record $id.";           break;
        case "delete": $msg = "Deleted record $id.";         break;
        default:       $msg = "Unknown action — ignored.";
    }
}
?>

<h3>Record 17</h3>

<?php if ($msg): ?>
  <p style="background:#eef8f2;border-left:5px solid #1a7f4b;padding:8px"><?= htmlspecialchars($msg) ?></p>
<?php endif; ?>

<form action="" method="post">
  <input type="hidden" name="id" value="17">
  <p>
    <button type="submit" name="action" value="save">Save</button>
    <button type="submit" name="action" value="delete">Delete</button>
  </p>
</form>

Output sent to the browser:

<h3>Record 17</h3>

<form action="" method="post">
  <input type="hidden" name="id" value="17">
  <p>
    <button type="submit" name="action" value="save">Save</button>
    <button type="submit" name="action" value="delete">Delete</button>
  </p>
</form>

Pressing Delete sends the button's own name and value together with the hidden field:

The reply:

<h3>Record 17</h3>

  <p style="background:#eef8f2;border-left:5px solid #1a7f4b;padding:8px">Deleted record 17.</p>

<form action="" method="post">
  <input type="hidden" name="id" value="17">
  <p>
    <button type="submit" name="action" value="save">Save</button>
    <button type="submit" name="action" value="delete">Delete</button>
  </p>
</form>

docs.title: 3.12 Common mistakes to avoid
docs.text:
• Do not omit the name attribute. Without it the field is not submitted at all — no name, no data.
  • Do not read a checkbox with ==. Use isset(), and ?? [] for a name[] group.
  • Do not forget the [] on a multiple select or a checkbox group. Without it PHP keeps only the last value.
  • Do not trust required, pattern, maxlength or a dropdown's list of options. All of them live in the browser, and the browser belongs to the user.
  • Do not echo user input without htmlspecialchars(), including inside value="" attributes on a sticky form.
  • Do not output anything before session_start(), setcookie() or header() — not even a newline after ?>.
  • Do not leave out exit; after a redirect.
  • Do not use a GET for anything that changes data. Browsers and crawlers follow links on their own.
  • Do not use empty() to mean "was it filled in". The strings "0" and "0.0" are legitimate answers, and empty("0") is true.
  • Do not put a password in a GET form. It ends up in the address bar, the history and the server's access log.
  • Do not forget enctype="multipart/form-data" on a form with a file input — without it $_FILES is empty and nothing says why.
  • Do not save an uploaded file under the name the browser supplied, and do not believe the type it claims.
  • Do not assume $_POST["marks"] is a number. It is the string "82"; cast it when you need arithmetic.

docs.title: 3.13 Summary
docs.text:
The key points of the unit, each stated as something you should now be able to do.

  • You can write a form whose data actually reaches PHP, and you know the name attribute is the whole mechanism: it becomes the key in $_GET or $_POST, and every value arrives as a string.
  • You can say exactly what travels for each method — the query string after ? for GET, the request body for POST — and choose between them on the grounds that matter: visible or not, bookmarkable or not, safe to repeat or not.
  • You can answer "is POST more secure?" correctly: no, it merely keeps values out of the address bar, the history and the logs, and only HTTPS makes a request private.
  • You can name the superglobals and use the four that matter, and you know $_SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] is the test that makes a self-processing form possible.
  • You can read every kind of control, including the two that catch everyone: an unticked checkbox sends nothing, and a group of them needs [] in the name and ?? [] in the handler.
  • You can write the standard form shape — check the method, collect and trim, validate into an $errors array, then act or redraw — and make the redrawn form sticky for text fields, selects, radios and checkbox groups alike.
  • You can explain why client-side validation is a courtesy rather than a defence, and demonstrate an XSS hole and close it with one function call.
  • You can keep a user signed in with a session, guard a page with three lines at the top, and say what is stored where.
  • You can use post/redirect/get so that refreshing a page does not save a second copy, and you know why exit; after header() is not optional.
  • You can accept a file upload: the enctype the form needs, the five keys in $_FILES and which of them a browser controls, the five checks in order, and the three rules — invent your own name, keep uploads out of an executable folder, and never trust the claimed MIME type.
  • And you can read the "headers already sent" warning as what it is: a message naming the file and line where a stray byte escaped.

docs.title: 3.14 Exercises
docs.text: Try each exercise on paper before you open its answer.

docs.title: Quick check — GET and POST
docs.text:
Exercise 3.1. A form has <input type="text" value="Zoya"> with no name attribute. After submitting, what is in $_POST?

  • (a) Nothing from that field at all
  • (b) $_POST[0] = "Zoya"
  • (c) $_POST["text"] = "Zoya"
  • (d) $_POST["Zoya"] = ""
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Right. The browser only sends fields that have a name — the name is the key. This is the number one cause of 'my value does not arrive'.
  • (b) There is no positional fallback; unnamed fields are simply not submitted.
  • (c) The type is not used as a key.
  • (d) The value never becomes the key.

Exercise 3.2. Which of these should be a POST?

  • (a) A link that deletes a student record
  • (b) A search box on the library catalogue
  • (c) A link to page 3 of the results
  • (d) A dropdown that changes the sort order
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Correct. Anything that changes data must be a POST — a GET can be pre-fetched by a browser or crawler, and refresh repeats it silently.
  • (b) A search is safe and repeatable, and a GET makes the results shareable and bookmarkable.
  • (c) Pagination is a GET, so page 3 has its own address.
  • (d) Sorting changes nothing on the server, so GET is right and the sorted view gets its own URL.

Exercise 3.3. Is POST more secure than GET?

  • (a) No — but it keeps values out of the address bar, history and server logs
  • (b) Yes — POST data is encrypted
  • (c) Yes — POST data cannot be intercepted
  • (d) No — they are identical in every way
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Exactly the right answer, and the one examiners look for. Both send data in plain text unless the connection is HTTPS.
  • (b) Nothing about POST encrypts anything. Only TLS does that.
  • (c) The body is as readable as the URL to anyone on the network path.
  • (d) They differ in visibility, size, caching and refresh behaviour; those differences matter, they are just not encryption.

Exercise 3.4. A page is opened directly, with no form behind it. What does echo $_POST["name"]; do in PHP 8?

  • (a) Prints nothing, and emits Warning: Undefined array key "name"
  • (b) Prints nothing, silently
  • (c) Throws a fatal error and stops
  • (d) Prints NULL
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Correct — it is a warning, not a fatal error, so the page continues. Guard it with isset() or ?? to keep the log clean.
  • (b) PHP 8 warns about undefined array keys; PHP 5 issued a quieter notice, which is why old code gets away with it.
  • (c) Only undefined functions and similar are fatal.
  • (d) The expression is null and echoing null prints an empty string.

docs.title: Predict the output — reading form data
docs.text:
Exercise 3.5. The form was submitted with no checkbox ticked. What does this print? It receives a POST request with sname = Zoya.

<?php
$sub = $_POST["subjects"] ?? [];
echo count($sub), "\n";
echo isset($_POST["newsletter"]) ? "subscribed" : "not subscribed", "\n";
var_dump(empty($_POST["subjects"]));

Hint: An unticked checkbox is simply not sent. The key does not exist.

Answer

The script prints:

0
not subscribed
bool(true)

This is why a checkbox is read with isset() and a checkbox group with ?? [] — so that the count and the loop that follows both work when nothing was ticked.

Exercise 3.6. A number field containing 0 was submitted. What does this print? It receives a POST request with marks = 0.

<?php
$m = $_POST["marks"];
if ($m) echo "A: truthy\n"; else echo "A: falsy\n";
if ($m !== "") echo "B: has a value\n";
if (isset($m)) echo "C: is set\n";
var_dump($m);

Hint: What type is a submitted 0, and is that value truthy?

Answer

The script prints:

A: falsy
B: has a value
C: is set
string(1) "0"

The string "0" is one of PHP's falsy values, so test A wrongly reports an empty field. For form input, test against "" or use isset() — never plain truthiness.

Exercise 3.7. This page was reached with ?q=PHP&page=2. What does it print? It is requested as ?q=PHP&page=2.

<?php
echo $_GET["q"], "|", $_GET["page"], "|";
var_dump($_GET["page"]);
var_dump($_GET["page"] === 2);
var_dump((int) $_GET["page"] === 2);

Hint: What type does a query-string value have?

Answer

The script prints:

PHP|2|string(1) "2"
bool(false)
bool(true)

Everything from the URL is a string. Compare with ==, or cast first — which is the safer habit, because it also makes the value ready for arithmetic.

docs.title: Write it — form handling
docs.text:
Exercise 3.8. Read $_GET["marks"] and print the grade: A for 80 and above, B for 60–79, C for 40–59, F below 40. If marks is missing or is not a number between 0 and 100, print invalid instead. Print the grade and nothing else.

Remember that everything in $_GET is a string, and that the key may not be there at all.

Starting point:

<?php
// your code here

Your script is tested with these cases:

Case Expected output ?marks=91 A ?marks=60 B ?marks=40 C ?marks=0 F ?marks=101 invalid ?marks=abc invalid nothing at all invalid Answer

A solution:

<?php
$m = $_GET["marks"] ?? "";

if (!is_numeric($m) || $m < 0 || $m > 100) {
    echo "invalid";
} elseif ($m >= 80) {
    echo "A";
} elseif ($m >= 60) {
    echo "B";
} elseif ($m >= 40) {
    echo "C";
} else {
    echo "F";
}

Validate first, then grade. The ?? "" handles the missing key without a warning, and is_numeric catches "abc" before the comparisons — a comparison against a non-numeric string in PHP 8 would compare as text and give a surprising answer.

The ?marks=0 case is the one that catches people: a naive if (!$m) or if (empty($m)) would call a legitimate zero invalid.

Exercise 3.9. A form posted subjects[] checkboxes. Print the chosen subjects as a comma-separated list. If nothing was ticked, print none. The page must produce no warnings when the key is absent.

Expected: PHP, MySQL for the first test, none for the second.

Starting point:

<?php
// your code here

Your script is tested with these cases:

Case Expected output two ticked PHP, MySQL one ticked jQuery none ticked none sent as a plain string none Answer

A solution:

<?php
$subjects = $_POST["subjects"] ?? [];

if (!is_array($subjects) || count($subjects) === 0) {
    echo "none";
} else {
    echo implode(", ", $subjects);
}

?? [] is what makes this warning-free, and the is_array guard matters because a request can send subjects=hello as a plain string even though your form would never do so.

Look at the last test case: a request that sends subjects=hack as a plain string rather than an array. Your form would never do that, but a request is not obliged to come from your form — which is why the is_array guard is there and not merely tidy.

Exercise 3.10. Write a validator: read $_POST["email"] and $_POST["phone"]. Print ok if the email is valid and the phone is exactly 10 digits starting 6–9. Otherwise print one line per problem: bad email and/or bad phone, email first.

So a request with both wrong prints two lines. Use filter_var for the email and a regular expression for the phone.

Starting point:

<?php
// your code here

Your script is tested with these cases:

Case Expected output both good ok bad email bad email bad phone bad phone both bad bad email bad phone nothing posted bad email bad phone Answer

A solution:

<?php
$email = trim($_POST["email"] ?? "");
$phone = trim($_POST["phone"] ?? "");

$errors = [];
if (!filter_var($email, FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL)) $errors[] = "bad email";
if (!preg_match('/^[6-9]\d{9}$/', $phone))      $errors[] = "bad phone";

if ($errors) {
    echo implode("\n", $errors);
} else {
    echo "ok";
}

Collecting into an $errors array rather than printing as you go is what makes "report every problem, in order" easy — and it is exactly the structure the sticky form above uses.

Note the anchors in the phone pattern. Without ^ and $, "abc9812345670xyz" would pass.

docs.title: Fill the blanks — a self-processing form
docs.text:
Exercise 3.11. Complete the handler so that it only runs on a submission, reads the field safely, and prints Hello, Zoya. The script receives a POST request with sname = Zoya.

The blanks are marked ___1___, ___2___ and so on.

<?php
$name = "";

if ($_SERVER["___1___"] === "POST") {
    $name = ___2___($_POST["sname"] ___3___ "");
}

if ($name !== "") {
    echo "Hello, " . ___4___($name);
}
Answer
  • Blank 1: REQUEST_METHOD
  • Blank 2: trim
  • Blank 3: ??
  • Blank 4: htmlspecialchars (also e)
<?php
$name = "";

if ($_SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] === "POST") {
    $name = trim($_POST["sname"] ?? "");
}

if ($name !== "") {
    echo "Hello, " . htmlspecialchars($name);
}

It prints:

Hello, Zoya

Four habits in four blanks: check the method, trim the input, default it with ?? so a missing key is not a warning, and escape it on the way out.

Exercise 3.12. Complete the sticky field so the user's answer survives a failed submission, and cannot break out of the attribute.

The blanks are marked ___1___, ___2___ and so on.

<?php $posted = "O'Brien"; ?>
<input type="text" name="sname"
       value="<?= ___1___($posted, ___2___) ?>">
Answer
  • Blank 1: htmlspecialchars
  • Blank 2: ENT_QUOTES
<?php $posted = "O'Brien"; ?>
<input type="text" name="sname"
       value="<?= htmlspecialchars($posted, ENT_QUOTES) ?>">

It prints:

<input type="text" name="sname"
       value="O'Brien">

ENT_QUOTES escapes single quotes as well as double ones. It has been the default since PHP 8.1, but naming it explicitly means the code is right on any version — and O'Brien is exactly the name that exposes the difference.

docs.title: Put it in order — validate then redirect
docs.text:
Exercise 3.13. These lines make up a correct post/redirect/get handler. Put them in the only order that works.

    if ($note !== "") {
        exit;
        $_SESSION["saved"] = $note;
}
session_start();
    $note = trim($_POST["note"] ?? "");
        header("Location: done.php");
<?php
    }
if ($_SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] === "POST") {
Answer

The lines in working order:

<?php
session_start();
if ($_SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] === "POST") {
    $note = trim($_POST["note"] ?? "");
    if ($note !== "") {
        $_SESSION["saved"] = $note;
        header("Location: done.php");
        exit;
    }
}

session_start() must come first, because it sends a header and nothing may be output before it. exit must come immediately after header(), or the script carries on running after telling the browser to leave.

docs.title: Quick check — forms, sessions and safety
docs.text:
Exercise 3.14. Why must exit; follow header("Location: next.php");?

  • (a) Because header() only queues the header — the rest of the script still runs, and may save the record twice or leak output
  • (b) Because the header is not sent without it
  • (c) Because PHP throws an error otherwise
  • (d) It is only needed when the target page is on another server
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Correct. The redirect takes effect in the browser, but PHP has no reason to stop on its own.
  • (b) The header is sent either way, at the end of the script.
  • (c) There is no error — which is precisely what makes the bug hard to find.
  • (d) It is needed every time.

Exercise 3.15. A page starts with a blank line and then <?php session_start(); ?>. What happens?

  • (a) A warning: headers already sent — the blank line was output
  • (b) Nothing — leading whitespace is ignored
  • (c) A parse error
  • (d) The session works but is empty
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Right. A single byte before the PHP tag is content, and once content has gone the headers are fixed.
  • (b) PHP sends everything outside the tags verbatim, including a newline.
  • (c) It parses fine; the problem is at run time.
  • (d) The session fails to start at all.

Exercise 3.16. Which is the correct test for a single checkbox called agree?

  • (a) isset($_POST["agree"])
  • (b) $_POST["agree"] == "on"
  • (c) $_POST["agree"] === true
  • (d) !empty($_POST["agree"])
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Right — an unticked box sends nothing, so existence is the only question worth asking.
  • (b) Works when ticked, warns when not, and breaks if you set your own value attribute.
  • (c) Form values are always strings; there is no boolean true to compare with.
  • (d) Nearly right, and it silences the warning — but it fails if the checkbox's value is "0", which is falsy.

Exercise 3.17. What is stored in the visitor's browser when you use a PHP session?

  • (a) Only an opaque session id, in a cookie
  • (b) The whole $_SESSION array
  • (c) Nothing at all
  • (d) The user's IP address
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Correct. The data itself lives in a file on the server, keyed by that id.
  • (b) That is how cookies work, not sessions.
  • (c) Something must identify the visitor across requests — that is the session id.
  • (d) PHP does not use the IP to identify a session; that would break on mobile networks.

Exercise 3.18. A sticky form redraws a submitted name with value="<?= $_POST['sname'] ?>". What is wrong?

  • (a) A quote in the value escapes the attribute, allowing injected markup — it needs htmlspecialchars(…, ENT_QUOTES)
  • (b) Nothing — value attributes are safe by definition
  • (c) It should use $_GET
  • (d) It needs urlencode()
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Correct, and it is the most common XSS hole in student projects: the site attacks its own users with their own input.
  • (b) The browser parses the attribute exactly as it parses everything else.
  • (c) The superglobal is not the issue.
  • (d) urlencode is for URLs; inside HTML it would show %20 in the box.

Exercise 3.19. Which statement about $_REQUEST is true?

  • (a) It merges GET, POST and cookie data, so you can no longer tell where a value came from
  • (b) It is a faster alternative to $_POST
  • (c) It contains only POST data
  • (d) It is automatically sanitised
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Right, and that ambiguity is why it is best avoided — a value you expected from a POST can be supplied in the URL instead.
  • (b) Speed is not the issue.
  • (c) It contains GET, POST and COOKIE, in an order set by php.ini.
  • (d) Nothing in PHP sanitises input automatically.

docs.title: Practice problems
docs.text:
Exercise 3.20. Build a form with two text boxes and a button named "Evaluate" that adds the two numbers and shows the result on the same page.

Answer

This is the self-processing form of Listing 3.6. Its essential logic is:

<?php
$message = "";
if ($_SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] === "POST") {
    $a = (float) ($_POST["a"] ?? 0);
    $b = (float) ($_POST["b"] ?? 0);
    $message = "$a + $b = " . ($a + $b);
}
?>
<form action="" method="post">
  <input type="text" name="a" value="<?= htmlspecialchars($_POST["a"] ?? "") ?>">
  <input type="text" name="b" value="<?= htmlspecialchars($_POST["b"] ?? "") ?>">
  <button type="submit">Evaluate</button>
</form>
<?php if ($message): ?><p><?= htmlspecialchars($message) ?></p><?php endif; ?>

The empty action posts back to the same file; the test on REQUEST_METHOD tells a submission from a first visit; the casts turn the two strings into numbers; and the values are put back into the boxes, escaped, so the user's typing survives. Entering 12 and 30 prints 12 + 30 = 42.

Exercise 3.21. Extend the registration form so that it also asks for a password twice and rejects the submission unless the two match and the password is at least eight characters.

Answer

Add two password fields to the form and two checks to the validation step:

$password = $_POST["password"] ?? "";
$confirm  = $_POST["confirm"]  ?? "";

if (strlen($password) < 8) {
    $errors["password"] = "At least eight characters";
} elseif ($password !== $confirm) {
    $errors["confirm"] = "The two passwords do not match";
}

<input type="password" name="password">
<input type="password" name="confirm">

Two points belong with the answer. First, a password is never placed back in a value attribute when the form is redisplayed, so the user types both again. Second, when the form finally passes, the password is stored as password_hash($password, PASSWORD_DEFAULT) and never as plain text (Unit 4 returns to this).

Exercise 3.22. Write a page that accepts ?n=5 and prints the multiplication table of n, defaulting to 2 and rejecting anything that is not a number between 1 and 20.

Answer 
<?php
$n = $_GET["n"] ?? "2";

if (!preg_match('/^\d+$/', $n) || $n < 1 || $n > 20) {
    echo "<p>n must be a whole number from 1 to 20.</p>";
    exit;
}

$n = (int) $n;
echo "<h3>Multiplication table of $n</h3>\n";
for ($i = 1; $i <= 10; $i++) {
    echo "$n x $i = ", $n * $i, "<br>\n";
}

With no parameter the table of 2 is printed; ?n=4 prints the table of 4; and ?n=abc, ?n=25 and ?n=-3 all print the error message. The pattern rejects anything that is not a string of digits before the range check, so no non-numeric text is ever compared with a number.

Exercise 3.23. Explain why <input type="hidden" name="price" value="500"> is not a safe way to carry a price to the payment page. What should carry it instead?

Answer

A hidden field is hidden only from the page as displayed. The user can see it with "View source", change it with the browser's developer tools, or send a request with any value at all using a tool such as curl. A user could therefore pay 1 instead of 500.

The payment page should receive only an identifier, such as product_id=17 and a quantity, and then look the price up itself on the server, from the database or from an array in the script. The price is then never a value the browser is trusted to supply.

Exercise 3.24. Write a login page with a session guard, so that dashboard.php redirects to login.php when nobody is signed in.

Answer

The guard, at the very top of dashboard.php and of every other protected page:

<?php
session_start();
if (empty($_SESSION["user"])) {
    header("Location: login.php");
    exit;
}
?>
<h3>Welcome, <?= htmlspecialchars($_SESSION["user"]) ?></h3>

The login page, which sets the session variable that the guard looks for:

<?php
session_start();
$error = "";

if ($_SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] === "POST") {
    $u = trim($_POST["username"] ?? "");
    $p = $_POST["password"] ?? "";

    if ($u === "zoya" && $p === "hunter2") {   // in Unit 4 this is a database lookup
        session_regenerate_id(true);
        $_SESSION["user"] = $u;
        header("Location: dashboard.php");
        exit;
    }
    $error = "Wrong username or password";
}
?>
<?php if ($error): ?><p><?= htmlspecialchars($error) ?></p><?php endif; ?>
<form method="post">
  <input type="text" name="username">
  <input type="password" name="password">
  <button type="submit">Sign in</button>
</form>

exit after each header("Location: …") is not optional: without it the rest of the page still runs, and a protected page would still be built for a visitor who was meant to be turned away.

Exercise 3.25. A feedback form has a textarea. Show the submitted text back to the user with line breaks preserved and all markup neutralised. (Hint: nl2br(htmlspecialchars($t)), in that order. Explain why the other order is wrong.)

Answer 
<?php
$t = $_POST["feedback"] ?? "";
echo "<p>", nl2br(htmlspecialchars($t)), "</p>";

htmlspecialchars first turns any <, >, & and quotes typed by the user into harmless entities; nl2br then adds real <br /> tags at the line breaks. In the other order, nl2br inserts <br /> first, and htmlspecialchars then escapes those tags too, so the page would show the literal text <br /> after each line instead of a line break.

Exercise 3.26. Draw the table of what $_GET, $_POST and $_REQUEST contain for a GET form, a POST form, and a POST form whose action already has a query string on it. Then verify it with Listing 3.4.

Answer Form $_GET $_POST $_REQUEST method="get" the form fields empty the form fields method="post" empty the form fields the form fields method="post" with action="save.php?id=5" id only the form fields id and the form fields

The third row is the one that surprises people: the query string in the action address is read into $_GET even though the form is posted, while the fields typed by the user arrive in $_POST. $_REQUEST merges the sources, and which one wins when a name appears in both depends on the request_order setting; for that reason it is better to read $_GET or $_POST by name.

Exercise 3.27. Build a two-page wizard: page 1 collects a name, page 2 collects a course, page 3 shows both. Do it once with hidden fields and once with a session, and say which you would ship.

Answer

With hidden fields. Page 2 receives the name from page 1 and must pass it on, so it prints it back inside its own form:

<input type="hidden" name="sname" value="<?= htmlspecialchars($_POST["sname"] ?? "") ?>">
<select name="course"> … </select>

Page 3 then receives both sname and course in $_POST.

With a session. Each page stores its answer and the last page reads them all:

// page 1 handler
session_start();
$_SESSION["sname"] = trim($_POST["sname"] ?? "");
header("Location: page2.php");
exit;

// page 3
session_start();
echo htmlspecialchars($_SESSION["sname"] ?? ""), " / ", htmlspecialchars($_SESSION["course"] ?? "");

Which to ship. The session version. The hidden-field version re-sends every earlier answer on every step, and each of those values can be edited by the user before it is submitted, so each step must validate everything again. In the session version the earlier answers are checked once, are kept on the server, and cannot be tampered with between steps.

Exercise 3.28. Add a photograph field to the registration form. Accept only JPEG and PNG under 1 MB, store the file as roll_number.jpg, and show the picture back on the confirmation page. What goes wrong if two students upload on the same day and you name files by date alone?

Answer

The form needs enctype="multipart/form-data" and a file input:

<form action="" method="post" enctype="multipart/form-data">
  <input type="file" name="photo" accept="image/jpeg,image/png">
  ...
</form>

The handler applies the checks of Listing 3.11 in order:

$file = $_FILES["photo"] ?? null;
if ($file && $file["error"] === UPLOAD_ERR_OK) {
    if ($file["size"] > 1024 * 1024) {
        $errors["photo"] = "The photograph must be under 1 MB";
    } else {
        $info = getimagesize($file["tmp_name"]);          // looks at the real content
        if ($info === false || !in_array($info[2], [IMAGETYPE_JPEG, IMAGETYPE_PNG], true)) {
            $errors["photo"] = "Only JPEG and PNG pictures are accepted";
        }
    }
}
// when everything has passed:
$name = $fields["rollno"] . ".jpg";                       // our own name, never the browser's
move_uploaded_file($file["tmp_name"], "uploads/" . $name);

The confirmation page then shows <img src="uploads/<?= e($roll) ?>.jpg">. (A strict version converts a PNG to JPEG, or keeps the extension that matches the detected type.)

If files are named by the date alone, two students who upload on the same day produce the same name, and the second upload silently overwrites the first, so one student's photograph disappears or is shown against the other student's record. A name built from something unique to the student, such as the roll number, or a name made with uniqid(), avoids the collision.

docs.title: Examination questions
docs.text: These are questions in the shapes this course uses, grouped by the marks they carry. A two-mark question wants a definition and one concrete example, a five-mark question wants structure, and a ten-mark question wants an answer with parts.

docs.title: Two-mark questions
docs.text:
Exercise 3.29. (2 marks) What are superglobals? Name any four.

Answer

Built-in arrays that PHP fills in before your script runs and that are visible in every scope — inside functions too — without a global declaration.

  • $_GET — parameters from the query string
  • $_POST — fields from a posted form
  • $_REQUEST — GET, POST and cookies merged
  • $_SERVER — information about the request and the server
  • $_SESSION, $_COOKIE, $_FILES, $GLOBALS

Exercise 3.30. (2 marks) Which attribute of a form field determines the key in $_POST?

Answer

name. <input name="rollno"> arrives as $_POST["rollno"]. A field with no name attribute is not submitted at all — neither id nor value substitutes for it, and this is the commonest reason a value "does not arrive".

Exercise 3.31. (2 marks) How do you check whether a checkbox was ticked?

Answer

With isset(). An unticked checkbox sends nothing at all — the key is absent from $_POST, rather than being empty or "off".

if (isset($_POST["agree"])) { /* it was ticked */ }

For a group named subjects[], read $_POST["subjects"] ?? [] so the loop that follows works when nothing was ticked.

Exercise 3.32. (2 marks) What is $_SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] used for?

Answer

To tell a first visit from a submission, which is what makes a self-processing form — one file that both draws the form and handles it — possible.

if ($_SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] === "POST") {
    // handle the submission
} else {
    // draw the empty form
}

Exercise 3.33. (2 marks) Why must session_start() appear before any output?

Answer

Because it sends a Set-Cookie HTTP header carrying the session id, and headers must precede the body. Once a single byte of output has gone — even a blank line before <?php or a newline after ?> in an included file — the headers are already sent and PHP warns "Cannot modify header information". The same applies to header() and setcookie().

docs.title: Five-mark questions
docs.text:
Exercise 3.34. (5 marks) Differentiate between the GET and POST methods.

Answer GET POST Data travels in the URL, after ? the request body Visible in the address bar Yes No Bookmarkable / in history Yes No Size limit about 2000 characters in practice effectively unlimited (post_max_size) Can upload a file No Yes, with enctype="multipart/form-data" Cached / re-sent on refresh Yes, silently No; the browser asks first Read in PHP from $_GET $_POST Use for asking: search, filter, sort, page number changing: register, log in, save, delete

Is POST more secure? No. It only keeps values out of the address bar, the history and the server log. The body is equally readable to anyone watching the network — only HTTPS makes a request private. State this explicitly; it is often the mark that separates answers.

Exercise 3.35. (5 marks) Differentiate between sessions and cookies.

Answer Session Cookie Stored on the server in the browser What the browser holds only an opaque session id the actual value Can the user read or edit it No Yes Size as large as you like about 4 KB Lifetime until the browser closes or the server expires it whatever expiry you set Created with session_start(), then $_SESSION["k"] setcookie("k", $v, time()+3600) Use for login state, a cart, a CSRF token "remember me", theme, language

Note that a session uses a cookie to carry its id, so the two are related rather than alternatives: the session is where the data lives, the cookie is how the visitor is recognised.

Exercise 3.36. (5 marks) What is form validation? Differentiate client-side and server-side validation.

Answer

Validation is checking that submitted data is acceptable — present, the right shape, within range — before acting on it.

Client-side Server-side Runs in the browser (HTML attributes, JavaScript) on the server, in PHP Speed instant, no round trip needs a request Can be bypassed Yes — the browser belongs to the user No Purpose convenience security and correctness

Both, always — and never only the first. required, pattern, maxlength and the options in a dropdown can all be edited or ignored before a request is sent, and a request need not come from your form at all.

$errors = [];
$name = trim($_POST["name"] ?? "");
if ($name === "")                              $errors[] = "Name is required";
elseif (!preg_match('/^[A-Za-z ]{3,50}$/', $name)) $errors[] = "Letters only";
if (!filter_var($_POST["email"] ?? "", FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL))
                                               $errors[] = "Invalid email";
if (!$errors) { /* safe to save */ }

Collect all the errors into an array rather than stopping at the first, and redisplay the form with the user's answers still in place.

Exercise 3.37. (5 marks) What is a sticky form, and how do you make one?

Answer

A form that redisplays the values the user already typed when validation fails, instead of clearing itself. Without it, one bad field costs the user the whole form.

Text fields — echo the submitted value back into value, escaped:

<input type="text" name="sname"
       value="<?= htmlspecialchars($_POST['sname'] ?? '', ENT_QUOTES) ?>">

Select — mark the matching option selected:

<option value="UG" <?= ($_POST['course'] ?? '') === 'UG' ? 'selected' : '' ?>>UG</option>

Radio and checkbox — mark them checked, using in_array() for a group.

The htmlspecialchars is not optional: without it a quotation mark in the value escapes the attribute, turning your own sticky form into an XSS hole.

docs.title: Ten-mark questions
docs.text:
Exercise 3.38. (10 marks) Design a student registration form and validate it with PHP. Show the form, the validation and the output.

Answer

Structure your answer in four parts — it is the structure the marks follow.

1. The form, with an appropriate control for each field:

<form action="" method="post">
  <input type="text" name="sname"  value="<?= e($f['sname']) ?>">
  <input type="text" name="rollno" value="<?= e($f['rollno']) ?>">
  <input type="text" name="email"  value="<?= e($f['email']) ?>">
  <label><input type="radio" name="gender" value="F"> Female</label>
  <select name="course">…</select>
  <input type="checkbox" name="subjects[]" value="PHP"> PHP
  <button type="submit">Register</button>
</form>

2. Collect and clean — one array, everything trimmed:

if ($_SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] === "POST") {
    $f = [
        "sname"    => trim($_POST["sname"]  ?? ""),
        "rollno"   => trim($_POST["rollno"] ?? ""),
        "email"    => trim($_POST["email"]  ?? ""),
        "gender"   => $_POST["gender"] ?? "",
        "subjects" => $_POST["subjects"] ?? [],
    ];

3. Validate, collecting every error:

    $errors = [];
    if (!preg_match('/^[A-Za-z ]{3,50}$/', $f["sname"]))  $errors["sname"]  = "3-50 letters";
    if (!preg_match('/^\d{7}$/', $f["rollno"]))           $errors["rollno"] = "7 digits";
    if (!filter_var($f["email"], FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL))  $errors["email"]  = "Invalid email";
    if (!in_array($f["gender"], ["F","M","O"], true))     $errors["gender"] = "Choose one";
    if (count($f["subjects"]) < 2)                        $errors["subjects"] = "Pick two";
}

4. Act or redraw — if $errors is empty, save (Unit 4) and redirect; otherwise redraw the form with the messages beside the fields and the values still in place.

Points to mention for the remaining marks: every value arrives as a string; an unticked checkbox sends nothing; validation must happen on the server because the browser can be bypassed; and every echoed value needs htmlspecialchars().

The complete running version is in Unit 3.

Exercise 3.39. (10 marks) Explain file uploading in PHP. What does $_FILES contain, and what checks must a handler perform?

Answer

The form needs two things — POST, and the multipart encoding:

<form action="upload.php" method="post" enctype="multipart/form-data">
  <input type="file" name="photo">
  <button type="submit">Upload</button>
</form>

Without enctype="multipart/form-data", $_FILES is empty and nothing explains why.

$_FILES["photo"] holds five keys: name (the visitor's file name), type (the MIME type the browser claimed), tmp_name (where PHP parked it), size (bytes), and error (0 = UPLOAD_ERR_OK). Only tmp_name, size and error are trustworthy; the other two come from the browser.

The handler:

$f = $_FILES["photo"];

if ($f["error"] !== UPLOAD_ERR_OK)        exit("Upload failed");
if ($f["size"] > 2*1024*1024)             exit("Too large");

$ext = strtolower(pathinfo($f["name"], PATHINFO_EXTENSION));
if (!in_array($ext, ["jpg","jpeg","png"], true)) exit("Type not allowed");
if (!is_uploaded_file($f["tmp_name"]))    exit("Not an uploaded file");

$target = "uploads/" . uniqid("img_") . "." . $ext;   // OUR name, not theirs
move_uploaded_file($f["tmp_name"], $target);

Three security points worth the marks: never store the file under the name the browser supplied (../../index.php is a valid string); never put uploads in a folder the server will execute; and never trust the claimed type. The temporary file is deleted automatically when the script ends, so it must be moved during that request.

Unit 3 has the runnable version.

docs.title: Unit 1: Introduction to PHP
docs.text:
This unit introduces PHP, the language in which the rest of the course is written. It starts with what a server-side language is and what it is not, takes you through installing a local server and running a first file, and then covers the language itself: syntax, variables and constants, the eight data types, arrays, operators, decisions, loops, functions, and the splitting of a program across files.

Everything in the later units (forms, strings, databases, JSON) is built from these constructs, so it is worth reading this unit slowly and running every example. It corresponds to Unit 1 of the course, Introduction to PHP, which is allotted 7 lecture hours.

Learning outcomes

Work through this unit and you should be able to do all of the following without looking anything up.

  • Explain what a server-side language is, and say exactly which parts of a request PHP touches and which parts it never sees.
  • Write, save and run a PHP file, and read the error message when it does not run.
  • Declare variables and constants, and say which of the eight types a value has.
  • Build indexed, associative and multidimensional arrays, and walk them with foreach.
  • Predict the result of any expression, including the ones where PHP quietly converts a string into a number — and say why == and === disagree.
  • Choose between if, switch and match, and between while, for and foreach, and justify the choice.

docs.title: 1.1 What PHP does, and where it runs
docs.text:
The idea, first

You already know HTML and CSS. Those are files the server hands over unchanged: the same bytes reach every visitor, and the page cannot know who asked, cannot remember anything, and cannot look anything up. That is the ceiling this course removes.

PHP is a program that runs on the server, before the reply is sent. The browser asks for marks.php; the server notices the .php, runs the file through PHP, and sends the result — which is ordinary HTML. The browser never sees a line of PHP. Choose "View source" on a PHP-generated page and there is no PHP in it, which is exactly why passwords may sit in a PHP file and must never sit in JavaScript.

So PHP's whole job is to build a string of HTML and hand it over. Everything in this unit — variables, arrays, loops, conditions — exists to make building that string depend on something: on who asked, on what they typed, on what is in the database. A loop over a database result is an HTML table that grows when the data grows. That is the entire trick, and the rest is detail.

Figure 1.1. One request, one reply. PHP sits inside the server box and its only output is text. Unit 5 comes back to the left-hand box, where jQuery runs.

Where the name comes from

PHP began in 1994 as Rasmus Lerdorf's "Personal Home Page Tools". The name now stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor — a recursive acronym, and a fair description: it processes a file before the hypertext is sent.

docs.title: 1.2 Getting a server and running your first file
docs.text: The listings in this book can be read without a server, but your practical file and your examination will use a real one. Set up the real thing once, now, and keep it.

docs.title: Install XAMPP
docs.text:
1. Get XAMPP from apachefriends.org and install it. It bundles Apache (the web server), MySQL/MariaDB (the database), PHP and Perl — the X is for cross-platform.
  2. Open the XAMPP Control Panel and press Start next to Apache and MySQL. Both should turn green.
  3. Find the htdocs folder — on Windows it is usually C:\xampp\htdocs. Everything you want the server to serve lives here.
  4. Make a folder inside it for your work, say htdocs\ge5b.
  5. Open http://localhost/ge5b/ in a browser.

The mistake everybody makes once

Opening the file by double-clicking it, so the address bar reads file:///C:/xampp/htdocs/ge5b/hello.php. The browser then shows your PHP source code, or offers to save the file, because nothing ran it. The address must start with http://localhost/. That is the difference between opening a file and asking a server for a page.

docs.title: Your first file
docs.text:
Save this as htdocs\ge5b\hello.php and visit http://localhost/ge5b/hello.php.

Listing 1.1. hello.php — the first program

<!doctype html>
<html>
<head><title>My first PHP page</title></head>
<body>
  <h1>Hello from the server</h1>

  <?php
    $name = "Riya";
    echo "<p>Good morning, $name.</p>";
    echo "<p>This page was built at " . date("H:i:s") . ".</p>";
  ?>

  <p>This last line is plain HTML again.</p>
</body>
</html>

Output sent to the browser:

<!doctype html>
<html>
<head><title>My first PHP page</title></head>
<body>
  <h1>Hello from the server</h1>

  <p>Good morning, Riya.</p><p>This page was built at 09:41:07.</p>
  <p>This last line is plain HTML again.</p>
</body>
</html>

The output is exactly what the server sends down the wire, and the browser then renders it. It contains no PHP at all. The time shown is the time at which the page was built, so it changes with every request.

What the visitor sees and what View source shows

What a visitor sees is the browser's rendering of the output above, and what "View source" would show them is that output itself. The PHP block has vanished from both and been replaced by its output. Everything else passed through untouched. That, mechanically, is all PHP does.

docs.title: The tags
docs.text:
PHP code lives between <?php and ?>. Outside those tags, the file is sent out as-is. A file may switch between the two as often as it likes.

Form Means Use it? <?php … ?> The standard opening and closing tag Always <?= $x ?> Short echo tag; identical to <?php echo $x; ?> Yes, inside HTML templates — it is always enabled since PHP 5.4 <? … ?> Short open tag No. It depends on a setting that is off by default and it clashes with XML File ends with no ?> Perfectly legal in a file that is all PHP Yes — preferred, because a stray blank line after ?> gets sent to the browser and breaks header() later

docs.title: Statements, semicolons and comments
docs.text:
Every statement ends with a semicolon. The last statement before a closing ?> may omit it, but do not rely on that. Whitespace is free; PHP does not care about indentation, though the next person to read your code will.

Listing 1.2. Comments, echo and print

<?php
// A single-line comment, to the end of the line.
# This also works, and is a leftover from shell scripting.

/* A block comment
   over several lines. */

echo "echo takes several arguments: ", 1 + 1, "\n";
print "print takes exactly one, and returns 1.\n";

$used = print "print is an expression\n";
echo "print returned $used\n";

echo "Nothing after a closing tag is PHP's business.\n";

Output:

echo takes several arguments: 2
print takes exactly one, and returns 1.
print is an expression
print returned 1
Nothing after a closing tag is PHP's business.

Deleting a semicolon from this listing produces a parse error. PHP reports the line where it first noticed the problem, which is usually the line after the missing semicolon.

echo print Arguments One or many, comma separated Exactly one Returns Nothing (it is a language construct, not a function) 1, so it can sit inside an expression Speed Marginally faster; nobody has ever noticed — In practice Use echo Use it when you need a value, which is almost never

docs.title: Case sensitivity — the rule people get wrong
docs.text:
Case-insensitive (both work) Case-sensitive (must match) Keywords: IF, if, While Variable names: $name and $Name are two different variables Function names: strlen(), STRLEN() Constants defined with define(), unless you ask otherwise Class names Array keys: $a["x"] ≠ $a["X"]

Listing 1.3. Case sensitivity, demonstrated

<?php
$name = "Aman";

ECHO "Keywords do not care about case.\n";   // fine
echo STRTOUPPER("nor do function names"), "\n";  // fine

echo "But variables do: [$Name]\n";   // a different, empty variable

Output:

Keywords do not care about case.
NOR DO FUNCTION NAMES

Warning:  Undefined variable $Name in case.php on line 7
But variables do: []

The warning is PHP telling you that $Name was never given a value. This single rule accounts for a large share of "my page is blank" problems.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
A variable is a name for a value. In PHP the name always starts with $, then a letter or underscore, then any letters, digits or underscores. There is no declaration step and no type to write: assigning a value creates the variable, and assigning a different kind of value later is allowed.

Rule: Valid variable names

$name ✓ $_total ✓ $roll2 ✓ $firstName ✓$2roll ✗ (starts with a digit) $first name ✗ (space) $first-name ✗ (a hyphen is the minus operator)

Listing 1.4. Variables: create, change, inspect

<?php
$roll   = 2231045;          // an integer
$name   = "Zoya Khan";      // a string
$marks  = 78.5;             // a float
$passed = true;             // a boolean

echo "$name ($roll) scored $marks\n\n";

// Assigning again simply replaces the value — and may change the type.
$marks = "seventy-eight";
var_dump($marks);

// Copying takes a copy: $a and $b are independent afterwards.
$a = 10;
$b = $a;
$b = 99;
echo "\n\$a is $a and \$b is $b\n";

// Everything about a value, at a glance:
var_dump($roll, $passed, null);

Output:

Zoya Khan (2231045) scored 78.5

string(13) "seventy-eight"

$a is 10 and $b is 99
int(2231045)
bool(true)
NULL

var_dump() is the tool to reach for whenever you are not sure what you have: it prints the type and the value, and for strings it prints the length too.

Assignment copies, and that matters later

$b = $a copies the value. This is true for numbers, strings, booleans and arrays — PHP arrays are value types, unlike JavaScript arrays or Python lists. Objects are the exception; they are handled by reference. The array section below shows the difference, and it catches everyone once.

docs.title: Constants
docs.text:
A constant is a name whose value is fixed for the run of the script. Two ways to make one, and note that a constant has no $.

Listing 1.5. Two ways to define a constant

<?php
define("COLLEGE", "Example College");   // works anywhere, even inside an if
const UNIVERSITY = "Example University"; // compile time, top level only

define("PASS_MARK", 40);

echo COLLEGE . ", " . UNIVERSITY . "\n";
echo "Pass mark is " . PASS_MARK . "\n";

// Constants are not interpolated into strings — this prints the word:
echo "Pass mark is PASS_MARK\n";

var_dump(defined("PASS_MARK"), defined("NOPE"));

// PHP defines plenty of its own:
echo "PHP version: ", PHP_VERSION, "\n";
echo "Largest int: ", PHP_INT_MAX, "\n";
echo "Line ending constant is ", strlen(PHP_EOL), " character long\n";

// PASS_MARK = 50;   // <- uncomment: Parse error, and rightly so

Output:

Example College, Example University
Pass mark is 40
Pass mark is PASS_MARK
bool(true)
bool(false)
PHP version: 8.2.0
Largest int: 9223372036854775807
Line ending constant is 1 character long

Uncommenting the last line of the listing gives a parse error, and rightly so: assigning to a constant is exactly what a constant forbids.

Variable Constant Written $passMark PASS_MARK Can change Yes No Scope Local to the function unless declared global Global everywhere, automatically In a double-quoted string Interpolated Not interpolated — concatenate it Convention $camelCase or $snake_case UPPER_SNAKE_CASE

docs.title: 1.5 Data types
docs.text:
PHP has eight types, in three groups. You never write the type down; PHP decides from the value, which is called dynamic typing.

Group Type Example Notes Scalar(one value) int 42, -7, 0x1A, 0b1011 64-bit on any machine you will meet; PHP_INT_MAX is 9223372036854775807 float 3.14, 1.2e3, .5 Also called double. Never compare two floats with == string 'hi', "hi $name" A sequence of bytes; Unit 2 is entirely about these bool true, false Case-insensitive: TRUE works too Compound(many values) array [1, 2, 3], ["name" => "Ana"] An ordered map. Covered below object new mysqli(...) Used in Unit 4; classes of your own are outside this course Special NULL null The type of a variable with no value. Exactly one possible value resource a file handle A handle to something outside PHP; you will rarely name it

Listing 1.6. What type is this?

<?php
$values = [42, 3.14, "42", "3.14 rupees", true, false, null, [1, 2], 7/2, 10/5];

foreach ($values as $v) {
    printf("%-16s => %-8s ", var_export($v, true), gettype($v));
    var_dump($v);
}

Output:

42               => integer  int(42)
3.14             => double   float(3.14)
'42'             => string   string(2) "42"
'3.14 rupees'    => string   string(11) "3.14 rupees"
true             => boolean  bool(true)
false            => boolean  bool(false)
NULL             => NULL     NULL
array (
  0 => 1,
  1 => 2,
) => array    array(2) {
  [0]=>
  int(1)
  [1]=>
  int(2)
}
3.5              => double   float(3.5)
2                => integer  int(2)

gettype() gives a word; var_dump() gives the word, the value and, for strings, the length in bytes. Changing the values changes the types reported.

Two results worth staring at

7/2 gives the float 3.5 — PHP does not do integer division with /; use intdiv(7, 2) for that. And 10/5 gives the integer 2, because PHP returns an int when the division comes out exact. So the type of a division depends on the values, not on the operator.

docs.title: Type juggling: PHP converting behind your back
docs.text:
When an operator wants a type it has not been given, PHP converts. This is convenient and it is the source of most surprises in the language, so learn the table.

Value as bool as int as string 0 false 0 "0" 1, -3, 0.5 true 1, -3, 0 "1", "-3", "0.5" "" (empty string) false 0 "" "0" false 0 "0" "0.0", "00", " " true 0, 0, 0 unchanged "abc" true 0 (with a warning in arithmetic) "abc" "12abc" true 12 (with a warning) "12abc" [] (empty array) false 0 "Array" + notice [0] true 1 "Array" + notice null false 0 ""

The seven falsy values

false, 0, 0.0, "", "0", [] and null. Everything else is truthy — including the string "false", the string "0.0" and the array [0]. The one that bites is "0": a student who types 0 into a form sends the string "0", and if ($_POST['marks']) then quietly treats it as empty.

Listing 1.7. Falsy values, all together

<?php
$tests = [0, 1, -1, 0.0, "", "0", "0.0", "00", " ", "false", "abc", [], [0], null];

echo str_pad("value", 12), str_pad("if()", 8), str_pad("empty()", 10), "isset()\n";
echo str_repeat("-", 40), "\n";

foreach ($tests as $t) {
    echo str_pad(var_export($t, true), 12);
    echo str_pad($t ? "TRUE" : "false", 8);
    echo str_pad(empty($t) ? "TRUE" : "false", 10);
    echo isset($t) ? "TRUE" : "false";
    echo "\n";
}

Output:

value       if()    empty()   isset()
----------------------------------------
0           false   TRUE      TRUE
1           TRUE    false     TRUE
-1          TRUE    false     TRUE
0           false   TRUE      TRUE
''          false   TRUE      TRUE
'0'         false   TRUE      TRUE
'0.0'       TRUE    false     TRUE
'00'        TRUE    false     TRUE
' '         TRUE    false     TRUE
'false'     TRUE    false     TRUE
'abc'       TRUE    false     TRUE
array (
)   false   TRUE      TRUE
array (
  0 => 0,
)TRUE    false     TRUE
NULL        false   TRUE      false

This is the table above, generated. If you remember only one line from this unit, remember that "0" is falsy and "0.0" is not.

docs.title: Casting: converting on purpose
docs.text:
Listing 1.8. Explicit casts

<?php
$s = "45.9 kg";

var_dump((int) $s);      // 45  — stops at the first non-numeric character
var_dump((float) $s);    // 45.9
var_dump((bool) $s);     // true
var_dump((string) 45.9); // "45.9"
var_dump((array) "solo");// ["solo"]

// The function forms do the same thing and read better in a chain:
var_dump(intval("2231045"), floatval("78.5"), strval(99), boolval("0"));

// intval() also takes a base — useful for form data in hex or binary:
var_dump(intval("ff", 16), intval("1011", 2));

// Checking, rather than converting:
var_dump(is_numeric("78.5"), is_numeric("78.5 kg"), is_int(5), is_string("5"));

Output:

int(45)
float(45.9)
bool(true)
string(4) "45.9"
array(1) {
  [0]=>
  string(4) "solo"
}
int(2231045)
float(78.5)
string(2) "99"
bool(false)
int(255)
int(11)
bool(true)
bool(false)
bool(true)
bool(true)

An explicit cast never warns — you have told PHP you meant it. That is the difference between (int)$x and $x + 0.

docs.title: 1.6 Arrays
docs.text: An array in PHP is not a list — it is an ordered map from keys to values. The keys may be integers or strings, mixed freely, and the order is the order you inserted them. Everything called a list, dictionary, stack, queue or record in another language is this one structure here.

docs.title: Indexed arrays
docs.text:
Listing 1.9. Indexed arrays

<?php
$subjects = ["PHP", "MySQL", "jQuery"];        // modern
$old      = array("PHP", "MySQL", "jQuery");   // identical, older syntax

echo $subjects[0], "\n";        // PHP        — counting starts at 0
echo count($subjects), "\n";    // 3

$subjects[] = "JSON";           // append: the next integer key, so 3
$subjects[9] = "AJAX";          // you may skip: key 9 exists, 4..8 do not
$subjects[] = "Sessions";       // the next key is now 10, not 4

print_r($subjects);

echo "\nLast key is ", array_key_last($subjects), "\n";
echo "Is there a key 5? ", isset($subjects[5]) ? "yes" : "no", "\n";

Output:

PHP
3
Array
(
    [0] => PHP
    [1] => MySQL
    [2] => jQuery
    [3] => JSON
    [9] => AJAX
    [10] => Sessions
)

Last key is 10
Is there a key 5? no

[] is the modern syntax; array() is the old one and still appears in every textbook. They are identical.

docs.title: Associative arrays
docs.text:
Give the keys yourself and the array becomes a record. This is the shape every database row arrives in, so it is worth being fluent.

Listing 1.10. Associative arrays

<?php
$student = [
    "roll"   => 2231045,
    "name"   => "Zoya Khan",
    "course" => "Computer Science (Honours)",
    "marks"  => 78.5,
];

echo $student["name"], " scored ", $student["marks"], "\n";

$student["grade"] = "A";          // add a new key
$student["marks"] = 82;           // overwrite an existing one
unset($student["course"]);        // remove one

print_r($student);

echo "\nKeys:   ", implode(", ", array_keys($student)), "\n";
echo "Values: ", implode(", ", array_values($student)), "\n";

// A missing key: warning, and null.
echo "\n", $student["email"] ?? "(no email on file)", "\n";

Output:

Zoya Khan scored 78.5
Array
(
    [roll] => 2231045
    [name] => Zoya Khan
    [marks] => 82
    [grade] => A
)

Keys:   roll, name, marks, grade
Values: 2231045, Zoya Khan, 82, A

(no email on file)

Note the arrow: key => value. Also note that a missing key is a warning and gives null, not a crash — which is why isset() and ?? matter.

docs.title: Multidimensional arrays
docs.text:
A value in an array may itself be an array. A table of students is an array of associative arrays — exactly what a SELECT returns in Unit 4.

Listing 1.11. A table as an array of rows

<?php
$students = [
    ["roll" => 2231045, "name" => "Zoya Khan",  "marks" => 82],
    ["roll" => 2231046, "name" => "Aman Verma", "marks" => 67],
    ["roll" => 2231047, "name" => "Riya Singh", "marks" => 91],
];

echo "<h3>Class list</h3>";
echo "<table>";
echo "<tr><th>Roll</th><th>Name</th><th>Marks</th><th>Result</th></tr>";

foreach ($students as $s) {
    $result = $s["marks"] >= 40 ? "Pass" : "Fail";
    echo "<tr>";
    echo "<td>{$s['roll']}</td>";
    echo "<td>{$s['name']}</td>";
    echo "<td>{$s['marks']}</td>";
    echo "<td>$result</td>";
    echo "</tr>";
}
echo "</table>";

$total = array_sum(array_column($students, "marks"));
echo "<p>Class average: " . round($total / count($students), 2) . "</p>";

Output sent to the browser:

<h3>Class list</h3><table><tr><th>Roll</th><th>Name</th><th>Marks</th><th>Result</th></tr><tr><td>2231045</td><td>Zoya Khan</td><td>82</td><td>Pass</td></tr><tr><td>2231046</td><td>Aman Verma</td><td>67</td><td>Pass</td></tr><tr><td>2231047</td><td>Riya Singh</td><td>91</td><td>Pass</td></tr></table><p>Class average: 80</p>

This is the shape of a result set. In Unit 4 the same loop will run over rows fetched from MySQL, and the HTML below will not change at all.

Curly braces inside a string

"{$s['roll']}" — the braces are needed because the key is quoted. Without them you would write "$s[roll]", with the key unquoted, which also works but reads badly and breaks the moment the key has a space in it. Use the braces.

docs.title: The array functions you will actually use
Arithmetic
docs.text: Operator Name $a = 7, $b = 2 + - * add, subtract, multiply 9, 5, 14 / divide — float unless exact 3.5 % modulus — integers only, sign of the left operand 1 ** exponent 49 intdiv($a,$b) integer division (a function) 3

docs.title: Assignment, and the shorthand forms
docs.text: Shorthand Means Notes $a += 5 $a = $a + 5 also -=, *=, /=, %=, **= $s .= "x" $s = $s . "x" the one you will use constantly when building HTML $a ??= 5 assign only if $a is null or unset PHP 7.4+; perfect for form defaults $i++, ++$i add one post- returns the old value, pre- returns the new one

docs.title: Comparison — the part that is examined
Logical operators
Precedence, briefly
docs.text: Highest to lowest, keeping only what you will meet: ** → ++ -- and casts → * / % → + - → . (since PHP 8) → < <= > >= → == != === !== → && → || → ?? → ? : → = += .= → and → or. When in any doubt, use brackets: they cost nothing and they are read by humans.

docs.title: if / elseif / else
docs.text:
Listing 1.16. Grading with if / elseif / else

<?php
$marks = 78;

if ($marks >= 90) {
    $grade = "O";
} elseif ($marks >= 80) {
    $grade = "A+";
} elseif ($marks >= 70) {
    $grade = "A";
} elseif ($marks >= 60) {
    $grade = "B+";
} elseif ($marks >= 40) {
    $grade = "P";
} else {
    $grade = "F";
}

echo "$marks marks -> grade $grade\n";

// Written the other way round, everybody gets a P:
if ($marks >= 40)      { $wrong = "P";  }
elseif ($marks >= 70)  { $wrong = "A";  }
elseif ($marks >= 90)  { $wrong = "O";  }
echo "Tests in the wrong order give: $wrong\n";

Output:

78 marks -> grade A
Tests in the wrong order give: P

The order of the branches matters. The first true condition wins and the rest are skipped, so the tests must go from the strictest to the loosest. Changing $marks moves the result to a different branch.

elseif or else if?

Both work with braces. Only elseif works with the colon syntax (if (…): … elseif (…): … endif;), so prefer elseif and you never have to think about it.

docs.title: The alternative syntax, for templates
docs.text:
Inside HTML, braces get lost among the tags. PHP offers a colon form that names its own end, and it is much easier to read in a template. You will use this constantly in Units 3 and 4.

Listing 1.17. Alternative syntax inside HTML

<?php $marks = 78; $name = "Zoya"; ?>

<h3>Result</h3>

<?php if ($marks >= 40): ?>
  <p style="color:green">Congratulations <?= $name ?>, you passed with <?= $marks ?>.</p>
<?php elseif ($marks > 0): ?>
  <p style="color:#c0392b">Sorry <?= $name ?>, you scored <?= $marks ?>.</p>
<?php else: ?>
  <p>No result recorded.</p>
<?php endif; ?>

<hr>

<?php
// The same thing with braces and echo, for comparison:
if ($marks >= 40) {
    echo "<p>Braces version: passed with $marks.</p>";
} else {
    echo "<p>Braces version: failed.</p>";
}
?>

Output sent to the browser:

<h3>Result</h3>

  <p style="color:green">Congratulations Zoya, you passed with 78.</p>

<hr>

<p>Braces version: passed with 78.</p>

Compare the two halves. In a real template the second form wins every time, because endif tells you what is closing — a bare } twenty lines down does not.

docs.title: switch
docs.text:
Listing 1.18. switch, and why break matters

<?php
$grade = "A";

switch ($grade) {
    case "O":
    case "A+":
        echo "Outstanding\n";
        break;
    case "A":
        echo "Very good\n";
        break;
    case "B+":
    case "B":
        echo "Good\n";
        break;
    default:
        echo "Grade not recognised\n";
}

// Deliberate fall-through, grouping cases — the only respectable use:
$day = 6;
switch ($day) {
    case 6:
    case 7:
        echo "Weekend\n";
        break;
    default:
        echo "Working day\n";
}

// The trap: switch uses loose comparison.
$value = 0;
switch ($value) {
    case "hello":  echo "matched the string!\n"; break;   // PHP 5/7 did match here
    case 0:        echo "matched zero\n";        break;
}

Output:

Very good
Weekend
matched zero

Deleting a break makes execution fall through into the next case, which is occasionally useful and usually a bug. Note also that switch compares with ==, not ===.

docs.title: match — PHP 8's tidier switch
docs.text:
Listing 1.19. match is an expression, and it is strict

<?php
$grade = "A";

$remark = match ($grade) {
    "O", "A+" => "Outstanding",
    "A"       => "Very good",
    "B+", "B" => "Good",
    default   => "Grade not recognised",
};
echo $remark, "\n";

// It is strict, so this does NOT match "0":
$v = 0;
echo match (true) {
    $v === "0" => "the string zero\n",
    $v === 0   => "the integer zero\n",
    default    => "something else\n",
};

Output:

Very good
the integer zero

Three differences from switch: it is an expression so it returns a value, it compares with ===, and there is no fall-through so no break. Not in the course, but it turns up in modern code.

docs.title: The ternary and null-coalescing operators
docs.text:
Listing 1.20. ?: and ?? — and how they differ

<?php
$marks = 35;

$result = $marks >= 40 ? "Pass" : "Fail";
echo "$result\n";

// Shorthand ?: gives the left side when it is truthy
$name  = "";
echo ($name ?: "Anonymous"), "\n";

// ?? gives the left side unless it is null or undefined
$input = ["marks" => 0, "name" => null];

echo "with ?: -> ", ($input["marks"] ?: "missing"), "\n";   // "missing" — wrong!
echo "with ?? -> ", ($input["marks"] ?? "missing"), "\n";   // 0        — right

echo "name  ?? -> ", ($input["name"]  ?? "Anonymous"), "\n";
echo "email ?? -> ", ($input["email"] ?? "none"), "\n";      // no warning at all

// They chain:
$display = $input["nickname"] ?? $input["name"] ?? "Guest";
echo "chained -> $display\n";

Output:

Fail
Anonymous
with ?: -> missing
with ?? -> 0
name  ?? -> Anonymous
email ?? -> none
chained -> Guest

?: asks "is it truthy?"; ?? asks "does it exist and is it not null?". For form input, ?? is almost always the one you want, because a submitted 0 is a real answer.

docs.title: 1.9 Constructs for iterations
docs.text:
Four loops. They can all do the same jobs, but each one is the natural fit for a different question.

Loop Use when Shape while You do not know how many times — you have a condition while (cond) { … } do…while The body must run at least once do { … } while (cond); for You are counting, and you know the range for (init; cond; step) { … } foreach You are walking an array — the one you will use most foreach ($arr as $k => $v) { … }

Listing 1.21. All four loops, same output

<?php
echo "while:    ";
$i = 1;
while ($i <= 5) { echo $i, " "; $i++; }

echo "\ndo-while: ";
$i = 1;
do { echo $i, " "; $i++; } while ($i <= 5);

echo "\nfor:      ";
for ($i = 1; $i <= 5; $i++) { echo $i, " "; }

echo "\nforeach:  ";
foreach (range(1, 5) as $i) { echo $i, " "; }

echo "\n\nThe difference between while and do-while, when the condition starts false:\n";
$n = 10;
while ($n < 5)  { echo "  while body ran\n"; break; }
do { echo "  do-while body ran once anyway\n"; } while ($n < 5);

Output:

while:    1 2 3 4 5
do-while: 1 2 3 4 5
for:      1 2 3 4 5
foreach:  1 2 3 4 5

The difference between while and do-while, when the condition starts false:
  do-while body ran once anyway

Four ways to print 1 to 5. Notice how much of the for loop is bookkeeping, and how foreach has none at all — that is why it wins whenever there is an array.

docs.title: foreach, properly
docs.text:
Listing 1.22. foreach: values, keys, and by reference

<?php
$marks = ["Zoya" => 82, "Aman" => 67, "Riya" => 91];

echo "values only:\n";
foreach ($marks as $m) { echo "  $m\n"; }

echo "\nkey and value:\n";
foreach ($marks as $name => $m) { echo "  $name: $m\n"; }

echo "\nmodifying by reference (add 5 grace marks):\n";
foreach ($marks as &$m) { $m += 5; }
unset($m);                        // <- always, after a by-reference foreach
print_r($marks);

echo "\nnested, for a table:\n";
$class = [
    "Sem 5" => ["Zoya" => 82, "Aman" => 67],
    "Sem 3" => ["Riya" => 91],
];
foreach ($class as $sem => $students) {
    echo "  $sem\n";
    foreach ($students as $name => $m) {
        echo "    $name -> $m\n";
    }
}

Output:

values only:
  82
  67
  91

key and value:
  Zoya: 82
  Aman: 67
  Riya: 91

modifying by reference (add 5 grace marks):
Array
(
    [Zoya] => 87
    [Aman] => 72
    [Riya] => 96
)

nested, for a table:
  Sem 5
    Zoya -> 82
    Aman -> 67
  Sem 3
    Riya -> 91

The unset($m) after a by-reference loop is not superstition. Without it, $m is still a reference to the last element, and the next loop that reuses the name overwrites that element, which is a famous PHP bug. Deleting the unset makes the bug show in the output.

docs.title: break and continue
docs.text:
Listing 1.23. break, continue, and their level argument

<?php
echo "continue skips the rest of this turn:\n  ";
for ($i = 1; $i <= 10; $i++) {
    if ($i % 2 !== 0) continue;      // odd -> skip
    echo $i, " ";
}

echo "\n\nbreak leaves the loop entirely:\n  ";
foreach ([4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42] as $n) {
    if ($n > 15) break;
    echo $n, " ";
}

echo "\n\nbreak 2 leaves both loops:\n";
for ($i = 1; $i <= 3; $i++) {
    for ($j = 1; $j <= 3; $j++) {
        echo "  i=$i j=$j\n";
        if ($i * $j >= 4) break 2;
    }
}
echo "  out\n";

Output:

continue skips the rest of this turn:
  2 4 6 8 10

break leaves the loop entirely:
  4 8 15

break 2 leaves both loops:
  i=1 j=1
  i=1 j=2
  i=1 j=3
  i=2 j=1
  i=2 j=2
  out

break 2 leaves two loops at once. It is rare, it is legal, and it is examined.

docs.title: Loops that build HTML
docs.text:
This is what loops are for in a web program: turning a list of data into a list of tags. Everything in Units 3 and 4 is a variation on it.

Listing 1.24. A loop that builds a table and a dropdown

<?php
$courses = ["CS Hon", "BA Economics", "BCom Hons", "BA English"];
$chosen  = "BCom Hons";

$fees = [
    "CS Hon"       => 21000,
    "BA Economics" => 14500,
    "BCom Hons"    => 15800,
];
?>

<h3>Pick a course</h3>
<select name="course">
<?php foreach ($courses as $c): ?>
  <option value="<?= $c ?>" <?= $c === $chosen ? "selected" : "" ?>><?= $c ?></option>
<?php endforeach; ?>
</select>

<h3>Fee structure</h3>
<table>
  <tr><th>Course</th><th>Fee</th></tr>
<?php foreach ($fees as $course => $amount): ?>
  <tr>
    <td><?= $course ?></td>
    <td style="text-align:right">₹ <?= number_format($amount) ?></td>
  </tr>
<?php endforeach; ?>
  <tr>
    <th>Total</th>
    <th style="text-align:right">₹ <?= number_format(array_sum($fees)) ?></th>
  </tr>
</table>

Output sent to the browser:

<h3>Pick a course</h3>
<select name="course">
  <option value="CS Hon" >CS Hon</option>
  <option value="BA Economics" >BA Economics</option>
  <option value="BCom Hons" selected>BCom Hons</option>
  <option value="BA English" >BA English</option>
</select>

<h3>Fee structure</h3>
<table>
  <tr><th>Course</th><th>Fee</th></tr>
  <tr>
    <td>CS Hon</td>
    <td style="text-align:right">₹ 21,000</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>BA Economics</td>
    <td style="text-align:right">₹ 14,500</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>BCom Hons</td>
    <td style="text-align:right">₹ 15,800</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <th>Total</th>
    <th style="text-align:right">₹ 51,300</th>
  </tr>
</table>

These are two patterns you will reuse endlessly: a <tr> per row, and an <option> per choice with the current one marked selected.

docs.title: Nested loops: the pattern questions
docs.text:
Listing 1.25. The four patterns every practical asks for

<?php
$n = 5;

echo "1. Right triangle of stars\n";
for ($i = 1; $i <= $n; $i++) {
    echo str_repeat("*", $i), "\n";
}

echo "\n2. The number pyramid (a practical favourite)\n";
for ($i = 1; $i <= $n; $i++) {
    for ($j = 1; $j <= $i; $j++) {
        echo $i;
    }
    echo "\n";
}

echo "\n3. Centred pyramid\n";
for ($i = 1; $i <= $n; $i++) {
    echo str_repeat(" ", $n - $i), str_repeat("*", 2 * $i - 1), "\n";
}

echo "\n4. Multiplication table\n";
for ($i = 1; $i <= 10; $i++) {
    printf("%2d x %d = %3d\n", $i, 7, $i * 7);
}

Output:

1. Right triangle of stars
*
**
***
****
*****

2. The number pyramid (a practical favourite)
1
22
333
4444
55555

3. Centred pyramid
    *
   ***
  *****
 *******
