The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Without the second argument json_decode builds objects, so property syntax is right.
  • (b) That needs json_decode($json, true).
  • (c) That is JavaScript. In PHP the dot is concatenation.
  • (d) That is for class constants and static members.

Exercise 5.4. A PHP endpoint returns JSON but the browser shows it as plain text and $.getJSON fails. The most likely cause is:

  • (a) The script did not send header("Content-Type: application/json");
  • (b) json_encode is deprecated
  • (c) jQuery cannot read JSON
  • (d) The array had string keys
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Right — and remember it must come before any output.
  • (b) It is not.
  • (c) Reading JSON is exactly what $.getJSON is for.
  • (d) String keys are fine; they become a JSON object.

Exercise 5.5. Why is echo json_encode($row); safe from XSS while echo $row["name"]; in HTML is not?

  • (a) json_encode escapes the characters that matter for JSON — but it is only safe because the output is consumed as data, not inserted as HTML
  • (b) json_encode strips all HTML tags
  • (c) JSON cannot contain HTML
  • (d) It is not safe either, in every circumstance
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. The precise answer. If you then do $("#out").html(data.name) in the browser you have reopened the hole; use .text().
  • (b) It does not remove anything; a name containing <b> comes through intact.
  • (c) A JSON string can contain any characters at all.
  • (d) Closer to the truth than the other wrong answers — which is why the correct option says what the safety depends on.

docs.title: Write it — JSON endpoints in PHP
docs.text:
Exercise 5.6. Print the JSON for an object with the keys name (Riya Singh), marks (91) and subjects (an array of PHP and MySQL), in that order and with no spaces.

Expected: {"name":"Riya Singh","marks":91,"subjects":["PHP","MySQL"]}

Starting point:

<?php
// your code here
Answer

A solution:

<?php
$data = [
    "name"     => "Riya Singh",
    "marks"    => 91,
    "subjects" => ["PHP", "MySQL"],
];

echo json_encode($data);

String keys make it a JSON object; the inner list has keys 0 and 1, so it becomes a JSON array. json_encode preserves the insertion order of a PHP array, which is why the keys come out in the order you wrote them.

Note that 91 comes out as a number, not "91" — because it was an integer in PHP. Feed it a string and JavaScript will have to convert it before doing arithmetic.

Exercise 5.7. Query the database for every student with marks of 80 or more and print a JSON array of objects, each with name and marks, highest first. marks must be a JSON number.

Expected:[{"name":"Riya Singh","marks":91},{"name":"Meera Joshi","marks":88},{"name":"Zoya Khan","marks":82}]

Starting point:

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

// your code here
Answer

A solution:

<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

$sql = "SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks >= 80 ORDER BY marks DESC";
$result = mysqli_query($conn, $sql);

$rows = [];
while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)) {
    $row["marks"] = (int) $row["marks"];
    $rows[] = $row;
}

echo json_encode($rows);

$rows[] = $row; gives keys 0, 1, 2 — a gapless list — so json_encode produces a JSON array rather than an object. That is what the JavaScript $.each on the other end expects.

The cast to (int) matters more than it looks: without it a real mysqli returns every column as a string, and data.marks + 5 in JavaScript would give "825" instead of 87.

Exercise 5.8. Read the JSON in $json and print the name of every student who passed (marks 40 or more), one per line.

Expected:ZoyaRiya

Starting point:

<?php
$json = '{"students":[{"name":"Zoya","marks":82},{"name":"Kabir","marks":38},{"name":"Riya","marks":91}]}';

// your code here

Your script is tested with these cases:

Case Expected output decode and filter Zoya Riya Answer

A solution:

<?php
$json = '{"students":[{"name":"Zoya","marks":82},{"name":"Kabir","marks":38},{"name":"Riya","marks":91}]}';

$data = json_decode($json, true);

foreach ($data["students"] as $s) {
    if ($s["marks"] >= 40) {
        echo $s["name"], "\n";
    }
}

The true is what makes $s["name"] work. Without it you would write $s->name and $data->students.

Decoding to arrays keeps the rest of the code looking like every other PHP array you have written. Decoding to objects is equally valid — just do not mix the two in one script.

docs.title: Predict the output — JSON in PHP
docs.text:
Exercise 5.9. What does this script print?

<?php
$a = ["x", "y", "z"];
echo json_encode($a), "\n";
unset($a[1]);
echo json_encode($a), "\n";
echo json_encode(array_values($a)), "\n";

Hint: What are the keys after the unset?

Answer

The script prints:

["x","y","z"]
{"0":"x","2":"z"}
["x","z"]

After removing key 1 the keys are 0 and 2 — not a gapless list — so json_encode switches to an object to preserve them. array_values() renumbers and restores the array form. This bites whenever you filter rows before encoding them.

Exercise 5.10. What does this script print?

<?php
$json = '{"name":"Zoya","marks":"82"}';
$d = json_decode($json, true);
var_dump($d["marks"]);
var_dump($d["marks"] + 5);
var_dump($d["marks"] === 82);

Hint: Look carefully at the quotes around 82 in the JSON.

Answer

The script prints:

string(2) "82"
int(87)
bool(false)

The JSON said "82" with quotes, so it decodes to a string. PHP will still add 5 to it, but the identity test fails — and in JavaScript the same value would have made marks + 5 produce "825". Cast on the server, before encoding.

Exercise 5.11. What does this script print?

<?php
var_dump(json_decode("{'a': 1}", true));
var_dump(json_decode('{"a": 1,}', true));
var_dump(json_decode('{"a": 1}', true));

Hint: Two of these three are not valid JSON.

Answer

The script prints:

NULL
NULL
array(1) {
  ["a"]=>
  int(1)
}

Single quotes and a trailing comma are both fine in JavaScript and both invalid in JSON. json_decode returns null rather than throwing, so a script that does not check gets a mystifying error one line later.

Exercise 5.12. What does this script print?

<?php
$rows = [
  ["name" => "Zoya", "marks" => 82],
  ["name" => "Riya", "marks" => 91],
];
echo json_encode($rows, JSON_PRETTY_PRINT);

Hint: The outer array is a list; each inner one has string keys.

Answer

The script prints:

[
    {
        "name": "Zoya",
        "marks": 82
    },
    {
        "name": "Riya",
        "marks": 91
    }
]

This is the exact shape every AJAX table endpoint returns: a JSON array of JSON objects, which JavaScript receives as an array of objects and walks with $.each.

docs.title: Quick check — jQuery
docs.text:
Exercise 5.13. A button added by .append() after page load does not respond to $(".del").on("click", fn). Why?

  • (a) The handler was attached only to the buttons that existed when that line ran
  • (b) jQuery cannot handle dynamically created elements
  • (c) .append() strips event handlers
  • (d) The click event does not bubble
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Correct. Use delegation: $("#list").on("click", ".del", fn) attaches one handler to a container that does exist.
  • (b) It can — through delegation.
  • (c) It does not; there simply were none on the new element.
  • (d) Click does bubble, which is precisely what makes delegation work.

Exercise 5.14. Which sets the value of a text input?

  • (a) $("#name").val("Zoya")
  • (b) $("#name").text("Zoya")
  • (c) $("#name").html("Zoya")
  • (d) $("#name").attr("value", "Zoya")
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Correct — .val() is the accessor for form fields.
  • (b) .text() sets the text between the tags. An input has none, so nothing visible happens.
  • (c) Same problem; an input has no inner HTML.
  • (d) This changes the attribute, which sets the default. After the user has typed, the live value no longer follows it.

Exercise 5.15. What does $(document).ready() wait for?

  • (a) The HTML to be parsed, so every element exists — but not for images to finish loading
  • (b) Every image and stylesheet to finish loading
  • (c) All AJAX requests to complete
  • (d) The user to click something
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Correct, and that is why it fires sooner than window.onload.
  • (b) That is window.onload.
  • (c) That is $(document).ajaxStop().
  • (d) It is not an interaction event.

Exercise 5.16. $.getJSON("data.php", cb) — the network tab shows 200 but cb never runs. The most likely reason is:

  • (a) The response was not valid JSON — often a PHP warning printed before it
  • (b) The URL was wrong
  • (c) jQuery was not loaded
  • (d) The callback must be named
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Right. $.getJSON silently skips success on a parse error; add .fail() and you will see "parsererror".
  • (b) That would give a 404, not a 200.
  • (c) Then $ itself would be undefined and no request would have been made.
  • (d) An anonymous function is fine.

Exercise 5.17. Which line stops a form from reloading the page when it is submitted?

  • (a) e.preventDefault(); inside the submit handler
  • (b) return true;
  • (c) $("form").hide();
  • (d) Removing the action attribute
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Correct — it cancels the browser's default action for that event.
  • (b) Returning true allows the default; returning false would cancel it, but preventDefault is the explicit form.
  • (c) Hiding it does not stop a submission that has already begun.
  • (d) With no action the form posts to the same page, which is still a reload.

Exercise 5.18. You are inserting a student's name from an AJAX response into the page. Which is right?

  • (a) $("<div>").text(s.name).appendTo("#out")
  • (b) $("#out").html("<div>" + s.name + "</div>")
  • (c) $("#out").append(s.name)
  • (d) document.write(s.name)
Answer

The answer is (a).

  • (a) Correct. Correct. .text() escapes, so a name containing markup is shown rather than run.
  • (b) String concatenation into .html() renders any tags in the name — an XSS hole fed by your own database.
  • (c) append() parses a string that looks like HTML, so this has the same problem.
  • (d) document.write after load replaces the whole document, and does not escape anything.

docs.title: Put it in order — a JSON endpoint
docs.text:
Exercise 5.19. These lines make a working JSON endpoint. Put them in the only order that works.

    $rows[] = $row;
header("Content-Type: application/json");
}
$rows = [];
$result = mysqli_query($conn, "SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC");
echo json_encode($rows);
while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)) {
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");
<?php
Answer

The lines in working order:

<?php
header("Content-Type: application/json");
$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");
$result = mysqli_query($conn, "SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC");
$rows = [];
while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)) {
    $rows[] = $row;
}
echo json_encode($rows);

It prints:

[{"name":"Riya Singh","marks":91},{"name":"Meera Joshi","marks":88},{"name":"Zoya Khan","marks":82},{"name":"Sara Ali","marks":74},{"name":"Aman Verma","marks":67},{"name":"Dev Kapoor","marks":55},{"name":"Kabir Nath","marks":38}]

header() must come before any output. $rows = [] must exist before the loop appends to it. And the echo must come after the loop has finished collecting.

docs.title: Practice problems
docs.text:
Exercise 5.20. Write the four jQuery tasks of a typical practical list: change a paragraph's text colour and contents on a button click; select elements by id, class, tag and attribute; and run code on a click event.

Answer 
<p id="para" class="note">Original text</p>
<input type="text" name="city">
<button id="btn">Change</button>

<script>
$(function () {

    // 1. change colour and contents on a click
    $("#btn").click(function () {
        $("#para").css("color", "red").text("Changed by jQuery");
    });

    // 2. select by id, class, tag and attribute
    $("#para").css("font-weight", "bold");              // id
    $(".note").css("background", "#fcf1de");            // class
    $("p").css("padding", "6px");                       // element (tag)
    $("input[name='city']").val("Delhi");               // attribute

    // 3. run code on a click event
    $("#btn").on("click", function () {
        alert("The button was clicked");
    });
});
</script>

Everything is wrapped in $(function () { … }) so that it runs only when the page has been built and the elements exist.

Exercise 5.21. Build a table where clicking a column heading sorts the rows, using only jQuery, with no request to the server.

Answer 
$(function () {
    $("#t th").on("click", function () {
        var col = $(this).index();                 // which column was clicked
        var asc = !$(this).data("asc");            // flip the direction each time
        $(this).data("asc", asc);

        var rows = $("#t tr:gt(0)").get();         // every row except the header
        rows.sort(function (a, b) {
            var x = $(a).children().eq(col).text();
            var y = $(b).children().eq(col).text();
            var nx = parseFloat(x), ny = parseFloat(y);
            var r = (!isNaN(nx) && !isNaN(ny)) ? nx - ny : x.localeCompare(y);
            return asc ? r : -r;
        });
        $("#t").append(rows);                      // appending moves the existing rows
    });
});

The rows are collected into an ordinary array, sorted with a comparison function that compares numbers as numbers and everything else as text, and then appended back in the new order. Appending an element that is already in the page moves it rather than copying it.

Exercise 5.22. Write a "check if this roll number is already taken" box: on blur, ask a PHP endpoint and show a message beside the field.

Answer

The browser side:

$(function () {
    $("#roll").on("blur", function () {
        var roll = $.trim($(this).val());
        if (roll === "") return;

        $.getJSON("roll_taken.php", { roll: roll }, function (res) {
            $("#roll-status").text(res.taken ? "Already taken" : "Available");
        });
    });
});

The server side:

<?php
header("Content-Type: application/json");

$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");
$roll = (int) ($_GET["roll"] ?? 0);

$stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn, "SELECT 1 FROM students WHERE roll = ?");
mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "i", $roll);
mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt);
$taken = mysqli_num_rows(mysqli_stmt_get_result($stmt)) > 0;

echo json_encode(["taken" => $taken]);

For roll 2231045 the reply is {"taken":true}; for an unused number it is {"taken":false}. The check is a convenience only. The insert that finally saves the student must still refuse a duplicate, because two people can pass the check at the same moment.

Exercise 5.23. Take the search example of Listing 5.10 and rewrite the results loop so that it uses .text() throughout. Then register a student called <b>test</b> and confirm the difference.

Answer 
$("#results").empty();
$.each(data, function (i, s) {
    var line = $("<div>");
    line.append($("<b>").text(s.name));
    line.append(document.createTextNode(
        " \u2014 " + s.course + ", " + s.marks + " marks, " + s.city));
    $("#results").append(line);
});

Every piece of data goes in through .text() or a text node, so the browser never parses it as markup. In the original, a student whose name is <b>test</b> appears as the word test in bold, because the string is concatenated into HTML and read as tags. With the rewrite the line shows the literal characters <b>test</b>. A name containing <img src=x onerror=…> would run script in the original and does nothing in the rewrite.

Exercise 5.24. Write a PHP endpoint that returns the class average as JSON, and a page that shows it and refreshes every ten seconds with setInterval.

Answer

The endpoint:

<?php
header("Content-Type: application/json");

$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");
$row  = mysqli_fetch_assoc(mysqli_query($conn,
    "SELECT AVG(marks) AS average, COUNT(*) AS n FROM students"));

echo json_encode([
    "average" => round((float) $row["average"], 2),
    "count"   => (int) $row["n"],
]);

On the seven students of Unit 4 it replies {"average":70.71,"count":7}. The page:

<p>Class average: <b id="avg">…</b></p>

<script>
function refresh() {
    $.getJSON("average.php", function (d) {
        $("#avg").text(d.average + " (" + d.count + " students)");
    });
}
refresh();                       // once at once
setInterval(refresh, 10000);     // then every ten seconds
</script>

Exercise 5.25. Explain, in three sentences, why $.getJSON needs no JSON.parse while $.get may.

Answer

$.getJSON(url, data, callback) is shorthand for $.ajax with dataType: "json", so jQuery parses the response body itself and passes your function a ready-made JavaScript object. $.get hands over the response as it arrives: with no dataType, jQuery guesses from the Content-Type header, so a reply that is not declared as JSON reaches the callback as a string that needs JSON.parse. The practical rule is to send Content-Type: application/json from the endpoint and to use $.getJSON, so that the intention is explicit and does not depend on a guess.

Exercise 5.26. Convert the live search from $.getJSON to fetch() with async/await, and say which you find clearer.

Answer 
async function search(term) {
    const response = await fetch("search.php?q=" + encodeURIComponent(term));
    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error("The server answered " + response.status);
    }
    const data = await response.json();

    const html = data.map(s =>
        "<div><b>" + s.name + "</b> \u2014 " + s.course + ", " + s.marks + " marks, " + s.city + "</div>"
    ).join("");
    $("#results").html(html);
}

Most people find the async/await form clearer, because the steps read from top to bottom like synchronous code and there is no nesting of callbacks. It asks for more care in two places, however: fetch does not treat a 404 or 500 reply as a failure, so response.ok must be tested by hand, and the query string must be encoded by hand with encodeURIComponent, where $.getJSON does both for you. (The string-building in this version has the same weakness that the previous exercise removed.)

Exercise 5.27. A page loads 500 rows and filters them in the browser as the user types. A second page asks the server on each keystroke. When is each the better design?

Answer

Filtering in the browser is better when the whole set is small enough to send once (500 rows is) and is not secret. Each keystroke is answered instantly, with no network delay and no load on the server, and it keeps working if the connection drops. Its costs are the initial transfer and memory, and the fact that every row, including any the user was not supposed to see, has been sent to the browser.

Asking the server on each keystroke is better when the set is large (thousands of rows or more), when it changes while the user is typing, or when access rules mean that the user may see only some of it, because the server decides what to send. It costs a request per keystroke, which is why the typing should be debounced, and it feels slower on a poor connection.

docs.title: Examination questions
docs.text: These are questions in the shapes this course uses, grouped by the marks they carry. A two-mark question wants a definition and one concrete example, a five-mark question wants structure, and a ten-mark question wants an answer with parts.

docs.title: Two-mark questions
docs.text:
Exercise 5.28. (2 marks) What is jQuery? Write the syntax to include it.

Answer

A JavaScript library that shortens DOM selection, event handling, animation and AJAX, with a single entry point — the $ function.

<!-- from a CDN -->
<script src="https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.7.1.min.js"></script>

<!-- or a local copy, which is what a practical file should use -->
<script src="js/jquery-3.7.1.min.js"></script>

It must be loaded before any script that uses $, or the console reports "$ is not defined".

Exercise 5.29. (2 marks) What is $(document).ready() and why is it needed?

Answer

It defers your code until the HTML has been parsed, so every element exists before a selector looks for it. A script in <head> runs before the body exists, so $("#result") would match nothing and — because jQuery fails silently on an empty selection — nothing would happen and no error would appear.

$(document).ready(function () { … });
$(function () { … });          // the shorthand, identical

Unlike window.onload, it does not wait for images to finish loading.

Exercise 5.30. (2 marks) What is JSON? Give an example.

Answer

JavaScript Object Notation — a lightweight, language-independent text format for structured data, and what a server sends when it is answering a program rather than a person.

{"roll": 2231045, "name": "Zoya", "subjects": ["PHP", "MySQL"], "active": true}

Rules that catch people out: keys and strings must use double quotes, and there may be no comments and no trailing comma — all three are legal in JavaScript and invalid in JSON.

Exercise 5.31. (2 marks) Differentiate json_encode() and json_decode().

Answer
  • json_encode($value) — PHP value → JSON string. A PHP array with gapless integer keys becomes a JSON array; anything else becomes a JSON object.
  • json_decode($string) — JSON string → PHP. By default it produces objects (read with ->); pass true as the second argument for associative arrays (read with []).
echo json_encode(["name" => "Zoya"]);   // {"name":"Zoya"}
$d = json_decode('{"name":"Zoya"}', true);
echo $d["name"];                        // Zoya

Exercise 5.32. (2 marks) What is AJAX? What does the acronym stand for?

Answer

Asynchronous JavaScript And XML — a technique, not a library, in which JavaScript requests data from the server in the background and updates part of the page without reloading it. The XML in the name is historical; JSON is what is actually used.

The underlying object is XMLHttpRequest; jQuery wraps it as $.get, $.post, $.getJSON and $.ajax, and modern JavaScript offers fetch().

Exercise 5.33. (2 marks) Difference between .text() and .html() in jQuery.

Answer

.text() sets or reads the element's text, escaping any markup so tags are shown as characters. .html() sets or reads the inner HTML, so tags take effect.

$("#p").text("<b>hi</b>");   // shows:  <b>hi</b>
$("#p").html("<b>hi</b>");   // shows:  hi   in bold

Use .text() for anything that came from a user or a database; .html() only for markup you built yourself, or you have an XSS hole.

docs.title: Five- and ten-mark questions
docs.text:
Exercise 5.34. (5 marks) Explain jQuery selectors with examples.

Answer

A selector is passed to $() and returns a jQuery object holding every matching element — zero, one or many — which is why jQuery code needs so few loops. A selector matching nothing is not an error; it returns an empty collection and every method on it silently succeeds.

Selector Matches $("p") every <p> — by element name $("#total") the element with id="total" $(".error") every element with class="error" $("[data-role='box']") by attribute $("ul li") / $("ul > li") descendant / direct child $("tr:even"), $("li:first"), $("input:checked") by position or state $(this) inside a handler, the element the event happened on 
$(".info").css("color", "red");        // all of them at once
console.log($(".info").length);        // how many matched

Exercise 5.35. (5 marks) What is event delegation in jQuery, and why is it needed?

Answer

$(".del").on("click", fn) attaches a handler to the elements that exist at that moment. An element created later — by .append() or from an AJAX response — never had one attached, so it does not respond.

Delegation attaches one handler to a container that does exist, and the container checks on each click whether what was clicked matches the selector:

// direct — only works for rows present when this line ran
$(".del").on("click", function () { $(this).closest("li").remove(); });

// delegated — works for rows added at any time
$("#list").on("click", ".del", function () { $(this).closest("li").remove(); });

It works because a click bubbles up from the element to its ancestors. Any list built from AJAX data needs this, and it is also more efficient: one handler instead of one per row.

Exercise 5.36. (10 marks) Explain AJAX. Write a program in which a jQuery page fetches data from a PHP script as JSON and displays it without reloading.

Answer

What AJAX is. Asynchronous JavaScript And XML: JavaScript makes an HTTP request in the background, the server replies with a small piece of data (almost always JSON), and a callback updates part of the page. The user sees no reload. "Asynchronous" means the script does not wait — which is why everything that depends on the answer must go inside the callback.

The server side — students.php, which answers a program, so it sends JSON rather than HTML:

<?php
header("Content-Type: application/json");

$conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college");

$course = $_GET["course"] ?? "";
$stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn,
    "SELECT roll, name, marks FROM students WHERE course = ? ORDER BY marks DESC");
mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "s", $course);
mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt);
$result = mysqli_stmt_get_result($stmt);

$rows = [];
while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)) {
    $row["marks"] = (int) $row["marks"];      // so JavaScript gets a number
    $rows[] = $row;
}

echo json_encode(["ok" => true, "count" => count($rows), "students" => $rows]);

The client side:

<select id="course"><option>BSCCS</option><option>BAECO</option></select>
<button id="load">Load</button>
<table id="out"></table>

<script>
$(function () {
    $("#load").on("click", function () {

        $.getJSON("students.php", { course: $("#course").val() })
            .done(function (data) {
                var rows = "<tr><th>Roll</th><th>Name</th><th>Marks</th></tr>";
                $.each(data.students, function (i, s) {
                    rows += "<tr><td>" + s.roll + "</td><td>" +
                            s.name + "</td><td>" + s.marks + "</td></tr>";
                });
                $("#out").html(rows);
            })
            .fail(function (xhr) {
                alert("Request failed: " + xhr.status);
            });
    });
});
</script>

Points that carry marks: the endpoint sends Content-Type: application/json before any output; $.getJSON parses the reply for you, so no JSON.parse is needed; the failure case is handled; and the values are cast to integers on the server so JavaScript receives numbers rather than strings.

Unit 5 runs this example for real.

docs.title: Who this book is for
docs.text:
This book is a complete treatment of an advanced university course in web programming. It is written for a student who knows HTML and CSS, which is the prerequisite of the course, and who wants to learn to build interactive, data-driven websites: pages that react to what a visitor types, remember things, and talk to a database.

The course is worth four credits, three of lecture and one of practical, and its eligibility condition is a pass in Class XII. This book covers the lecture part, forty-five hours of it; it does not contain a laboratory manual. Its worked examples and exercises nevertheless include the programs that a practical examination typically asks for, such as a form that adds two numbers, a registration form, a login with a session, and the four operations on a database table.

By the end of the course, in the words of the course outline, a student should be able to:

  • develop interactive and dynamic websites;
  • write programs to communicate with the server using the GET and POST methods;
  • learn to connect to and manipulate databases using MySQL;
  • validate server-side (back-end) data.

docs.title: How the book follows the course
docs.text:
The five units of the book follow the five units of the course in order, and each unit assumes the one before it. The hours are those of the course scheme.

Course unit Hours Course text Covered in 1 7 Introduction to PHP: basic syntax, defining variables and constants, data types including arrays, operators and expressions, decision making statements, constructs for iterations Unit 1, Introduction to PHP 2 5 String Handling: creating a string and accessing its content, searching and replacing content of a string, and other built-in functions Unit 2, String Handling 3 12 Handling HTML Form with PHP: creating a form, submitting data to the server at the backend using GET and POST methods, GET vs POST methods, PHP global functions Unit 3, Handling HTML Forms with PHP 4 15 Database: connectivity with MySQL: connectivity with database, database creation, creating tables, create, retrieve, update, and delete (CRUD) operations Unit 4, Database: MySQL Connectivity 5 6 jQuery and JSON: introduction to jQuery syntax (selectors, events, AJAX, JSON) Unit 5, jQuery and JSON

Functions and the splitting of a program across files are not named in the course outline, but every later unit uses them, so Unit 1 teaches them. Regular expressions and the escaping of output, likewise, are treated in Unit 2 because the form validation of Unit 3 needs them.

docs.title: How to use this book
docs.text:
Install the real thing first. Section 1.2 walks through installing XAMPP, which bundles the Apache web server, the MySQL database and PHP. Your practical file and your examination expect these on your own machine, and a page of PHP cannot be tried by opening the file in a browser: it has to be requested from the server through an address that begins http://localhost/.

Type the listings. Each unit contains numbered listings (Listing 1.1, 1.2, and so on) that are complete programs. Each is followed by the output it produces, so you can check your own result against it. Where a program takes input from a form or from the address, the book shows the request and the reply. Change a value, predict the new output, and then run it; this is the quickest way to learn a language in which so many surprises hide in small rules. Details that depend on the version of PHP (the wording of a warning, for example) can differ a little on your installation.

Read the boxes. Notes give definitions and asides, tips name the idea to take away, and warnings mark the mistakes that cost students marks and, in real applications, cost users their data.

Work the exercises. Every unit ends with a Summary and an Exercises section. The exercises include short questions with reasons given for every option, programs to predict, blanks to fill, lines to put in order and programs to write, followed by practice problems and by questions in the shape of the examination paper. Each exercise has its answer folded below it. Attempt it on paper first: reading a model answer and nodding at it produces a feeling of understanding that does not survive the examination hall, whereas writing an answer and then comparing it does.

The back of the book has two further parts: a Reference (error messages and what they mean, syntax and function summaries, a security checklist), and a Glossary and Further Reading.

docs.title: Answering examination questions
docs.text:
The questions in the exercises are grouped by unit and by size, because the size tells you what the examiner wants.

  • A two-mark question wants a definition and, ideally, one concrete example, not a paragraph.
  • A five-mark question wants structure: a table for a "difference between", or three or four labelled points.
  • A ten-mark question wants an answer with parts: explain, then illustrate with code, then say when it fails.

Four habits earn marks in all of them.

Always name the function

"We can validate the email" earns less than "we call filter_var($e, FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL), which returns the address or false".

Always give an example

Two lines of code in a two-mark answer is usually the difference between full marks and half.

Use a table for comparisons

A "difference between" answer in a table with three or four rows is faster to write and faster to mark.

Say what breaks

Naming the failure ("without enctype, $_FILES is empty") shows understanding rather than memory.

The split of marks between internal assessment, the end-semester theory paper and the practical examination is set by the institution and changes from year to year, so check the current scheme with your teacher. What does not change is the shape of the questions.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: This part collects what you need to look up while you work: the error messages PHP and MySQL give and what causes them, one-screen summaries of PHP, SQL and jQuery, the built-in functions grouped by the job they do, a security checklist, and a quick reference for XAMPP. Near the end are two lists for revision: the pairs of things that examinations ask you to distinguish, and the programs that a student should be able to write from memory.

docs.title: Error messages, decoded
docs.text:
Start here. Nearly every hour lost on this course is lost to one of these eight, and each has one usual cause.

Message Means Usually Parse error: syntax error, unexpected … PHP could not read the file at all; nothing ran A missing ; or } — and it is usually on the line before the one named, because that is where PHP first noticed Warning: Undefined variable $x Read before it was written A typo in the name, or a form field that was not submitted. Use ?? "" Warning: Undefined array key "x" That key is not in the array An unticked checkbox, a misspelt name attribute, or the page opened directly with no form behind it Warning: Cannot modify header information — headers already sent by (output started at file:line) Something was output before header(), session_start() or setcookie() A blank line before <?php, or a newline after ?> in an included file. The message names the real culprit — read the file and line in the brackets Fatal error: Uncaught Error: Call to undefined function foo() No such function A misspelling, or an extension that is not enabled Fatal error: Uncaught Error: Call to a member function query() on bool You called a method on false The connection or the query failed and its return value was never checked mysqli_fetch_assoc(): Argument #1 must be of type mysqli_result, bool given The same thing, procedurally mysqli_query() returned false. Print mysqli_error($conn) Uncaught ReferenceError: $ is not defined jQuery is not there yet Your script tag comes before jQuery's, or jQuery failed to load — check the Network tab

The four-step debugging routine

1. Read the message, all of it, including the file and line in brackets. 2. echo or var_dump() the value just above the failing line — never guess what a variable holds. 3. For a query, print the SQL and paste it into phpMyAdmin. 4. For anything in the browser, open the console (F12) before saying "nothing happens".

put this at the top while developing

<?php
// Show every error while you are building. Never on a live site.
error_reporting(E_ALL);
ini_set('display_errors', 1);

XAMPP shows errors by default. A blank white page usually means they have been turned off — turn them back on before doing anything else.

docs.title: PHP syntax, on one screen
docs.text:
everything.php

<?php                                   // open. Close with ?> only if HTML follows

// ---- variables and constants ----
$name   = "Zoya";                       // no type declared
$marks  = 82;                           // case-sensitive names
define("PASS", 40);                     // constant: no $, global
const  COLLEGE = "Example";           // top-level only

// ---- strings ----
echo 'single: $name';                   // literal
echo "double: $name and {$arr['k']}";   // interpolated
echo 'joined ' . "with a dot";          // . not +
$s .= "appended";

// ---- arrays ----
$list  = [1, 2, 3];                     // keys 0,1,2
$assoc = ["name" => "Zoya", "marks" => 82];
$table = [["a" => 1], ["a" => 2]];      // rows
$list[] = 4;                            // append

// ---- conditions ----
if ($m >= 90)      { }
elseif ($m >= 40)  { }
else               { }

switch ($g) { case "A": break; default: }
$r = $m >= 40 ? "Pass" : "Fail";        // ternary
$v = $input ?? "default";               // null coalescing

// ---- loops ----
while ($i < 5)          { $i++; }
do { $i++; } while ($i < 5);
for ($i = 0; $i < 5; $i++) { }
foreach ($assoc as $k => $v) { }
foreach ($list as &$v) { $v *= 2; } unset($v);   // by reference

// ---- functions ----
function grade($m, $pass = 40) { return $m >= $pass ? "P" : "F"; }
function addOne(&$x) { $x++; }          // by reference
function total(...$n) { return array_sum($n); }
$double = function ($x) { return $x * 2; };
$triple = fn($x) => $x * 3;

// ---- the alternative syntax, for templates ----
?>
<?php if ($m >= 40): ?>
  <p>Passed with <?= $m ?></p>
<?php else: ?>
  <p>Failed</p>
<?php endif; ?>

<?php foreach ($rows as $row): ?>
  <tr><td><?= htmlspecialchars($row["name"]) ?></td></tr>
<?php endforeach; ?>

docs.title: SQL, on one screen
docs.text:
everything.sql

-- ---------- databases and tables ----------
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS college;
USE college;
SHOW TABLES;
DESCRIBE students;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS students;

CREATE TABLE students (
    roll   INT          PRIMARY KEY,        -- or: INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY
    name   VARCHAR(50)  NOT NULL,
    course VARCHAR(10),
    marks  INT          DEFAULT 0,
    email  VARCHAR(60)  UNIQUE,
    joined DATE,
    fee    DECIMAL(8,2),                    -- money: never FLOAT
    FOREIGN KEY (course) REFERENCES courses(code)
);

ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN city VARCHAR(30);
ALTER TABLE students DROP COLUMN city;

-- ---------- create ----------
INSERT INTO students (roll, name, marks) VALUES (2231045, 'Zoya', 82);
INSERT INTO students (roll, name, marks) VALUES (1,'A',50), (2,'B',60);   -- many rows

-- ---------- retrieve ----------
SELECT * FROM students;
SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks >= 40;
SELECT DISTINCT city FROM students;

--   the clause order is fixed:
SELECT   c.title, COUNT(s.roll) AS n, ROUND(AVG(s.marks)) AS avg_marks
FROM     courses c
LEFT JOIN students s ON s.course = c.code
WHERE    c.fee < 25000
GROUP BY c.title
HAVING   COUNT(s.roll) > 0
ORDER BY avg_marks DESC
LIMIT    5 OFFSET 0;

--   WHERE operators
WHERE marks BETWEEN 40 AND 59
WHERE course IN ('BSCCS', 'BCOM')
WHERE name LIKE 'A%'          -- % any run, _ exactly one
WHERE email IS NULL           -- never  = NULL

-- ---------- update and delete ----------
UPDATE students SET marks = marks + 5 WHERE course = 'BAECO';
DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 40;
TRUNCATE TABLE students;      -- empties it, keeps the structure

Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after.

docs.title: The security checklist
docs.text:
Six lines. Every one of them is a question an examiner may ask, and every one is a real hole in a real student project.

Where the value goes What protects it What happens without it Into an HTML page htmlspecialchars($v) Cross-site scripting: the visitor's browser runs someone else's markup Into an HTML attribute htmlspecialchars($v, ENT_QUOTES) and quote the attribute The same, escaping out of value="…" Into an SQL query a prepared statement SQL injection: the data becomes part of the program Into a table or column name a whitelist — placeholders cannot bind names The same, by another route Into a URL urlencode($v) A broken link, or a parameter smuggled into the next one Into JavaScript json_encode($v), and .text() not .html() at the other end XSS again, delivered through your own API

And two rules that are not about escaping

Never trust anything the browser sends — required, maxlength, a dropdown's options and a hidden field are all editable. And never store a password you can read: password_hash() on the way in, password_verify() on the way out.

Change Apache to 8080 in httpd.conf, then use http://localhost:8080/ Back up a database phpMyAdmin → the database → Export → Go. Keep the .sql file with your practical file

docs.title: The ten most-asked questions
docs.text:
If time is short, these ten are the ones to be certain of. Every one has appeared in some form in almost every paper on this course.

  2. What is SQL injection, and how does a prepared statement prevent it? (Unit 4)
